div.p: VottrV._

DEATH AND LILIES. A plot of lilies swaying to and fro, A plot of garden lilies all a-blow, With dewy faces drinking in the light Behold my stainless lilies how they grow— Had ever earthly field so fair a show? Like summer seas of scented foam and white. What's this? A shadow on their virgin snow— Whence comest thou. dread harbinger of woe,
With chilly breath my winsome blooms to blight? Alas! my shining lilies are laid low. Well! flowers must fade, andhuman tears must flow, The brightest sun must set—then comes the night. E. S.

div.head: Varitties.
div.p: Varitties.

_ A young lady resembles ammunition because the powder is needed before the ball. A lady asked a clergyman, who was suffering with the influenza, what he took for his cod? Five handker- chiefs a day, ma'am," was the reply. "How much to take me to the cathedral?" asked a tourist of a hackman. Pat replied, " The meanest man I ever took gave me three shillings." . . . . .

A country squire asked a juggler why he played the fool. "For the same reason you do; out of want. You do it for want of wit; I for want of money." Lady: "These strawberries look very large and ripe." Little boy (who is selling strawberries for the first time) : • Yes, mum, the little ones are all underneath." "Why did you leave your last place, Sarah?" "Why, you see, mum, I was too good looking, and when I opened the front door folks took me for the missus." Cardinal Richelieu detected an adventurer, who was passing himself off for a nobleman, by his helping him- self to plives with a fork, the custom being to use one's fingers. A lady remonstrated with her butcher for his cruel treatment in putting little lambs to death. "Why. madam," said he, "you would not eat them alive, would you?" A traveller who had very large feet, asked a waiter to bring him a boot-jack. "What for ?" "To take off my boots." "Why. be jabers, sir, you'll have to go to the forks of the road to get them off." Lord Russell said, "Mr. flume, What do you consider theiobject of legislation ?" "The greatest good to the greatest number." "What do you consider the greatest number ?" "Number one" was" flume's reply. To love the public, to study universal good, and to promote the interest of the whole world, as far as lies within our power, is the height of goodness, and makes that temper which we call divine.—Shaftesburu. A poet was once walking with M. Talleyrand in the street, reciting some of his verses. Talleyrand, perceiv- ing at a short distance a man yawning, pointed him out to the poet, saying, "Not so loud, he hears you." "I have a wife and six children in New York, and have never seen one of them," said a gentleman. "Why, sir, how can that be?" said a travelling companion. " One of them was born, sir, after I left the city." • An orator, on commencing his speech, said he should -divide the subject into 13 heads. The audience be- ginning to murmur, the speaker continued, "But to prevent my being too prolix. I shall omit a dozen of them." At a dinner the host asked Quin to take a piece of pudding. A gentleman had just before helped himself to an immense piece. "Pray," said Quin, looking first at the gentleman's plate, and then at the dish, "which is the pudding." A witty clergyman, having buried five wives, was asked by a lady how lie managed to have such good luck. "Why, madam," said he, "I knew they could not live without contradiction, therefore I let them have their own way."

The first water mill ever built was erected on the river Tiber at Rome A.D. 50. Windmills were in original use in the twelfth century. Tidemills were operated in Venice about 1708. Sawmills are said to have been in use at Augsburg. Germany, about 1332. "Did you hear of the railroad accident to-day ?ivies al question asked of his father by Sammy Snaggs. "No. Sammy; where was it ?" "At our school. The teacher thrashed Jimmy Davis like anythins.." " What has that to do with railway accidents?" "Well, it was a miss- -placed switch, wasn't it?" Mrs. Cottonhack : This book for boys says the way 40 succeed in this world is to do two dollars' worth of -work for one dollar." Mr. Cottonback (great manufac- turer) : "That writer is way off. The way to succeed is to hire men to do two dollars' worth of work for one dollar, and then form a trust and sell it for five dollars." An Irish glazier was putting a pane of glass into a window, when a groom, who was standing by, began joking him, telling him to mind and put in plenty of putty. The Irishman bare the banter for some time, but at last silenced his tormentor by, " Arrah now, be off wid ye, or else I'll put a pain in your head widout any putty." When the great picture of the Court of Death was •exhibited in Boston, a ticket was sent to the Rev. Dr. Osgood, to admit the bearer to the Court of Death. The old gentleman was literally confounded, not having beard of the painting. "I expected to go before long, but I was not prepared for so abrupt a sum- - moos," said he. Ellenborough disliked travelling encumbrances. His wife once accompanied him on a circuit, and, while sitting in the carriage, Ellenborough's feet suddenly came in contact with a bandbox. Up went the window and out went the box. When they reached their desti- nation, Ellenborough could not find his wig. "Where is my wig ? " said he. "My lord," said a servant, "it vas in the bandbox." A servant girl came to her mistress one day and said, "I'm sorry. ma'am, but I'll have to leave you next month. Me and my young man are going to git married then." "Very well, Mary," replied the lady. "I hope, however, that you have given the matter careful con- sideration, and counted the cost in case one makes a mistake in marrying." "La, ma'am, it ain't going to -cost me anything!" was the immediate reply "He has to pay for it his own self, you know."

- AN OPEN QUESTION. "What shall We open now for tea?" Asked mother, as she stood Before the row of jars which held Preserves and jellies good. Beside her, with an eager face, Was cunning little Bess. Who answered, while she eyed the sweets, "Open our mouths, I guess." A CATERPILLAR WITH TUCKS.—On several occasions Jennie had watched her mother as she lengthened her dress by letting out the tucks. One morning she came into the house with a caterpillar rolled up into a ball. "Oh, put down that ugly worm !" cried her mother, in disgust. Jennie dropped the caterpiltar, whereupon it elongated, and began to crawl away. "Oh, mamma!" exclaimed Jennie, in childish surprise; "look at it letting out its tucks !" SOME Cuntous Igs3iss.—Everyone knows the story of the spendthrift who, happening to bear the unluckily suggestive name of "Owen More," was complimented by a bitter wag with the very appropriate epitaph—. Owen More has gone away, Owin' more than he could pay.

But such coincidences are by no means so rare as one might think. One of the newly-made nobles of Louis XV. was the Marquis of Avantiere (" Avant-hier," the day.before yesterday). The antagonistic names of Pitt and Fox, a century ago, gave rise to not a few jests as to whether "the fox would find the pit too deep for him." During Lord North's term of office, his chief friend was a Mr. Pole, and a persistent office seeker who haunted both was nick-named "Compass," as being "constant to' the North and always turning towards the Pole." One •of the French commanders deteated by Aldmiral Hawke bore a name signifying "Lark," and "the hawk pounc- ing on the lark," became:a favourite joke with the Eng- lish'sailors. The biting epigram that branded Napoleon's ungenerous gaoler, Sir Hudson Lowe, as "Lowe by name and by nature," is familiar to all. Nor are such cases less frequent in private than in public life. A tavern keeper named "Death," and a pastrycook named "Pill," were the jest of the Euston-road in London for many a year. The partnership of two lawyers, Ketcham and Cheetham, is still a standard joke, and anyone who has visited Western Australia must have heard of the mer- cantile house of Hogg, Bacon, and Fryer. The writer himself knows of two next-door neighbours called Mrs, i.Blood and Mrs. Gore. and two young ladies, way"- -"1s of eacll pt4r, wbose rearA^t;-- : initials were C. A. T. an“ ;7 nut of all these queer coincidences the most striking was the case of a British frigate that figured in the American War of Independence, which was for some time left almost without a crew, owing to the superstitious terror of English seamen for the cluster of ominous names which chance had gathered on board of her. And well it might be so; for the ship's name , was the Sepulchre, her commander was Captain Death, ,1 her first Lieutenant William Devine, and her surgeon I John Ghost !—Cassell's Saturday Journal for July. div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."

Mr. Adolphus Vane-Tempest, who has commenced the forlorn hope in Mid-Durham in the Unionist interest, is the son of Lord Adolphus of that ilk, brother of the Marquis of Londonderry. He is a young man, and his political record consists of a defeat in this same constituency, which he con- tested in 1880.

One of the men who has come to the front a great deal in the House of Commons this session is Mr. Henry Fowler. He is a little heavy in manner, and does not seem to be able quite to shake off the dust of the provincial attorney's office. But he evidently has a large share of solid ,good sense, and is capable of making a clear, intelligible speech on the spur of the moment.

The members of the committee sit at a horseshoe table; but Mr. Gladstone takes a place in the centre besides the clerk. From this point of vantage he is able to hear and make himself heard. Mr. Gosch en, the chahman, is quiet, hardly logical, rather de- pressed. Mr. Balfour manifests that extraordinary good humour which has been his characteristic since Mr. Goschen was humiliated, and the post, ponement of the Land Purchase Bill brought all the present ills on his colleagues.

The venerable Sir Edwin Chadwick has died after an unusually long and useful career. Ile may well be regarded as the pioneer of sanitary reform, which has done so much during the last half cen- tury to lower the death rate and increase the health and happiness of the people. As the "Daily News" admirably puts it :—" Had he killed in battle as many as he saved by sanitation, be would have had equestrian statues by a dozen put up to his memory." As it is, perhaps the nation may find some worthier means of commemorating him.

It is feared that Sir James Stephen will not be able to return to his judicial duties. The malady from which he is suffering is of such a character as to preclude him from transacting even the most ordinary business; indeed, it is said that he is un- able even to go through the formula of sending in his resignation. With business in the courts in such a congested state as it is at present, and with the bwansea Assizes coming on, the continued absence of even one judge is severely felt, and is a state of things not likely to be tolerated for any length of time.

The members of the Committee on the new Stand- ing Order speak with awe of the industry, the vigi- lance, and the profound love of work- which Mr. Gladstone has exhibited. Be has been in his place as regularly as the youngest member, and has watched everything that has gone on with lynx-like eye. The other day he had to attend the funeral service to Lord Carnarvon ; but he promised to be back in an hour and a half; and, sure enough,.when the hour and a half was up, there appeared at the door Mr. Gladstone—puffing, pale, panting,. but punctual—and ready to dash once more intco the fray.

The mania—for it can hardly be called anything else—for the edition de lure of Stanley's "In Darkest Africa" seems to be not yet at its height, for I hear that ..£2O is now tha price demanded for a hook which was published only a few days ago at £lO 10s. The two-guinea edition of the work has been exhausted in a week, and the publishers are certainly to be congratulated on the celerity with which 18,000 copies have been snapped up by the trade, the libraries, and private purchasers. It may be added, that the edition was neither more nor less —in spite of statements to the contrary—than 18,000

Lord Tennyson has been spending a day or two in town as the guest of Mr. James Knowles, of the Nineteenth Century, at the latter's house in (en Anne's Mansions. For many years Mr. Knowles acted as Lord Tennyson's man of business, and this fact alone affords a sufficient explanation of the intimate relations in which they stand to each other. Last week Mr. Gladstone dined with Mr. Knowles in company with Lord Tennyson. I am glad to be in a position to state that Lord Tennyson is now in the enjoyment of the best of health.and is feeling much stronger than he did a year or two ago.

Great Scot! there is a comic paper in Edinburgh ! It is called the "Great Scot," and it WEIEt started on the assumption that it would' be " grandly success- ful "; but the public did not see the fun of it. One of its great achievements has been to get itself into trouble and the Court of Cession for not paying its printer's bill. The gain to Scotch humour was not stated in court, but the loss on the working of the "Great Scot" was said to be ..£769 9s. 11(I. It was also stated that the writers agreed to do the brain- work for nothing." That is where the difficulty came in, and the fun was left out. The public had to turn out their brain power at high pressure, and then don't seem to have seen the jokes.

Those who wish to know something a the move- ment which has sprung out of "Looking back- ward," will find it in Mr. Edward Bellamy's article in this month's "Contemporary," on P'What Nation- alism Means." As Mr. Bellamy's ideal consists of organising all industry on a national basis by inviting all the people to use their collective power to promote the common welfare—it is appropriately enough known in America as Nationalism. There are many Nationalist clubs, societies, and news- papers in existence, and courses of lectures are delivered in the lyceums on Nationalism. Mr. Bell- amy's article is a reply to an attack by M. Emile de Laveleye.

Mr. Bellamy, whose book has now made him famous, is of old New England stock, and is the son of a minister. He wrote several novels before he produced "Looking Backward," but these did not find public favour until after his masterpiece had been published. Mr. Bellamy was formerly on the staff of the New York " Evening Post." It is stated that about 200,000 pirated copies of "Looking Backword" have been sold in this country. It would be interesting to know how much money Mr. Bellamy has received from the publishers. You see that our publishers are not above doing a little pir- ating business when they can get hold of an American work likely to have a large sale.

At the State ball, the other nigh t,the best displays of diamonds were shown by the Duchess of Bedford and the Duchess of Abercorn. Just as the Royal procession reached the dais an unfortunate accident occurred. Lord Lathom, the most graceful and Court-like of Lord Chamberlains, was walking backwards before the Prince of Wales and the Grand Duchess of Mecklenburg-Schwerin when, miscal- culating his distance, he tripped against the edge of the dais and came down on his back as one falls on a skating-rink. For a moment blue arms and white legs struggled in the air, but he recovered himself with dexterous grace, and though Lord Cross might have " heard a smile," the Royal party kept their countenances with commendable gravity.

The Leeds Forge Company's Brass Band, which played at the ceremony of laying the foundation-stone Of 0(.3 PLYaI College of Music,has carried off a great Many ya!llable prizes in the North of England. Mr. Samson Fox, assisted by his brother William—who is an excellent amateur musician—established the band in 1882, and by the liberality of the former the members (27) were provided with new silver-plated instruments at a cost of £3OO, as well as a complete set of uniform. After the band had begun to con- test for the much-coveted prizes in 1884, and went on well, securing victory after victory, the coffers became filled, and they are now in a position to pay their own way, both for new music and travelling expenses. Their total prizes gained up to date amount to no less than £920. They are all hard- working men—strong, healthy Yorkshire lads. The band is conducted by Mr. Alexander Owen.

Whilst the promoters of the nine new supply associations have been flooding London with en- ticing prospectuses well loaded with the statistics of northern co-operation, the condition of many of the workmen's co-operative stores in the capital has been going from bad to worse. It is said that the Southern Sectional Board of Co-operators and the directors of the Co-operative Wholesale Society are concerting measures with a view to remedy this state of things, a course in which they are sustained by a resolution of the North-western Section promising active support and co-operation. With the help of the co-opera- tors of Lancashire thus guaranteed, the outlook is more hopeful than it would otherwise be. Much criticism has been excited in the co-operative move- ment by the appearance of the names of two repre- sentative northern co-operators on the directorate of one of the new supply associations. Co-operators appear to entertain a strong objection to their move- ment .being exploited for the benefit of "those ' more illicit and less constitutional associations," as Lord Rosebery dubs the joint-stock stores.

A few days ago the Bishop of St. Asaph referred, in the course of a speech at some function in his diocese, to" his younger and rasher days," but the local papers reported him as having deplored his " younget and masker days ! "

There are some Tories who look on obstruction as a pure gain to Conservative principles. I met one of those philosophers yesterday, and he said, "1 don't blame the Opposition : on the contrary, I ap- plaud their action. They are preventing my party from rushing into rash legislation." "Then what do you consider the duty of a Tory. Government ?" I asked. "Never to legislate," said he. "The Tory who legislates is lost."

Mr. George Augustus Sala has been writing on small newspapers, and has crept into a small error. "The Petit Journal has a circulation of a million, and a splendid property is the Petites Afflehes," he says, citing examples of the successful small newspapers. But the Fetites A.ffiches is not small. It is forty pages, if it is one. We have nothing like it In London. It is published daily, and contains noth- ing but advertisements.

Even the most intemperate of temperance advo- cates might feel a touch of regret at the extinction of the Horse and Trumpeters, Crutch ed Friars, which has sold the accursed thing without let or hindrance since the year 1555. Though not as old by almost two centuries as the famous Seven Stars at Man- chester, which has held a license since 1350, and holds it still, the Horse and Trumpeters deserves the consideration du,e to its venerable age. But the requirements of the district seemed to have changed, and the old hostelry was no longer needed.

Lord Rosse has been appointed to the vacant knightship of St. Patrick. Lord Rosse is a great scientist, and looks like one. He is the owner of a noble beard and of an immense telescope, which his grandfather erected at a prodigious cost at Parsons- town. Hence the lines of the Rosse family have lain largely in astronomical paths. Not that Lord Rosse is merely a stargazer, as he is admirably qualified to participate in various mundane affairs, and is an admirable judge of horseflesh,. besides a noted connoisseur on all matters agricultural.

Mr. Thomas Greenwood has brought out a new edition of his most useful book. on publie libraries. Mr. Greenwood has re-written most of his work and brought it down to date. He gives n list of the libraries which have been founded by Mr. Andrew Casnegie, which shows that the "'lron Ling has already spent L 160,000 in providing free reading for the'people. His benefactions in America are the Allegh any City Library, £60,000;. Carnegie Library, Braddock's. Johnstown Library, £2,000, Pittsburg Library £200,000; and in Scotland the Carnegie Library at his native place, Dunfermline, which cost .£B.OOO, and the Edinburgh Public- Library, which was £50,000; not to mention large contribu- tions to other libraries.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 12, 1890
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 12, 1890

MR. SCHNADHORST AND THE BARROW ELECTION. LErTER TO LYMM LIBERALS. The Lymm District Liberal Association of the Altrinc- ham division of Cheshire passed a resolution at a meet- ing held on Monday last, applauding the determination shown by the Barrow Liberal Association in insisting on putting up a distinctively Home Rule candidate at recent election, and heartily congratulating them on their success in carrying their man under peculiarly ad- verse circumstances. A copy of this resolution was for- warded to Mr. Sehnadhorst, who has returned the fol- lowing reply :--

- • "National Liberal Federation, "Loudon, S.W., July 9, 1890. " Dear Sir,—l beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter, enclosing me copy of a resolution passed by your Association, with the purport of which resolution I cor- dially agree. The suddenness of Mr. Caine's resignation, and the circumstances under which it took place, occa- sioned great perplexity in the minds of many Liberals, I and it is. perhaps, hardly surprising that there was I much difference of opinion au to the right policy to be pursued. This differetre of opinion was manifested in the Liberal' Frees—the majority I of London Liberal newspapers deprecating op- position to Mr. Caine,—among leading politicians in the country, among all sections of the Liberal party in Parliament, on the front Opposition Bench and below the gangway alike. For myself, Ihad not a moment's hesit- ation as to the course which ought Lobe adopted, and, as I had opportunity, warmly commended the decision of the Liberal Association of Barrow tcr run their selected candidate. My opinion was based ozureasons having no relation to the possible result of the election, and would have been unchanged had Mr. Wainwright, instead of Mr. Duncan, been returned. I believe- that any ether , policy than that pursued would have livriv a demoralising I effect on Liberal workers throughout thercountry, espec- , iaily in those constituencies now represented by Dissenti- ent Liberals. I join heartily, therefore your congrat- ulations to the Liberal Association of iparow and to its 'leaders. They have earned our admiiintion by their pluck, determination, and fidelity. Pt should be a matter of satisfaction to all who have contended for the representative principle in relation to party manage- ment and for the independence of local organisations that when the Barrow Liberal Associationi finally deter- rtheed to contest the seat thd leaders of thelfarty gave it their loyal and hearty support. —I am,, yours faithfully,. F. Scluesnlionor.. ".J. R. Swanwick, Esq., Lymm District Liberal Asso- ciation."

SOUT.H-WEST MANCHESTER LIBERATIa AT CR9FT. The- annual picnic of the members of the South-,west Manchester Liberal Association. took- place on.. Saturday. The party numbered about 300. From the Central. Station. they went by train to Culcheth, and thence by. roadto-Croft, The afternoon and evening werespentim the neighbourhood of the General Elliott Hotel. First there was a series of sports, then tea, followed bra <little speechmaking, 'then dancing. Among the gentlemen present were Mr. Jacob Bright, the member for, the divi- sion, Mc. H. J. Roby, Mr.E. J. Broadfield, Dr. Woodcock, Mr. Councillor Gibson, Mr. Council/or Norris, Mm.Coun- cillor.Baia,,Mr. J. Wigley, Mr. R. Cachart, Mr. Councillor Tatton„Mr. F. Drummond, Mr. J. Appleton, Mr; -L., D.. Frince,,Mr. J. Gamble, Dr. Worswiok, and Mr.R..Ander- son. For the speechmaking the chair was taken by Dr. Woodcock.—Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P., said his notion of a Government,. whether it were Liberal or Tory, . was that it should. at least have capacity, and not only capacity"but'claaracter. Well, a Gowernthent of broken pledges could have hardly character enough , to excite thorespect of the country., . The present Govern - Talent was.. essentially a Government of broken pledges:. It came into,office as a non-coercion,Government, passed a.Goercien bill which, as far es it could, it Made perpetual. In the very first week after it came into power the. Government declared emphatically that . Local Government Bill should be passed for Ireland at the same time as, for England and Scotland. No Local Government Bill for Ireland was forthcoming, and even' ' politician knew that no. such bill would:be introduced by the present,Government.. So much for itsepledges. As to its capacity,, it, had broliendown irretrievably during the pize sentSessien. The explanation,he believed,was extremely simple. The Governmentwas absolutely, ignorant of the- country it undertook to,govern. He knew it was true, but he hardly expected his audience to believe it, that when the Government brought their Fl,blic-house En- dowment Bill into the-House of Commene they thought that the country,,ttcs- temperance party'. .and the best.' people of. England would accept it with jny and thanks- giving—(laughter),—though they were doubtful tvliethen- it would be acceptedby the publicans.--(tLaughter.) stronger proof could be given of their ignorance of what. was in the minds of the English people. How, was it that suchimiorance•existed ? It was because the Gov- ernment had been largely led by Mr. Goachen, who had, no sympathy with orconfidence in the -people. When& the Liberals handed Mr. Goschen over: to the Tories, they did the best thing they could for themselves and a. very dangerous thing for the enemy.—(ll.aughter.) He suspected. that thiafeeling was now widely entertained by the Tony. party. (Cheers and laughtsy4-/-The party returnedto town ima train which left Cutcheth at nine- o'clock.

CANAL.
SOME, INTERESTING DETAILS.

Under. the auspices of the Liverpool, Engineering; Society, ,a. largo party of engineers left Liverpool, OM Wednesday morning, for thepurpose of making an inspec- tion of the Manchester Ship Canal works, under ti' guidance.of Mr. E Leader Williams, the chief engine, of the-Ship Canal. Proceeding by train to Manchester, the party were conveyed to Pomona, where, under the guidance of Mr-Williams, the special features of engineer- ing interest were explained, and the magnitude and. ingenious construction of the dock walls and gates were. subjects of greatadmiration. A special train, consisting: of two saloons,and an open wagon, was , placed at the, service of the pesty, and in this they proceeded on to, Latchford locks,. Mr. Williams leaving the company, under.the guidance of Mr. Cecil Brown, the resident engineer for, this section of the canal. At letchford great, interest was excited at the huge locks—magnificent. specimens of engineering skill. Of the two locks one is. 600ofeet long and, 65, feet wide, and the other 350 fast long,and 45 feet wide, and each can be emptied by enimv- mous culvertain the space of five minutes. The great feature, however„ in these and the other locks of the• canal is that the level of the lower sill Isl 3 feet 10 inches below the old-dock datum, and, theref.ire, deep enough, to allow the largest vessel built to pass through them. The mornirg,having passed very pleasantly in viewing! I this end of the canal, the party proceedsd to Wilderspoel,, where, at the Saracen's Head Hotel, they were served. with an excellent dinner at the hands .of the proprietor,. Mr. .I'. o..Speakman—After dinner therresident. H. West,. proposed the health of Mr. Leader Williams. The toast was cordially drunk, afterr which Mr. Cecil Brown„the resident engineer at the Lntchford sectiOn.of the works, thanked, them all on behalf of the Manchester. Ship Canal for the kind way in which they had wished success to the undertaking. With regard to his motioi. of the work, he would give them some figures which might prove of interest as to the best day's work and the number of hands employed. There were four stearin Inavvies.at work, of which Lubeck: machine hadlrnada The hest day's work (ten hours) 0f.24,400 cubic yards, or an average of 1,900 yards. The-number of men and boys employed at this machine was 22. Rushton. and Procter's machine has made a test day's worhet 1,920 cubic yards ; average 750 yards.;, the number,- of men and boys employed at this machine was 17. Whit-taker's excavator had made a best daywittork of 718 eulltic yards; average 320- yards, with ten men and boys. Priestrvan's grab h had made a best days work of 362 cubic yards; average 324 yards, with several men and boys.empleyed around it. In his section the total excavation,babe done was .6 million cubic yards and of these 41 million yards had already been excavated.—" The President 'barring been drunk, the party left the hotel and again jpined the train, which was to take them towards Runcorn. In the run between Warrington and 'Runcorn the great obstacles. which the Manchester Ship ' Canal will have to surmount are strikingly prominent. Great interest was centred in the work going on at Fiddlers' ferry in connection with the Vyrn.wy scheme. Here, it will be remembered, the tunnelis. after being carried 50 feet beneath the river, Was flooded, and had to be abandoned. Owing to the" quicksanely " nature- of the soil pumping was of no avail, and the new con, tractors, we are told„ will have to sink a fresh shaft and begin practically allover again. A mile or two further- down Runcorn was passed, and the party alighting from, the carriages, were treated to a pleasant cruise in a steam launch down, the Weaver. Landing at Weston Point, an laspectiamwas made of the remarkable sluices at the mouth of the Weaver, and the formidable-lookhag, tidal gates thronghwhich communicationwill be effected between the Weaver, the Mersey, and the canal. The section bet Ween this point and Runcorn practically runs alongside of the-Mersey, from which it will be separated by a hugeseawall,which at present is hardly compienced. Having spent the afternoon in viewing this part of the canal, the party once more embarked in the special train, which moved off in the direction of Runcorn, where the company, having spent a most enjoyable day, separated for their various destinations.

.k.FTER DARK. "T's ready, father," cried the pretty slim girl about seventeen years old as she stood in the garden of the little cottage on the same evening itpon which this tale opened. There was no answer to her appeal, so she called again. "Tea's ready, father, and it will soon be time for you to go on again." "I'm meomin', my dear. I'm a-comin'," replied Raymond, and in a moment more the person to whom the voice belonged appeared carrying a hoe. "So tea's ready for me is it, Lucy? Well, and I'm ready for tea.. So we're quits on that point, my girl." "Come along, father. I've made the toast and put lots of butter on it, and the teapot is on the hot steaming, like Bill's engine does. Make haste, rot I'm hungry." "So am I," replied her father. " I'rcr as hungry as a famished hanak, and sharp set as a saw, I am. Why, there's a picture! Lucy, you're the best gir; alive, and you'll make a first-rat, wife soma day l" "Perhaps I shan't," replied Lucy, blhshing little. "Why are you always tellina me that?" "Because I want to see ye happily married, my girL Ye know I love ye, Lucy; don't ye, now?" For an answer the girl went up, and perching her- self upon his knee, kissed him heartily. And he who spoke of her as his chiiiikissed her respectfully,as a comparative stranger might have done, upon, her smooth forehead, and looked into her deep brown
ks-4
teerri

eyes. There was something in his giw, that struck the girl, now budding into a lbvely womanhood, her ttim gure indicating a more than usual symmetry than is usually found in girls of her station. Her bands were small and well formed,, though evidently not these of an idler. Her well-turned ankles ana small

feet were fully visible beneath her stuff dress; and; her dark hair was bound up plainly, and Owl, with scarlet ribbon. A small blush rose was fastened at her throat, and matched tbo, glowing of her soft and nounded cheeks. She' was a striking girl, and onr whose face indicated', firmness as well as beauty; passion at rest, and a will scarce formed, but still existent, as the moutit.• and chin could show. Just thim she was all tender-

The Londommail train had passed through the cutting. Perched.upon the submit of the embankment, the main line of a great and prosperous railway running underneath and out of sight, the', cottage was a. picturescgm object in the landscape: It was 'em.- ,bosomed in honeysuckle and roses,/ which climbed and twined lovingly around the lattice windows or peepedi slyly intota the bedroom through the white dimity curtain which shrouded Laity's toilet table, as she. dressed la the early morning.. The old signalman proceedetraleng the narrow. path leading through the plantation that crossed the railway embankment, and desceaded the slope to the signal-box perched upon the grassy slope. Tholine curved somewhat at this pointeand a deep-mouthed : tunnel yawned widely in thb opposite direction. Above the tannel, which had been cut through the kill for a mile and a half, were dark ventilatornlike short chimneys; and children who notice/ the' smoke rising therefrom at tintes,, believed the stories , told by nervous matrons, that a giant lived below, and stnoked, his pipe. Facing the signal-box & publle road ran around the hill opposite, and above, the road the trees sur- rounded a house or two; while in the valise/a° the left, as you looked beyond the curve, lay tin village - of Blenheim., its square-towered old church: , dome- nating red roofs and slates and thatch. Behindi the signal-box a canal carried on its alaggish, waters many a laden barge and grimy flat, while coal-heavers, with masculine-looking wives., andt children, dirty as the flats themselves, passed' and repassed day and night, with horses tugging lard in fear of cracking whips and growling, swearing drivers' from Landstene town. Hidden away upon; the embankment, in. close, proximity to the high road, yet invisible from it and shaded from the canalty the trees, the signalman's. little cottage and potato patch was., situated; and when the setting sun poured its crimson, beams right up the line, even illuminating the dark, wide ineuth of the great Blexham Tunnel, the acne from the cottige down the incline towards the village was as pretty a piece of scenery as one coull wish to view. And then the heaving seat' In the distance, above the trees tall chimneys rose by day, vomiting smoke and clouding the setting sun. At night the flames ascended with a roar from these great shafts, and throw a glare upon the clouded sky at times as if Par.demonitra, had opened a trap-door and let the fire have free vent. Clanging hammers rang down them iet the "shops" all day, and round the works the cottages had risen in rows so like each other and in such regular lines that they might almost have been thought toys set down upon the ground by children a a largo! growth. The sun was dipping down behind the western hills 'when the signalman, Jack, as his comrades called him, entered his box, and was gladly wel- comed by his mate. "Good time, Jack," said the latter; "I must say ye always are in ta time. The mall's just gene up. She ain't cleared the tunnel yet." "All right," replied Jack, as he took off his coat, "leave her to me; get ye home and sleep till Itlerning, and if ve see Tone Throwgood, tell hiM not t came lastat,Maid ,a, repliedt h i to be late again to-morrow. "It ain't all of us as has such a lass to keep house as you Jack Eaemond," "Never you mind my caughter, Dick, but beware of the Village Maid.' Her' tap' is worse than any knock-down blow. A lick of the 'fist is done with and over; a drunk Mei sosg put off, and you tell Tom so from me." **Good nizbt. Jack" said his mate. "I'm blest

if ye am' tinned toteetaller or Methody all of a sudden," he muttered to himself, as he descended. He had not gone half way along the path, when he heard Raymond calling to him to come back. "Look here, mate, let me see ye a minute. 'Have you seen anyone hanging about theline this evenin' ?'• asked the old man. _ _

"Hanging about—on the railway?" "Aye, any loafing fellow—a tallish man. I've once or twice seen him a crossing the line when I was attendin' to the points, and I've checked the , train for fear he might be killed." "Ha, ha, we heard o' that game. Co it was you, Jack, that stopped the fast train for nothing, was it P "Not for nothing, Dick. It were the life of a fellow creature, and it's a dreadful thing to be took sudden like that." "Aye, it is," assented Dick, seriously. "But, mate, not for them as is prepared to go. Why, I declare' to ye this minute that if I was ready and could defy the devil and his angels, I'd as lief die than live." "Then get ready, Dick," said the old man. "We never know what may befall. Why, my wife, Lucy's mother there—ah, she was a frolicsome woman, mate' to the last—and she was took as sudden as a wink. Poor thing! She give one gasp and died, sciildin' me to the last, and findin' fault with her -very. latest-breath." "We never knew," assented Dick, more cheerfully; "but what, makes ye think of this to-night?" •• "I don'thrightly know, Dick. I can't tell ye for certain., ißut lately I've seen things. Hush! pve seen.thinks on the railway. I've noticed sharAs-- the .man—ghost I call it—and a white figure, sometimes alone, sometimes close together. They're warnixes, Dick—warnin'e," "Nonsense, man, ye're over-worked. Go and get a holiday and one of Dame Jones's big pills. that don't make ye a ghost it'll clear them out of your head. One or two taken fasting nearly killed Abraham Timhs, and Ee-was a knowledgeable man, too." "Very well, mate, you'll see some day. Now mind ye avoid the Maid.' Women is ticklish cattle at the best o' times; but. when ye call a public a 'Village Maid,' ye add all the seclueings of liquor to the sex. Come early in the mornin', if ye can, or tell Tom to be in time as you; arrange it. Good night." 'Goodnight, Jack. Newer mind the women." ". Good by, old friend," said Raymond, the points- roam holding out his hand.: "Good night. (live us yer fiat." The men exchanged a hearty grip, and Dick went hearse unwillingly. "I wish:l-hadn't left him alone," he muttered. "He's gettinrfanciful,and no good will come of it."
CHAPTERz IV.
A GHOSTLY WARNING.

.Jecx„ left alone, received the signal from the man. :at the end of the tunnel, telling him that the mail .had passed through, and, as he had no warning just then, he opened the sliding window and looked out. Evening was closing in, but there was plenty of light, and in the gloaming -nem- the tunnel the signalman perceived the figure of a man. A sudden tremor shook Raymond's limbs. He gazed at the figure intently as ifthe could not believe his eyes, and yet to an ordinary observer there was nothing to alarm anyone in the appearance of the person upca the railway. To..the signalman the figure was a tall, well-formed young man, of military appearance, and yet the gloom near the mouth of the tunnel rendered his face indistinct.. But there was nothing in the general appearance of the man to alarin any one. And yet Raymond was very much alarmed indeed. His hands shook, and had he soave ghost he could scarce have been paler. The man stood upon the line for a few seconds, and then approached the signal-box upon the up metals—those farther from the box; and just then a train was signalled on as coming on that line. The signalman replied, and catching up a flag, waved it to the man upon the railway. He took no notice, except to hold up his arm, and pursued his way along the line. The signalman called out, knowing the train was rapidly approaching. He could see the steam of the engine come round the curve; and determined to warn the driver. He hastily snatched up a red flag and put his signal at danger. A whistle told him he had done so only just in time—if it were in time. Another second or two would decide it. All this time the trespasser was walking on the metals; gliding along quietly, quite unconcerned . and carn, as if no such things as trains existed. But the warning came too late. The speed could not be slackened ' sufficiently. The express came rushing en, and in a moment had'run over the spot where the man had been standing. As the train gulled up, Raymond ran out and down to the line. "You've killed him," he exclaimed. "Poor - fellow ! " _ .

"Killed who? What's up?" inquired the driver as Raymond approached. Many people put their heads out of the windows and eagerly inquired if there was an accident. "What's up, mate ?" inquired' the.flreman, who with the engine-driver descended from the engine. " Why, I tell you you've run over a man just this moment—a tall youngfellow. Come back here with me." "We didn't see any one on tho line," replied the drive' r • did we Ned? We only saw the signal put upall of a sudden and your flag." Raymond made no answer, but le& the way to the rear of the train, where he encountered a guard and several passengers who had alighted. Many inquiries were immediately addressed to the signalman' who answered that he was afraid a marshad been killed on the line. "I warned him time enough, but he took no notice, and then I put up the signal to warn the driver."

Thoguareturned back, , and the others went also towards the spot indicated, and, examined the ground. , Not a trace of any human being could be fcund. The ballast of the permanent way was not in any way disturbed, nor had any blood been spilt. "Well, this is a rum start," said the guard. "The driver and fireman looked at each other and laughed. "Jack's been dinia' out," said Ned. "Been raisin' a bit. Eh, Jaek ? " rve touched nothin' but tea this week," re- plied the trembling signalman. "It's the warnin' again." "The warnin' I" exclaimed the guard. "What, the spirit we heard ,ed ? Gt out:" he added, scorn- fully. "Spirits and water, I'm afraid," remarked one of the passengers. "I'm sorry to. see the lives of people are trusted to a tipsy signalman." "I'm not tipsy, sir," replied Jack, res7ectfully; "tor was I ever drunk in my life. You can have me, on-mined, if you, please. I saw the appearance on; the line as sure as I stand here."'

"Nonsense, my good fellow," replied another gentleman. "I think you are overworked—you fancy things. Take a rest—get off dutyfor a week, and have a change of air. 1 can see you are sober enough." "Jack's sober enough always." said the engine- driver. "se's stopped us before like this. Mere may be soraethinF in it, but we saw nobody." "Not a soul,' said Ned, confirming his mate't remarks, as,in duty bound. The guard also said the same. "Then there's something going to happen. You may depend warnings dont come for nothin'. Loot out aheed„ driver; youi may find it affects yew too," said Jack, shaking his.head. "Gain' to happen, is there? Do ye think that theres,ghosts about than?" asked the driver,scorn- " That's just what Ido believe. I've, seen the figure afore, and he always vanishes in. front of a train. Look ahead, mate.' "All right, Jack; don't alarm yourself. 11 he's a.gbeet I run him down. If he's a man I won't. Good night." Jack stood at the window of the box and watched the train. The steam rose in lurid clouds in the light of the setting sun, and vanished into ths tunnel. The figure had disappeared, and. when the man hurried up from the tunnel to ask if anything was the matter, Jack turned the subject, and said it was." all right." Yet, notwithstanding his convi-tions, Jack Ray- mond could not shake off the dread that oppressed him as night came on. The sun disappeared in fiery clouds, and made .the discs of the signals blood-red danger lights, even when green or white were dis. lilayed. All tile atmospherical concomitants were ir favour of nervous associations. The air was stib and sultry; scarce a sound was heard—the birds were hushed—the insects forgot to hum—a weird and alarming sensation of solitude crept over Tack, and ever and anon a cold and unaccountable shiver ihurried through his limbs, as if he had suddenly walked into a fog. The heavy masses of cloud came piling themselves up on the horizon, and sent out light scouts of vapour like pilot balloons to see which way the wind blew. And yet the great masses did not always take advantage of the information, for some of them went slowly away in another direction, and left their mountainous companions putting out tendrils of their own, and grumbling loudly as the 3 west,

All this while not a breath of wind was stirring. and yet the branches of the higher trees waved to and fro as if in sympathy„ with each other. The snails and such creeping things came under the signal-box as if for shelter, and in the light of his .band lamp he could see glistening streaks upon the woodwork. And had Jack Raymond' understood how,!well animals of a lower creation than he under stands the signs of coming rain and tempest, he might have been interested in watching his com- panions—two fine spiders. But when his attention was not directed to an al3- preaching train he was listless, and yet nervously alive to every sound. He could not help watching the line near the tunnel, as if he expected to see the ghostly figure in the gloom. Night came on, and as twelve o'clock approached, a distant sigbln4 mound was heard, and a flicker that:was not an engine's light or fire glittered across the rails. "A storm is comin' on," muttered Jack. "1 hope Lucy wen't be frightened—all alone. It'll wake her up, and I don't think she quite likes it. There's another—ah ! and that's thunder and no mistake." There could be no mistake as the deep' yet still distant boom of Heaven's artillery resounded through the pitchy darkness. Suddenly a vivid blaze of light showed the signal- man the kill and the trees, as if a transparency had been lighted up behind them. In that second he savr every object as distinctly, even more distindtly than at noon-day„ and then the thunder rumbled and finished with, a boom like a stroke upon an enormous

drum. - Then a blue and silvery gleam came shimmering' and zig-zagging through the sky, and danced from cloud to cloud. A rattling peal followed—the boom- ing stage was passed—the storm was approaching. Jack Raymond turned to shut the door of -the signal cabin whith had swung open, for the breeze was getting up i and, as he did so, a terrific light- ning flash leapet from the sky all green and blue and chain-like,arid in the vivid gleam he beheld a figure standing on the top step of his ladder, a figure all in white, but in the second of time he had recognised Lucy standing like al lovely statue against the landscape, the glinting rails, and distant yilluge! !muses, all of which were clearly visible

behind her in he light. " Lor a mercy, girl, you startled mtrfor a minute, I declare; ome inside. I was thinkin' of you. I thought ye'd be nervous, Lucy." She was very white as she stood there, very beau' tiful, and trembling in the dim light. "So I was, father. I'm glad I came. See! there's a flash! I couldn't sleep father, dear, and _,

so I thought I'd come to you." "Very glad ye earns, my girl. Why, Lucy, hacs ye been frightened? Are ye cryin', lovey ? That's a tear, or I'm a Dutchman." "Nothing, father—nothin' at all. I was a little frightened at first, but now I am here I feel safor: The thunder is going off, and I can soon get back• It will be daylight soon." But the storm still grumbled around, and man); vivid flashes darted across the black sky. In one _ _ . •

these Raymond called out, excitedly: - "There! look there! He's come againi. Don't ye see him—the appearance!" "Where, father ? "exclaimed Lucy, startled IT the suddennesa of her father's appeal am' the nature ' of it. "I don't see anything." "Not now ye couldn't, but I did. Well, warned him, and now he may take his There he he is still, crossing now." In the second that had elapsed every object wan as clear as noon-day, but now blackness had settled cloWn again. The thunder that followed the last flash was apparently nearer. "Get ye home, Lucy. I'll not be late. Have breakfast laid ready, there's a good lass. Run awil now." "Run away, father.. Why shouldJ?" she asked, playing upon the words with a strange pleasures and almost wishing he would detain her in the signal' tos by force till morning. "Go home, child," replied the old man, testily. "Leave me_; ran now before the rain comes worse; yy L ctlhaisileth' esti will. be wet. through. Good night, "Good nightir.and good bye,." she murmured, softly. "Give me your blessing, dear father." , " 0-od bless ye, girl, and send ye happinesss. A feel strange to-night myself. But go, and heaven preserve you, my girl.' She went reluctantly. Kissing him warmly, and then with slow unwilling steps, notwithstandingthe rain which had now recommenced, she. returned . homewai ds. 4 At the gate a man awaited her. Sbn almost *creamed at seeing him there. "Here I am, Lucy, darling, as.l said, punctual to the time. Halfret two.. Have yen put the thine n "Yes, Frank; but I do not think I can go lik* this. Why not wait and ask father and—" "George Collier, I suppose," sneered the man.; "Oh, certainly. Hadn't we better tell them all about it now i" "Don't be so cruel, Frank. You know what 1 have Mcriliced for you,, and yet I wish we could have acted differently.. But it is too late-°° late!" 11• - " Too early you mean, Lucy,"' cried the man impatiently. "It will. be daylight soon. We call cross tloe line, and in ten minutes we shall be in the trap. Came, darling Lucy, come." She still hesitated, and he. proceeded, "W°' then, I must go alone. The transport sails on the 26th, and I have only one more day. I re- ene'aqa as a married man, and am.on the•' strength' of the regiment." "I thought you was. an officer, Frank; you told me so. Are not you an officer ?" . "Yes, a' non-com.'.'—without a commission I mean; ' Now, my girl, no nonsense; pick up your spirits tie; your clothes and let'it be. off.. You must, you Abel' come v crye hear?" Lucy almost rebelled at these words, hat eon-- trolled her temper as she thought of the probablef• consequences. Then in.w.more submissive frame mind, she entered the cottage, and soon retur,no`' ,iyith a good-sized bundle. "Here are my things,' she said. "rye saved 9-11 the money I could, and have got it here." She touched her bosom as she spoke, and after fl' hurried glance around, the youthful pair hasteneo• dewn the path to the railway line. There was a sort of dim Tight from the eastern sky, and they were admonished there was no iil They crossed the railway unobserved as they fancied and were at once hidden in. the deep shadows ef the trees. But Raymondthad perceived from his elevated niche the gliding figures. He was certain this WM!' that his eyes had not deceived him. In a roomeil; he was on the line hurrying towards the tunnel- He had made up his mind to find out the mystOrYi His brain was in a 'whirl. He fancied he recognised , a female form,like Lucy's. He must be gcing ri'll b le A sudden scream—a roar—a rush—a terri_ grinding, rasping sound in his ears. He had ?I' Lime to turn round—no time to utter a cry for belP• The engine threw him aside with a horrible sweepilli action from the buffer and east him in the pertneoeni. way a mangled, dusty heap of matter., apparel)", no longer human.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four. TELEPHONE LICENSES.—The Duke of MARLBOROUGH Moved that it was advisable that licenses should be granted to responsible parties willing to undertake the business of forming new telephone companies on the expiration of the patents owned by the National Com- PallY, but after some remarks by Lord Jersey the motion Was withdrawn. THis EDUCATION Cos.—On the motion of Lord CHAN- BROOK, a hill to give effect to certain provisions in the Education Code, 1890, was read a second time, and re- ferred to a Committee of the whole House. A number of Bills were advanced, and the House adjourned at 5.15.
THE ANGLO-GERMAN AGREEMENT: STATEMENT HT LORD

SALISBURY. The Marquis of SALISBURY moved the second reading of the Bill to give effect to that part of the Anglo-Ger- man Agreement which provides for the cession of Heli- goland, he said the value of the island for strategic purposes has been generally recognised as very small ; and, holding that it was a distinct disadvantage if we had a possession contributing in no degree to the defence of the empire, without commercial or other value, and yet, in order to avoid a humiliating blow, requiring a naval force to defend it, the Government had come to the conclusion to cede it to Germany if they could obtain for it a satisfactory consideration. His Lordship referred at some length to the African branch of the bargain, and contended that an arrangement had been come to which would be for the benefit of both this country and Ger- many, each having gained that which was best suited to its own purposes, and come to an agreement which would remove all danger of disunion and conflict.—The Earl of ROSEBERY, while not disposed to carp at the Agreement, said that such arrangements could not but produce jealousy amongst those nations who were no par- ties to them. He held that it would be an advantage if they could receive the formal assent of all the European Powers. He thought, moreover, that the House ought to be informed of the opinions of the naval and military sexerts as to the value of Heligoland, and he drew atten- tion to the fact that the two guaranteeing Powers of Zanzibar were not Germany and the Sultan but England and France. After a few observations from Lord KNUTS- FORD and Earl GRANVILLE the second reading was agreed to without a division being challenged. The house rose at seven o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THMISDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. PRIVATE BILLS.—The Cheshire Lines Committee Bill was read a third time and passed. The Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Bill, which hal come down from the House of Lords, was considered and ordered for third reading. THE POSTMEN'S "STRIKE.—Mr. EAMES, replying to Mr. COnybeare, said that all the defections which took place at the Leicester-square Parcel Office had been more than provided for, and applicants had been turned away. No FACILITIES TOR WELSH SUNDAY CLOSING.—Mr. W. H. SMITH, replying to Mr. Roberts, said it was not in his power to grant facilities for passing the Welsh Sunday Closing Bill or any other bill. Purim BUSINESS.—Mr. SMITH then made a statement regarding public business, in the course of which he indicated that the Government had decided not to press the "hanging-up" standing order this Ses- sion. It followed that they would not proceed with the Land Purchase Bill or the Tithes Bill be- fore the prorogation, but intended to re-introduce them early in the next session, which they proposed should assemble at a much earlier period than hitherto. Mr. Gladstone thought that unless some further means were taken to ascertain the feeling of members on the well-intended plan of the Government, the early meet- ing would tend to prclong rather than shorten the don.

THE POLICE STRIKE.—Mr. H. W. LAwsoN asked the LlAnte Secretary as to the reported strike of the police- uteri at Bow-street Station, London.—Mr. MATTHEViS l'ePlied that the statements in the newspapers had been Much exaggerated. The fact was that 39 constables guilty of insubordination in refusing to go on duty on Saturday night had been dismissed the service. They *were all young men, and had not long been in the force. The constables of older standing and experience had behaved in a manner worthy the police, and they had exhibited no insubordination. The Chief Commissioner bad made every arrangement for the due performance Af the police duties throughout the metropolis.—ln 'reply to further questions by Mr. C. Graham and others, Mr. Matthews said the cause of dissatisfaction among the constables dismissed was the transfer from one division to another ot a constable who was improperly Asking for signatures to a certain petition among the Men at Bow-street, and who was also canvassing for sab- Acriptions. GRAHAM asked for information as to a rumour circulated by the Press As- sociation that a company in the 2nd Grenadier Guards had refused to parade for dutythat morning, and had Ire- to barracks;; also he asked if it were true that it Nvas in contemplation to order them for foreign service.— alt. STANHOPE : I have heard nothing of the matter.. If anything of importance had occurred I should haveileard of h.—Mr. C. GRKHAM : In view of threatened troubles With the police and the postmen, will the right hon.gen- tleman inquire into the matter ?—Mr. Stanhope made no GRATIAM I must insist on an answer. SMITH informed Mr. Sexton that he did not propose to make any statement tegarding the course of public business until the Com- mittee on procedure had reported. THE SLAVE Trwm.=Sir. J. PEROUSSON informed Mr. 8- Smith that a large traffic in the Red Sea was being done in slaves disguised as pilgrims and otherwise. Italy had acceded to the slave trade treaty between'England Mad Turkey, and concerted action was being taken as to the suppression of the trade. IRISH VOLUNTEER:I.—Mr. STANHOPE told MT. W. .8.• Macdonald that the reasons advanced by Mr- Gladstone some years ago against the formation of an 'lrish volun- teer force, namely, the existence of strong religiouailis- Tensions, still heffigood. SIIPPLY.—The House then went into Committee of supply on the chill service estimates, and on the vote of 089,490 for the Royal Irish Constabulary, Mr. Ellis complained of its great cost compared with that of the Metropolis and some •of the provincial towns.—Mr. itAtsoult defended the administration of the police, and, 'referring to ' shadowing," said that that system, which Was now so strongly objected to by the Opposition, was Practised by Mr. Gladstone and the Secretary to the :Lord-Lieutenant when the member for Midlothian was fl office,—Mr. GLADSTONE followed, and demanded Proofs for the statements made by the Chief-Secretary. —The remainder of the evening was occupied discussing thevote. _

The House adjourned at 112.50. HOUSE OF 'LORDS.—TITESDNY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at 'half-past five. THE RIOT IN BOND-ST. AND THE GRENADIER GUARDS.— The Marquis of SAINSBURY, in reply to Earl Granville, said it was undoubtedly true that there had been certain disaffection in a small and limited section Of the police, and it was in Bow-st. and its neighbourhood especially that the influence of the section was felt. 'Under the cir-, cumstances, and as a crowd Of a not very reputable char- acter assembled in and around that locality, the Assistant Commissioner thougkt it necessary to Bendier a squadron Of Life Guards. Their appearance was quite sufficient to restore order. With regard to the second question— the breach of discipline in the 'Grenadier Guards—that Was the subject of investigation, and it would be unde- tirable for him then to express an opinion on-a subject on Which evidence was being received and sifted, and the 'result of which would be made public before long. Any breach of military discipline was much to be deplored, Aind ought to be visited with proper punishment. Still, it would be absurd to lend any importance to what had 'taken place. (Hear, hear,) TIPPERARY.—EarI &MOGAN, in reply to the Earl of 'Camperdown, said that 25 outrages had occurred in or 'Dear the town of Tipperary since September last in 'reference to the Smith-Barry dispute. The House adjourned at ten minutes past six. HOUSE OF COINIONS.—TITESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three O'clock. 'LONDON Couxrr Cousimt, 13Tht..—The London County 'Council 8111 was ordered for third reading, after ,an bnportant amendment had been carried against the views of the promoters. TEE GUARDS.—Mr. Sraemore told Mr. Cunizighame 'Graham that some dissatisfaction existed among a num- lzeir of men belonging to the Guards Regiment on being ordered to attend parade, but the Whole of them after- 'wards paraded and marched off in perfect order for-duty. Inquiry was being made into the case. IlamooraND.—Mr. W. H. Ssurn„ in reply to Mr. Charming, said the natives of Heligoland and all their children born up to the date of the Anglo-German agree- Ment would be free from the obligation to serve in the naval or military forces. THE PUBLICANS' PETITION.—Sir Cnant.ns FORSTER , formed Sir W. Lawson that 7 per cent, of the signatures attached to the publican' petition were in the same handwriting and some few were fictitious. The Coin- Inittee on Public Petitions had ucanimously decided that,' the case was one calling for further action. ENGLAND AND THE TRIPLE ALLIANCE.—Sir J. PEROUSSON told Mr. Picton, in reference to the Anglo-German treaty, ' 'that the Government had entered into no new engage- ments on the eveht of war breaking out on the continent of Europe. "SBADOWINO."—Mr. SHAW LEFEVRE,OR the!Flousegoing into Committee of Supply on the Irish estimates, resumed the discussion on the Royal Irish Constabulary vote,and said that the force, instead of being impartial, had com- Meneed to display a purely partisan spirit, which he attributed largely to the speeches of Mr. Balfour in the House. He condemned " shadowing " as utterly futile, even from the point of view of the Government themselves.—Mr. Dii.tox believed that the day was at hand when the English people would have the stain of ,4 shadowing " on their honour removed.—The -discussion on the vote occupied the remainder of the sitting. The House adjourned at 12.55. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes past _ twelve o'clock, but it was not until 25 minutes to one that a quorum was made. BURNLEY RECTORY BILL.—The Burnley Rectory Bill Was considered, and ordered for third reading. THE BANKRUPTCY BILL. The Bankruptcy Bill as amended by the Grand Committee was considered. A new clause was agreed to providing that a landlord's Preferential claim to rent in bankruptcy cases should be reduced from twelve to six months. Clause 11 was so amended as to deprive the court of discretion, and to compel it to withhold its assent to any scheme or corn- Position or arrangement which was not reasonable or calculated to benefit the general body of creditors. The hill was read a third time and passed. PUBLIC HEALTH.—The Public Health Acts Amendment Bill passed through Committee, after Mr. Ritchie had thanked Mr. H. H. Fowler and Mr. Powell for the valu- able addition which was about to be made to the statute- book. THE Loin:Km Posratex.—On the motion for the adjournment of the House, Mr. CONSBEARE asked the Secretary to the Treasury, in the absence of the Post- master General, whether the statement was correct that the authorities had called on the postmen to sign a declaration that they would not come out on strike before the 21st July, the authorities in the meantime being at liberty to import outside labour, and that the men were Willing to sign provided the authorities on their part Would undertake not to introduce additional labour, and • that any such labour now employed should be dismissed. The hon. member complained that he had tbeen refused admission to the Post-office, and said that in view of the forthcoming discussion on the Estimates he should press his claim to view the working of the office.—Mr. J. ROWLANDS complained of the absence of the Post- master General, who must have known that ques- blahs on the subject would be asked.—Mr. JACKSON thought the Postmaster General had reason to complain that questions of this kind should be put without notice. As for himself (Mr. Jackson), he knew nothing whatever 0 the circumstances in question. The House adjourned at ten minutes to six. ROUSE OF LORDS, TILORSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took .his seat at a quarter-past our.

div.head: INSURANCE OF CHILDREN.
div.p: THE INSURANCE OF CHILDREN.
sessi

STARVED TO DEATH FOR A CROWN-PIECE. Evidence quite as remarkable as any that has yet been forthcoming was given on Tuesday before the Children's Life Insurance Bill Committee by two of Her Majesty's Judges. Mr. Justice Wills, who said he spoke not only for himself but for other Judges, said that no one who had sat in criminal courts in Lancashire, Yorkshire, Warwickshire, &c. could doubt that there was in the aggregate a considerable and lamentable amount of neg- lect and cruelty practised towards children. He had tried very many more cases of this kind into which the element of insurance did not enter than cases into which the element of insurance did enter. These cases occurred amongst "the residuum," and there could be no doubt that a great many of them were due to downright, wan- ton cruelty. He had no doubt, after making every Allow- ance which justice and charity suggested, that there was a considerable number of children in this country who were starved to death by parents who could prevent it if they chose. The percentage of people to whom his remarks applied might be very small, but in the aggre- gate the number was very large. In cross-examination he said it would be affectation to doubt that "there was an abundance of parents in this country who would starve their children for a crown-piece.' Mr. Justice Day confirmed the statements of Mr. Justice Wills.

div.p: THE CHESHIRE TINES FESTIVAL

Hesketh Bank was on Saturday the scene of the Cheshire Lines (Great Notthern, Manchester, Sheffield and Lincolnshire, and Midland Railways) 17th annual athletic festival. It may be stated that Hesketh Bank lies on the south shore of the Ribble,, at the mouth of the Douglas, and about halfway:, between Preston and Southport. The Douglas an , the days of battle has run red, but history was com- paratively silent regarding Hesketh Bank until the', West Lancashire Railway Company put a station., there. This railway is peculiar in having stOl refreshment rooms at any of its stations, and at, Heaketh Bank private enterprise has reared a towering hotel, the Becconsall. To fully provide for Saturday's gala day, however, a marquee was erected by the Southport Baths Cafe Company, and there were other tents, all of which seemed to be crowded. From Liverpool 3,500 railway employes and, their friends were stated to have come; from Preston 1,000, Southport. 1,000, Warrington 600, Stockport MO,' and Manchester 500.
