div.head: TUE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 12, 1890
div.p: TUE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 12, 1890

I He was connected with the firm of Messrs. BrDmilow, Foster, and Co., of the Ashton's Green Colliery, St. Helens, and of the Bickerstaffe Collieries, Skelmersdale. He was well known in Liverpool, and was frequently on 'Change, having business relations with several of the large steamship companies, to whom his firm was in the habit of supplying coal. A shrewd business man,he was associated with some large undertakings in the coal trade. He was of genial disposition, and his tragic end has caused a great sensation in commercial circles in Liverpool. Mr. Foster, who was unmarried, has relatives living in the neighbourhood of Waterloo, and for them the greatest sympathy is felt. He was one of the con- gregation worshipping in Rainford Parish Church, and attended Divine Service no later than Sunday evening.

RUMOURED CAUSE OF THE MURDER. The terrible murder seems to have been most cold- blooded and planned. It was the cause of considerable speculation in the surrounding country, and many theories have been advanced as to the motive for the crime. The female prisoner, while engaged as domestic servant to the deceased gentleman was, if rumour be correct, too intimately acquainted a.v t 1-1 him, and this circumstance is supposed to be the original cause of the terrible affair. The• couple, according to all accounts, went to Rainford on Sunday night with the specific pur- pose of shooting Mr. Foster, and this purpose they car- ried into execution with the result so well known. Up to Thursday morning the missing revolver' or revolvers, with which the deed was committed, had not been found, but bullets of two sizes had been picked up in the road near the scene of the murder, and these corres- ponded with cartridges found in the home of the pri- soners at Prescot.

bleeding from his right temple and his left hand. An alarm was then given. He.could not identify the man and woman.—John Grace, farmer, Rainford Junction, gave similar evidence. He assisted to take Mr. Foster to the railway station, where he was placed in the wait- ingroom.—Alfred Pennington, Muncaster Hall, said he was driving in his trap on Monday morning, and passed Mr. Foster walking on the road towards Rainford Junc- tion Station.—Thomas Seddon Pennington, of Muncaster Hall, brother of last witness, deposed that he saw the two prisoners running away from the direction of Rain- ford Junction. He was in the road, and they passed him. On hearing of the occurrence to Mr. Foster he in- formed Police-sergeant Smith, and they started in pursuit. —Ellen Wright, married woman, and Edward Davies, collier, spoke to finding two bullets, each of two sizes, near the scene of the tragedy.—Dr.Murdoch, of Rainford, gave medical evidence as to the injuries received by de- I ceased on the left temple, right shoulder' left hand, and left groin. They were wounds caused by bullets. He found a bullet (produced) in deceased's brain. That was the cause of death. Deceased had carried an overcoat, and this was cut and torn by a bullet which was found in the lining.—Superintendent Barker here submitted two boxes of cartridges, of two sizes, which he said were found in prisoners' house at Prescot. FULL CONFESSION. Sergeant Smith (stationed at Rainford), said prisoners were apprehended at Eccleston-lane-ends, near Prescot. They both denied having had revolvers, and when form- ally charged with the offence neither made any reply. On Tuesday morning the female prisoner said she wished to make a voluntary statement. She was cautioned that it might be used in evidence against her, but she made a statement, which was taken down in writing, read over to her, •Inct she signed it as correct. It was as follows : "Of my own free will 1 make this statement. On Sun- day last, the 6th inst., my husband threatened to shoot me if I did not go to Rainford to shoot Mr. Foster. I said I would. My husband has been jealous of him ever since we were married. We went together to Rainford. I went to Mr. Foster's house, but Mr. Foster was not in, and then we waited till morning. Then we met him by Rainford Junction, and my husband fired first, and then he made me fire after. We took the revolvers with us. We had each one. My husband fired five or six times. I only fired once. I fired the last shot." Wit- ness, continuing, said he found the boxes of cartridges produced at the house of prisoners. "WILFUL MURDER."

The prisoners had no questions to ask any of the wit- nesses, and did not wish to make any statement. The Coroner, in summing up, said that he was sure the jury would join with him in an expression of sympathy and condolence with the family of the deceased. He hoped that the jury would not allow any feeling against the prisoners to influence them in their verdict,but that they would be guided purely by the facts as presented in evid- ence. The statement of the female prisoner was not legally evidence against her husband, but against herself. It was for them to say whether the prisoners were guilty of murder with malice aforethought. The juryreturned a verdict of' Wilful murder" against both prisoners, who were committed for trial at the Liverpool Assizes. THE PRISONERS AT EARLESTOWN. At the inquest on Wednesday night, Mrs. Morris, landlady of the Old Saddle Inn deposed that in course of conversation with her the male prisoner stated that they were on their way back to Earlestown. It ap- peared from inquiries made by our reporter next day, that the two prisoners occasionally visited Earlestown, where a married brother of the male prisoner lives with his family and is employed by Mr. John Axon, boot and shoe maker. The prisoner's brother is named Elias Pickavance, and resides in Duke-st. Yesterday after- noon he was away at Prescot, having left .his work in order to see, if possible, his unfortunate brother John, who, with his wife, lies under the Coroner's committal for wilful murder. Mrs. Pickavance stated to our reporter that her brother-in-law was a frequent visitor at their house, and on three or four occasions he had been accompanied by his wife. The last time the male prisoner was at Earlestown was about a month ago. Asked if she and her husband were expecting the com- mitted coupled on Sunday or Monday last, she replied that they were not, but had since been informed by some relatives at Prescot that the prisoners had informed them they were going to Earlestown. She saw the two pri- soners the last time about a fortnight ago when she and they were at a funeral of a brother-in-law at Bolton. In reply to a question as to whether.she had ever suspected or noticed anything like jealousy on the part of the male prisoner she said he did not appear to have had the least jealousy. They had always seemed to be a perfectly happy, and comfortable couple. She was very friendly and intimate with the female prisoner,and the latter had never mentioned a word to her about her husband's jealously. She thought the female prisoner would have done so had there been any jealousy. About five weeks ago she and her husband were over at Prescot on a visit to the two prisoners. The two prisoners accompanied them on the return journey as far as St. Helens. On the road the two brothers walked in front and their wives followed a few yards behind. w They talked over family and domestic affairs but the female prisoner never once mentioned or suggested that her husband was jealous, or that he ill-treated her. The female prisoner had also given her to understand that she was happy and conten- ted. She had certainly never mentioned anything about Mr. Foster nor about Rainford. In the visits of the pri- soners to Earlestown, or whenever they had been in their company, the male prisoner had never once complained about his wife ln any shape or form. The male prisoner, she thought, always seemed reticent in regard to such matters and, she added, "he was always close-fisted." The first intimation she and her husband had of the , shooting affair was by reading of it in the evening papers. She had lately noticed that something had been preying

div.head: TERRIBLE HIGHWAY MURDER NEAR
div.p: TERRIBLE HIGHWAY MURDER NEAR
ST. HELENS.

A COLLIERY PROPRIETOR SHOT. There was a great sensation on Monday morning in the district of which Rainford (near St. Helens) is the centre, when it became known that Mr. Henry Grainger Foster, a well-known independent gentleman and col- liery proprietor, had been shot several times whilst walking al.ng the road, within a short distance of his own residence, and in broad daylight. The news spread with remarkable rapidity, and soon the residents of the district for many miles around were thrown into a state of the keenest excitement. The details of the occur- rence show that the affair was one of the most cold blooded attempts to take the life of a human being that could possibly be conceived, and the sensational circum- stances by which the affair is surrounded, . with the interesting relationships between the chief actors in the terrible tragedy, accord to it an importance which will probably make it rank as one of the most notable crimes of modern times.

div.head: DEED COMMITTED.
div.p: THE DEED COMMITTED.

Mr. Foster, who resided at Brook Lodge House, about midway beteen Rainford and Rainford Junction railway stations, left home about 8.40 in the morning and walked along the road in the direction of Rainford Junction/ station, where it was his intention to catch the 9-5 a.m. train to Liverpool. About midway between his house 1 and the station he was met by a man and woman. The residents of a farmhouse in the vicinity heard three or four shots, and on a farmer named Grace looking in the direction from whence the sounds proceeded, he saw two men struggling in the road, and a woman standing a few yards away. One of the men and the woman then made off, and the other man appeared to stagger in the road and fell to the ground. Grace and other persons went to the spot, and found Mr. Foster with serious in- juries to his head, back, groin, and hand. He was assisted to the railway station, and was shortly after- wards driven to his home. Medical aid was at once sought, and Dr. Murdock, of Rainford, was the first in attendance, while Dr. R. Parker, of Liverpool, was tele- graphed for. The injured man's condition grew most serious, and about an hour after the affair he became un- conscious. From the very first there seemed no hope of the injured gentleman's recovery. He bad lost a quant- ity of blood; at least two bullets were embedded in his temple and back, and after being removed home he lingered between life and death until nine o'clock in the evening, when he quietly expired. Drs. Murdock and Parker had beenin constant attendance, but their skill was unavailing.

AITAMMENSION OF A MAN AND HIS WIFE. The police were early acquaihted with the shooting affair. With commendable promptitude they took steps to secure the man and woman isklio had disappeared, and the various roads in the district were scoured by the local officers and others whose assistance was sought. Police Sergeant Smith and Constable Carter stopped a butcher's cart which was passing along the road, entered it, and, followed by a friend of the wounded man, upon horseback, went in the direction of Billinge. It soon appeared that the man and woman they were in search of had net gone that way, and they returned and took the Premot-rd. In afew minutes it was found that they were on the right scent. The man and woman had called at a public-house onthe way for a drink of water, and their description was given to the officers in pursuit. At Eccleston Church there were further traces of them, and finally they were overtaken at a place where several reads met, called Eccleston-lane ends, near Prascot. Whilst the couple were about a hundred yards in front they turned round, and seeing the officers in pursuit, ran down a 'back passage and made an effort to escape across the fields. The officers jumped onto! the trap and followed. The woman was first caught, and the hus- band, as he afterwards proved to be, seeing escape hope- less, stopped. He then said, "Oh, I'll give myself up; if I had had another hundred yards start you would not have caught me to-day." Both denied having had re- volvers, and the husband told his wife not to answer any questions. In the male prisoner's possession were hymn- books and papers relating to the Salvation Army, and his rnenibership card for a local Rechabites' lodge. The prisoners were identified as John Duckworth Pickavance, a cobbler and clogger, of 5, Houghton-st., Prescot, and his wife, Mary Jane. Pickavance is the son of Elias Pickavance, now dead, who was himself a shoemaker at the same hoase. Mrs. Pickavance. his mother, is still alive. The prisoner is a sallow complexioned man of medium height and square build • and 28 years of age. The family have hitherto been well respected in Present, but latterly Pickavance has been known to have pecu- lar ways. and his remarks to neighbours have been some- what extraordinary. His wife was, before marriage, named Hutchins, and is the daughter of a blacksmith, at Tarbuck. She was for some time a domestic servant with Mr. Foster, at Hyde Brow. She is 23 years of age, ,of good figure, and prepossessing appearance. After hiaving the service of Mr. Foster last October she went to live at Tarbuck, on the other side of Present. Here she seems to have met Pickavance, and they were. mar- ried last March, at Liverpool. Since then they have lived at the male prisoner's house in Houghton-st. Pres- cot. Small crowds of men and women were on Monday and Tuesday to be seen in the vicinity discussing the -strange event. Pickavance and his wife have bees on hood terms since their marriage, and the man has at- -tended to his work, notwithstanding rumours as to his mental condition. On Sunday afternoon they went to a "camp" meeting in cohnection with the Zion Chapel, .and they had dinner and tea togethemat their home. But in the evening they went away and locked their house up.
THE DECEASED GENTLEMAN. The deceased an was extremely well known.

div.head: MAGISTERIAL PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: MAGISTERIAL PROCEEDINGS.

At the PreseotPolice Court, early on Tuesday morn- ing, Pickavance and his wife were brought before Col. W. W. Pilkington and charged with the wilful murder of Henry Grainger Foster. Superintendent Barker said : These two prisoners, your worship, are charged with the wilful murder of Henry Grainger Forster, by shooting him with a revolver' yesterday morning. They way- laid him on his way to the station, and deliberately shot him, and he died last night. I must ask for a remand until the inquest has been held. The magistrate kto pri- soners).—You will be remanded till after the inquest. The prisoners were then removed. The male prisoner seemed a little nervous, but his wife seemed altogether indifferent, and wore a smile during the proceedings. Neither of the prisoners knew of the fatal result till charged with the murder. INQUEST AND VERDICT.

_ The interest which centred in the terrible shooting affair increased almost hourly. This was especially the case in the Rainford district, where trade and the ordin- ary daily avocations were temporarily paralysed by reason of the keen excitement which the unparalleled tragedy, as affecting the neighbourhood, had aroused. Pending the coroner's inquest and the succeeding magis- terial inquiry, the wildest rumours were afloat. The scene of the murder was visited by thousands of persons, and, on Wednesday night, a great crowd of villagers and people from a distance assembled in the village with the view of having a glimpse at the two prisoners. They were expected, and subsequently did attend the coroners inquest which was held to inquire into the cir- cumstances of the death. The remains of the late Mr. Foster were interred in Bickerstaffe Churchyard, on Thursday at noon. The inquest was held at the Muncaster Inn, ttainford village, on Wednesday night, before Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner for South-west Lancashire, and a jury of ,15 gentlemen, of whom Mr. B. Smith, surveyor and clerk to Rainford Local Board, was the foreman. Some hundreds of persons awaited the arrival of the two prisoners, who were driven from Prescot Police Station in a closed cab. They were in charge of Police-Superintendent Barker, Police-Sergeant Knott, and other officers. Immediately on stepping from the cab the female prisoner burst into tears and cried bitterly. She had to be assisted upstairs. Her husband wore a stern and determined look. They were both present during the proceedings. Superinten- dent Barker conducted the inquiry on behalf of the police authorities; Mr. Sear, barrister, instructed by Messrs. Oliver Jones, 13illson, Jones, and Madge, appeared on be- half of the relatives of the deceased. The Coroner in- formed the jury that the deceased gentleman had met with fatal injuries on the road near Rainford Junction Station, and it was for them to say if the two *prisoners were responsible for it.

div.head: SUSPICIOUS ENCIITI2IES.
div.p: THE SUSPICIOUS ENCIITI2IES.

- - Mrs. Ann Frood, wife of Colonel Frood, said she was the sister of the deceased, who was 35 years of age.— Alice Leigh, a housekeeper at Brook Lodge House, said on Sunday night the female prisoner knocked at the door of Mr. Foster's house. Witness answered the knock. The prisoner asked if Mr. Foster was in and she replied that he was not at home. She asked if he would be at home that night, and witness said he would be in about nine o'clock. The woman then went away, and she was accompanied by a man whom witness could not identify. Jane Morris, wife of Henry Morris, landlord of the Old Saddle Beernouse, Rainford, saidthe prisoners stayed at tier house all night on Sunday. Next morning she had some conversation with the prisoners. The male pri- soner said they had both come on one business, and would" do it before they went away." He added that they might never be through Rainford again. --------

div.head: THB FATAL STRAIGOLE.
div.p: THB FATAL STRAIGOLE.
QUEEN CHARLOTTE'S

John Wood, fireman at Rainford Colliery, said he was going to his work about nineeclock on Monday morning. When near Rainford Junction Station he heard shots in the road. He looked in that direction and saw two men and a woman. One of the men threw up his hands, and the other man and the woman then ran away. He ran, to the spot, and found the deceased lying on his back,

on the male prisoner's mind, and she had heard that it appeared as if he was being driven out of his mind. She had also heard that the male prisoner had said he was getting tired of his life and that he did not care whether he lived or died. She had also heard of the alleged intimacy between the female prisoner and Mr. Foster, but it was only what relatives and friends at Present stated.—Mr. Jahn Axon, lAoot and shoe dealer, Queen-st., Earlestown, who is the employer of Elias Pickavance, brother of the male prisoner, said the latter had several times visited his workroom to see his brother. The male prisoner seemed to be rather strange in his conversation and manner, though he was very sharp on some points. The prisoner's brother was at work with the other hands when the news of the shooting affair was received, and, though greatly surprised, he made a remark to the effect that he had always said their "Jack " would be hanged. Mr. Axon described the brothers (both shoemakers) as good workmen. FUNERAL OF THE VICTIM. The remains of Mr. Forster were interred on Thursday in the churchyard attached to Bickerstaffe Parish Church. The funeral cortege left the residence of the deceased, Brook Lodge, about ludf-past eleven. The departure was witnessed by a large number of the inhabitants of Rainford village. The coffin was borne from the house to the hearse by four employes of the deceased, and it was covered with a number of beautiful wreaths sent by relatives and friends There were six carriages in addition to the hearse, and they contained relatives and friends. The blinds of the great majority of the houses in Rainford were drawn down as the cortege passed along. The funeral was ac- companied from Rain ford by a large number of villagers, and at the Bickerstaffe Church there were other sym- pathisers waiting. The service which was semi-choral, WAS conducted by the Rev. W. Wall, vicar of Bickerstaffe. The coffin bore the inscription—" Henry Granger Foster. Born May 2, 1885, Died July?, 1890."

THE GRENADIER GUARDS REFUSE TO TURN OUT. An extraordinary scene occurred at the Wellington Barracks on Monday, the Second Battalion Grenadier Guards locking themselves in their rooms and refusing to come out when the bugle sounded to fall-in for a kit in- spection which had been ordered. The inspection was abandoned, and on Colonel Maitland addressing his men there was much hooting and hissing. An inquiry held at the War Office on Tuesday showed that the disaffected men had ground for complaint, owing to excessiveduties and the release of those confined to barracks was ordered.
EXTRAORDINARY USE OF A FORTUNE.

It was on Tuesday announced that Mr. John Hope, writer to the Signet, Edinburgh, has executed a trust deed, conveying a large portion of his means and estate, amounting to £84,459, to trustees, of which he is himself to be one, for advancing the cause of total abstinence at home and abroad from liquor, tobacco, and opium, and disseminating a knowledge of the anti-Scriptural char- acter of the Church of Rome.

div.head: LORD HARTINGTON AND IRISH. LAND
div.p: LORD HARTINGTON AND IRISH. LAND
PURCHASE.

Lord Hartington, writing on Wednesday to the Chair- man of the Bradford Liberal Unionist Association, says he has received a copy of the resolution recently passed by that body calling upon the Government to hold an autumn session in order to pass the Irish Land Purchase Bill. He entirely shares the opinion therein expressed of the paramount importance of passing the measure, and has no doubt the Government intend to use every effort to pas a it into law with the least possible delay.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE_ AND ,WELSEL DISES-
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE_ AND ,WELSEL DISES-
TABLISHMEN T.

Mr. Gladstone, writing to Mr. Gee, chairman of the Denbighshire County Council, on the subject of disestab- lishment in Wales, says that on the question of priority in time, as compared with Scotland, the inference to be drawn from his private conversation on the subject at Hawarden is that is impossible to determine any ques- tion of priority between them, nor yet among the various measures to which the Liberal party is pledged, for the sake not only of Scotland but also of Wales. He depre- cates any discussion, which would be premature and Injurious to both. The suggestion that by undertaking the Welsh question himself he would assist in surmount- ing the difficulties of the case he cannot accept, as he has gone a great length in undertaking to deal,even con- tingently, if his health is preserved with the Irish question.

div.head: AFRICAN ARRANGEMENT CON DEMNED BY MERCHANTS.
div.p: THE AFRICAN ARRANGEMENT CON DEMNED BY MERCHANTS.

--- A deputation of African merchants and others, headed by Sir Donald Currie, M.P., waited on Lord Salisbury at the Foreign Office on Tuesday for the purpose of laying before him their views as to the pending arrangements between Germany and England with regard to South Africa. With one accord the members of the deputation denounced the proposed arrangement, declaring that the extension of German influence would be injurious to the interests of the colony, and would stand in the way of that which the colonists so much desire, a united South. Africa. Lord Salisbury in his reply stated that the Government was not responsible for the presence of the Germans in South-west Africa, as they were there when the Government took office. He did not admit that the colonists' interests had suffered by what had just taken place, but said he eould not discuss the matter at length until it had been before the Houses of Parlia- ment.

div.head: POLICE AND PROCESSIONS IN
div.p: THE POLICE AND PROCESSIONS IN
/ LONDON.

The demonstration organised by the Right of Public Speech Committee was held on Saturday evening. Large crowds assembled at the starting point on Clerken- well Green at 4 p.m. Mr. William Saunders, an hour later, presided over a meeting on the Green, which was addressed by Mr. Conybeare, M.P. who said he was quite prepared to march with the meeting, as he was to Derry Gaol twelve months ago. Shortly before six o'clock a procession was formed and marched to Hyde Park, there being no interference on the part of the police. Three platforms had been erected in the park. Mr. Saunders, who presided at the chief platform, denounced the tryannical action of the late Chief Com- missioner of Police in prohibiting processions in the streets of London. They had now marched through the streets in processional order, which only a month ago were closed against them. Resolutions were adopted protesting against arbitrary attempts by any Govern- ment to infringe the rights of the people, and declaring a determination to resist an such attempts at all hazards. The meeting dispersed quietly.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT TO MR. F. BROOKS CLOSE.
div.p: THE FATAL ACCIDENT TO MR. F. BROOKS CLOSE.

Several weeks ago Mr. Frederick Brooks Close, a nephew of Sir William Cunliffe Brooks, M.P., was killed during a game of polo in Sioux City, United States. The " Sioux City Journal" of June 14 gives the following account of the unhappy accident : The polo game between Le Mars and Sioux City came to a disastrous end yesterday in an accident that resulted in the death of Fred Brooks Close. Close entered the game with his left arm in a sling, not having recovered fully from the effects of a fall while fox hunting in England last fall, and to that fact was probably due the fatal result of yesterday's game. Notwithstanding his reckless daring, Close was a splendid horseman, and had he had full use of his arm he might haveavoided the collison that caused him to be thrown anti crushed between the two falling horses. Ile Sioux City team had scored three goals,and Close wat congratulating his boys on their •excellent playing. Jack Watson, of the Le Mars tearn,was making a splendid run down the field when, for some unaccount- able reason, Close attempted to cross in front of him.and to the spectators it was evident that the two would can- non. An instant before the horses collided Fred was seen to sway in his saddle, and when the crash came he was already unseated. Watson's horsestruck Close's and the latter was thrown, and falling upon its rider' rolled clear over him. Then, as the horse struggled to regain his feet, Watson's horse fell over him, and he also rolled across the body of poor Close. Watson was thrown over his horse's head and escaped injury. Close never moved a muscle, and lay as one dead. A number of his friends rushed to his assistance, but he manifestedno sign of life. A young Norwegian physician who happened to be on the ground came to their assistance, and succeeded finally in restoriag circulation, but was unable to bring the unfortunate man back to consciousness. The immedi- ate cause of death was internal hemorrhage caused by the injuries to the chest. Among other projects which Close had formed was the organisation of the Freeland' Mortgage Company, representing above 3,000,000 dols. of English capital, which would have been incorporated under the law of lawa within a few days. But it is not the man of business that his friends will mourn, but rather the whole souled, enthusiastic, and sympathetic man. His young wife was on the grounds, but was not allowed to go near the tent. She refused to leave the ground, and her friends did all they could for her com- fort in the club-house."

div.head: MURDERER'S CONFESSION.
div.p: A MURDERER'S CONFESSION.

Thomas Byrne, the painter who has been eommitted for trial charged with the wilful murder by shooting of Elizabeth Grundy, at Greystones, county Wicklow, has made a written confession of his guilt. He says that the motive of his crima was jealousy, and that the girl and he were for some time acknowledged lovers. She, how- ever, showed preference for another, which so exasper- ated him that he was driven to taking her life.

TEN YEARS' PENAL SERVITUDE FOR MANSLAUGHTER. , At Cambridge Assizes, on Tuesday, William John ' Warren, alias Styles, aged 21, tanner, of Maidstone, was , indicted for the murder of Mrs. Elizabeth Barber, an elderly widow, at Bentinck-st., Cambridge, with whom he lodged. Prisoner whilst in goal wrote a circumstan- tial account of what occurred. He admitted having stolen Mrs. Barber's watch, and fearing detection when Mrs. Barber went upstairs, he dragged her down with the intention of gagging her. They both fell, and Mrs. Barber's head came in contact with a fender, causing her death. The jury returned a verdict of manslaughter, and prisoner was sentenced to ten years' penal servi- tude.

div.head: MURDER OF THREE CHILDREN
div.p: THE MURDER OF THREE CHILDREN

AT LIVERPOOL Tho adjourned inquest on the bodies of William Robert Charlton, Dorothy Bennett Charlton, and Barbara Bennett Charlton, children of a Customs clerk named Charles Arthur Charlton, residing at 16, Garmoyle-road, Wavertree, was resumed on Monday. It will be remem- bered that on the Bth of May the mother killed the children by cutting their throats with a razor, and has since been in a critical condition owing to an attempt sho immediately afterwards made on her own life. The jury insisted rather strongly on appending to their ver- dict of" Wilful murder" an expression of opinion that Mrs. Charlton was insane; but eventually, on the re- peated representations of the coroner that they had nothing to do with this, they refrained.

div.head: MR. PARNELL ON IRISPI EMIORATION
div.p: MR. PARNELL ON IRISPI EMIORATION
AND MIGRATION.

Mr. Parnell, in evidence given on Tuesday before the Select Committee of the House of Commons appointed to inquire into the subject of emigration and colonisation, said he did not think that as regards the congested dis- trict of Ireland there was as much immediate necessity for dealing with the condition of the population by emigration or migration as many people imagined. The congested population in the West of Ireland was really needed for the purposes of Ireland at home. It fornied a most valuable labouring population which he would prefer, if possible, to keep at home, as he believed that the resources of Ireland. including the fisheries, could. if properly developed, furnish abundant employment for these people. The money of the State ought to be spent in developing the resources of the country instead of in sending the people away to the colonies.

div.head: THREATENED STRIKE OF LONDON
div.p: THREATENED STRIKE OF LONDON
POSTMEN.

The agitation among London postmen has again reached an alarming crisis. A serious 'disturbance took place on Wednesday morning in the East Central sort- ing-room, and work was suspended for nearly two hours. In the parcel post department at Mount Pleasant there was a still graver development, for the union men turned upon the emergency hands who had been intro- duced, and eventually ejected them from the building. On Wednesday afternoon the postmen attached to the Central East-end office turned out on strike. It is stated on good authority that in the event of a general strike in London, the provincial Post Office employes will also cease work.

Though there was some delay in the delivery of letters in London on Thurday, and in some cases it was found necessary to make special arrangements for handing letters to callers at the district offices, there was no general response to the call made to the men engaged in the postal service to strike. The chief officials of the department had made it understood that they were deter- mined tot to dismiss the supernumeraries at the demand of the union men, and they gave further proof of this yesterday morning by dismissing or suspending all the hands who were deemed to have been guilty of insubordination. Altogether about 220 men were dis- charged. These formed themselves into a procession, which visited the various divisional sorting offices and , called upon the men at work to come out. This move, however, was attended with little success, and the offi- cials on Thursday night stated that the work in the offices was proceeding much as usual.

div.head: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
A TENANT FARMER CANDIDATE.
Mr. W. H. Lander, tenant farmer, Tibberton, was on Tuesday unanimously adopted by the Liberal Council as candidate for the Newport division of Shropshire. THE MID-DURHAM VACANCY.

A meeting of representatives of both sections of the Unionist party was held at Durham on Saturday, when Mr. Adolphus Vane-Tempest was adopted as a candidate for the vacancy created in the Parliamentary represent- ation of Mid-Durham by the death of Mr. W. Crawford. Mr. Gladstone has written to Mr. John Wilson, the Liberal candidate, offering heartiest good wishes for his success, and referring to his special qualifications as a successor in Parliament of the late Mr. Crawford.

SPEECH BY MR. JOHN MORLEY. The two candidates for the representation of Mid- Durham are hard at wurk. The miners of the consti- tuency have repented of their disposition to oppose Mr. Wilson, the Liberal candidate, in whose behalf they are nAw working. Mr. Wilson is also likely to obtain the temperance vote, as he has declared himself in favour of giving the ratepayers power to deal with the issue of licenses and against compensation to publicans. His opponent, Mr. Vane Tempest, tainks sobriety cannot be promoted by Acts of Parliament, and is against Parlia- mentary ihterference with "the trade." Mr. John Morley was the chiet speaker at a great Liberal meeting held in Durham Town Hall on Wednesday night in support Of Mr. Wilson's candidature. He expressed satisfaction that the election was to be fought on the question of Home Rule, and said he hoped Mr. Wilson would be returned by an overwhelming majority. Criticising the doings of the Government. he ridiculed the notion that the present Parliamentary deadlock was in any way due to obstruc- tion, and attributed it to the incompetence, the want of, foresight, and the vacillation of the Governments
TEE THREATENED BTEIRE: OP LONDON' ' POLICE. WHOLESALE DISMISSAL OF CONSTABLES.

The police difficulty in London had serious develop- ments on Saturday, the action of the night duty men at Bow-street causing much excitement. A rumour went round that the constables paraded had in a body refused to turn out, and although they were afterwards found on their 'beats there appears to havd been serious ground for the report which was widely circulated. The parti- cular matter which the men on this occasion complained of was the transfer of one of their numb:ir who had acted as a delegate in their interests to another division. , This movement was regarded in the light of a punish- ment which it was the business of the whole body to resent. Accordingly the men of the night duty sections, or the great majority of them ,declined to leave the station until some explanation had been given, and it is stated that it was only after considerable delay, and after a promise had been made by the superintendent to do all in his power to get the transferred officer recalled that the constables were induced to go on duty. The disaffection among the police increased in intens- ity throughout Monday, and in the evening had assumed a serious phase. The dismissal of nearly forty men dur- ing the day for participating in Saturday night's demon- stration Ead intensified the feeling of discontent. In anticipation of the strike which appeared inevitable, the authorities were busily engaged in enrolling new hands. These, who for the greater part were youths, have been provided with spare uniforms ; and it is stated that in consequence of the doubtful attitude of the troops in London, orders had been sent to the provinces for the military to be held in readiness.

Therei was n'o fuither---deiriOn-s-ti:a—tiOn by the London police n the morning or afternoon of Tuesday at any of the headquarters or divisions, but at night a renewal of the disturbances in Bow-st. and the neighbourhood oC- curred, although elaborate precautions had been taken to prevent disorder. In the afternoon a meeting of the men was held, at which it was evident that there was no organisation Among the men, and that the leaders of the agitation were acting without any definite plan. The meeting was in favour of a petition being forwarded to the Home Secretary and the Chief Commissioner. askiag for the re-instatement of the dismissed constables, and a good deal of recrimination was indulged in, hitter com- plaints being made that the men in several districts had failed to support the action taken in the E division.

• of those who serve under him, as so many of his predecessors have done, has contrived to make himself generally detested. Ho treats postmen as though they were his personal slaves. They

• are not to hold meetings, except by his high per- mission, and in presence of a reporter in his ser- vice. He assumes to control their actions when they are off duty; and punishes in the spirit of a tyrant those who dare to show a spark of independence in stating their grievances and defending their rights. Can it be wondered at, then, that the whole service is in a state of revolt? The Tories, on a celebrated occasion, jeered at Mr. GLADSTONE for referring to is fellow- countrymen as " our own flesh and blood " ; they Would have nothing to do with appeals on the ground of conimon humanity. That was a feature of Toryism then, and it is the feature which is Prominent in the Toryism which rules in high Places to-day. But there is a good deal of human nature in men—be they Irish peasants, English • Postmen, or Metropolitan policemen; and it is part of human nature to rebel against conduct which is tyrannical and unjust. Coercion never succeeded as a permanent policy, and it never will. It is a failure in Ireland; it has failed at the Post Office; and it fails with the Police. And what is the remedy ? • The remedy is to got rid of the Goer- eionist Government—the Government of Failures.
JEALOUSY and the madness which Rainford comes of jealousy would appear to Tragedy constitute the motive of the terrible
ras which was comrnitted near Rainfor'd Junction, _ _

•''°ll Monday night, in the murder of Mr. FOSTER, "of Brook Lodge, Rainford. Two persons—named and Mrs. PICKAVANCE—have been committed by a coroner's jury on a charge of wilful murder; 441.... d) assuming the truth of the confession made by 4111. PICKAVANCE, there is revelation of hatred and I,t desire for revenge on the part of the jealous ausband which has few parallels in fact or fiction. If) as stated, PICICAVANCH put it to his wife to kurder Mr. FOSTER, or be murdered herself, there is evidence of such "method in madness" as is— haPpily for the safety of society—an altogether IWlcernmon thing. That the murder was coolly Planned is shown by the prisoners staying all night 14. Bain' ford, in order that they might next morn- kg be in waiting for their victim. They slept 'oh the project, but that was not to alter it in the least, for it is affirmed that the husband fired five six shots, whilst the woman—held to her horrible 134gagement—fired once, and that was the last shot. Ilse confession, as the Coroner pointed out, was tldence only against the woman who made it— the wife not being permitted in such a case to give evidence against, her husband. But 4,the statement so fits in with other evidence, it will be strange, indeed, if both •Prisoners are not found guilty at the Assiz es. With regard to the deadly and consuming 7,_atred which PIOKAVANCE entertained towards mr. FOSTER, rumour has it that it had its origin in statements which had reaclied him of the 'deceased gentleman having been intimate with his Wife before her marriage. But jealousy sometimes laakes the meat it feeds on, and it may have been in this case. The murder, whatever the motive, Was undoubtedly deliberate and cold-blooded; and 4 is natural that it should have caused the utmost

He has come to see that what he VoB that "broken-down failure "—the present vernment, will never settle the Irish question, and he is right. Other Liberal Unionists will do Well to follow his example. "Come over and help us" St. Helens has furnished sundry patients for M. aateur. The Government have done one good thing; they have made a grant of £l5O to Mr. Ben Brierley, who is in ill health and necessitous cir- cumstances. The creator of " Ab-oth' -Yate " and the author of innumerable Lancashire tales and sketches, deserves the sympathy and help of the community. He has not only been a hard worker but a prudent one. A bad investment, however, ran away with what had been put by for a rainy day ; and he has since, like the brave man that he is, set to work again. He has given his country so much that the country may well give something in return.

The Publication Committee of the Society for the Promotion of Christian Knowledge have caught a Tartar. They have issued a report in which they invite suggestions as to their methods of work; and Mr. Walter Besant, the novelist, has responded with a pamphlet in which he accuses the Committee of being literary "sweaters." He re- fers to cases in which authors have been paid by the Committee about one-sixth of the profits made. This is a serious charge to make. "The labourer is worthy of his hire." There ought to be no divorce between Christian morality and "Christian Knowledge."

Our chief Lancashire watering places have faith in town improvements. The Marine Park, at Southport, has proved such a great attraction, and has, moreover, paid so well, that it has been decided to construct another and a larger. Marine Park on the other side of the pier. Blackpool has under consideration a scheme for dealing with the cliff walks, on the North Shore, in front of Claremont Park. It is proposed to make the cliffs safe froml the incursions of the sea, and provide a series of promenades one above the other. It is estimated that the cost of the scheme will exceed £70,000. But what of that? It will pay in the long run.

Seven per cent., that is 40,000, of the signatures to the monstre petition in favour of the Compen- sation Bill were, it has been ascertained, in the hand-writing of one person. It must have been very convenient to have such a ready writer at hand. There were odd doings at Warrington. We can vouch for a little scene as follows :—Tap-room where petition is lying for signature. Enter Man from the Street: I say, landlord, does it matter if I sign your sheet P I've signed at three other places."—Landlord: "All right, sign away." And he did sign. It is not stated how many gills he got for signing; but he has not yet "signed tee- total."

It appears from the analysis that the mussels which proved fatal to the family of Mr. John O'Connor, editor of "United Ireland," had devel- oped a special kind of poison through their impreg- nation with sewage. It is no uncommon thing for people who are staying at the sea-side to gather mussels or cockles; but it will be seen that if the fish are eaten the pastime becomes a most danger- ous one. What is called mussel-sting is in all probability a speqies of poisoning. The best thing is to leave mussels alone. Stich a terrible tragedy as that which occurred in Ireland ought to act as an interdict to this particular bivalve as an article of food. It is stated that £2O are being given for c‘dpies of the edition de luxe of Stanley's bnok, which was published at ten guineas. The craze is the craze of a season. There is evidently more money than wit among the Stanley worshippers. Next year the idol will be something or somebody else. When Salvini first came to London, he was the rage as an actor, and the theatre was crowded every night. He came again; but Society had in the meantime taken to another lion, and Salvini had to play to empty houses. This year Stanley is having his turn as the African "lion,' and he does well to make hay while the sun shines. It may not shine for him next season.

WIDNESIAWS AT CRYSTAL PALACE.

In the gr;ntiteinper-ance-fete, which took place at Crystal Palace on Tuesday, 50 Widnesians formed part of the choir of 5,000 voices. The Widnes contingent had rehearsed the music sung under the conductorship of Mr. G. W. Williams, to whom they had given every satisfaction.

TRE RUNCORN CORONER AND His COURT. At the conclusion of an inquest at Runcern, on Tues- day, Mr. Worsley, the Coroner, said the County Council had sent out a recommendation that in all cases where it was possible, inquests should be held in police courts instead of in public-houses. This recommendation, how- ever, did not apply to mortuaries whrre there was con- venience for holding inquests. Therefore, in future, in Runcorn, when the body was not lying at the Police Station, he should hold the inquest in the court-room.

JOINERS' WAGES AT WIDNES. The master builders and joiners of Widnes have de- cided to grant the joiners in the building trade an in- crease of one halfpenny per hour. The advance; how- ever, is subject to the condition that no workman shall undertake any private work after having done a day's work for his master. The representatives Qf the Amalga- mated Society of joiners and carpenters readily accepted this condition. Any workman committing a bteach of the agreement will render himself liable to instant dis- missal. _ . - _

THE INCORPORATION OF WIDNES.

The members of Widnes branch of the Irish National League spent several hours on Sunday afternoon at St. Paul's Chambers, discussing the advisability of obtaining a charter of incorporation for the town. In the end a resolution was passed in favour of such a course, and it was ordered to be forwarded to the chairman of the Local Board. Steps were also taken for presenting a requisition to that gentleman, praying him to call a public meeting in order to ascertain the feelings of the ratepayers ou: the questionv

At Widnes Potty Sessions, on Thursday, James Ince, Halewood, and John Farley, of Ditton,were charged with breaking into a hut and stealing one cwt. of lead and 401bs. of indiarubber, value £l, the property of Mark Smith. On the morning of the 9th inst. it was found that the hut had been broken into,and the lead and india- rubber removed. • GIRLS' FRIENDLY SOCIETY, nIiNCORN. About 140 members of the Girls' Friendly Society spent an enjoyable day at Halton and Norton Priory on Thurs- day. Proceedings commenced at three o'clock by a service in Halton Parish Church. the preacher being the Rev. S. Wilkinson,vic.ar of St. Paul's, Warrington. After- wards tea was proyided in the schoolroom.; and then the members were driven over to Norton Priory, where they spent a pleasant evening in the grounds. The Runcorn contingent were conveyed to and fro in waggonettes supplied by Messrs. Yarwood Brothers. SUMMER SALE now on at J. & W. Durrox's Sankey-at., Warrington.—Adet. TRIP Fnom Dtrrvon WORKHOUSE. The children of Dutton Workhouse had their third an- nual trip to the seaside on Wednesday last. Ample funds had been obtained froth the ex-officio Guardians, by Mr. Cunnali, the master, and the children, numbering 50, were conveyed in a specially reserved carriage to Llandudno. which was reached about noon. The party immediately sat down to a capital dinner in the Coffee and Cocoa Rooms, and afterwards the afternoon was spent on the beach in donkey riding, boating, bathing, &c. At four o'clock tea was provided, and their appe- tites sharpened by the pure air, the youngsters did ample justice to the good things provided. The return journey was commenced at 5p.m., and Sutton Weaver was reached at half-past eight. The children were accompanied by Mr. and Mrs. Cunnah (master and matron), Mrs. John J. Nuttall, (schoolmistress)., Mr. R. Naylor (schoolmaster), the Rev. J. D. Lyon Bennett, chaplain, Mrs. Bennett, and niece, and Dr. Robinson, medical officer. The arrangements had been admirably made by the master and matron, and thanks are due to Mr. Shaw, of Lime-st., for the exceptional railway facili- ties afforded to the excursionists. Messrs. Beecham, of St. Helens, the well-known pill manufacturers, gave their employes their annual treat on Saturday, when the day was spent at Blackpool. The company numbered about 100. including Mr.. W. Moss (manager), the office staff and the managers of the respective departments, and they journeyed from St. Helens by the 6.40 a.m. train. On Saturday evening Mr. Brunner, M.P., ad- dressed a large meeting of Temperance Socie- ties at. Northwich. He spoke in favour of local option, and referred with pleasure to the change that had taken place of late years in the popular feeling on the temperance question. Adverting to the large number of limited companies that had been floated to work breweriesi he remarked that a great many who had bought shares in breweries ha,l had cause to regret it. He counselled them never to buy from a rich man at his own price without careful enquiry. F.specially he asked them, not only for financial reasons, but for the sake of conscience, not to put any money in breweries, and declared that he would not take a dividend from a brewery company if it were to keep him out of the work- house. He felt convinced that no Government would remain in power for many years that did not propose remedial temperance legislation. BUMMER SALE ROW OD at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-4., Warrington.--Advt. THE REV. G. S. AND MRS. REANEY. In drawing attention to a series of services under- taken by Mrs. Reaney in the Theatre Royal. Black- pool, the "National Advance" says —" For the opportunities afforded by these services the visitors and townspeople of Blackpool have to thank the delicate health of Mrs. Reaney's youngest boy. It is owing to this circumstance, being under medical orders to remain at Blackpool that he may get the benefit of the sea air, that Mrs Reaney has been compelled for a few weeks to postpone removal to the scene of Mr. Reaney's curacy in Kent. We are in a position to offer an emphatic contradiction to the suggestion that in seceding to the Church of England Mr. Reaney was in any way influenced by the fact that Mrs. Keeney had never relinquished her membership with the Establishment, which dates back to her girlhood. Few, indeed, were T aware of the fact of such membership, for in MI chapel with which she has been associated she has worked as loyally and devotedly as any other minister's wife in the Kingdom.r IRON BEDSTEADS tt BEDDING.—GArIaIId. 51, Bridge-it., Warrington. PROPOSED GREAT ALKALI UN/ON. Referring to an announcement made the other day, the "Pall Mall Gazette" says :—NegotiationiS are proceeding for the combination of all the alkali works of the kingdom, which, if effected, will sur- pass anything of the kind hitherto attempted in this country. The Salt Union was floated with a capital of £4,000.000. but in the case of the alkali works £8,000,000 to £9,000,000 is the figure men- tioned. There are over 100 works in England. the largest groups being in East Lancashire and York- shire, Widnes, and the North of England. The products are caustic soda, bleaching powder, and chlorate potash. The amount of salt consumed last year in the manufacture of alkali amounted to no less than 800,000 tons. The industry at present is in a transition stage, the old or Leblanc process being gradually superseded by the ammonia-soda process, and a number of works have been closed in conse- quence. This circumstance has, of course, a direct bearing upon the ;value of the properties, for only a very few in number, although the most important in degree, have adopted the new method of manu- facture. It is said that the owners will be expected to accept a third of the purchase price in shares, so , that the capital which the public may be asked to subscribe is from five to six millions. The alkali manufacturers have had the success of the Salt ,Union impressed upon them' by the higher prices which that combination have been enabled to secure for their salt, that being the raw material of the I soda makers, and so they are in a mood to listen to the proposals which have been made to them by the financiers. If the negotiations are successful, the prospectus may be looked for in the autumn.

div.head: DR. PRESTON AND CARDINAL MANNING.
div.p: DR. PRESTON AND CARDINAL MANNING.

Mr. Gladstone has replied to the Rev. Dr. Preston, vicar of Holy Trinity, Runcorn, as Lord Salisbury had previously done, respecting the Lord Mayor's claim for giving precedenceto Cardinal Manning akter the Prince of Wales. He writes :—" Dear noer heard until your letter came of the statement attributed to the Lord Mayor, nor am I aware of having ever, tendered to her Majesty any advice of any kind regarding the place due to the name of Cardinal Manning, who, so far as I at aware, is not possessed of any temporal rank, whatever precedence may be accorded to him by courtesy.—Yours very obediently, W. E. GLADSTONE. Rev. Dr. Preston."
SUMMER SALE now on at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt. BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN.

The second pic-nic in connection with this class, took place on Saturday afternoon, when 40 members and friends were driven from Widnes to the picturesque. village of Hale, in vehicles supplied by Mr. Lea. Mr. B. Crosby and Mr. W. Millington had control of the arrange- ments, and under their guidance the party visited every- thing of interest in the locality. The greater part of the afternoon was spent in the fine old mansions Hale Hall, the residence of Colonel Blackburne, where there was much to interest and delight, and a stroll round the park and gardens amply repaid the party for the exertion. Occasionally the visitors awoke the echos with sacred melody, to the delight of those who were privileged to listen. The return journey waa accomplished by half- past nine, all being well pleased with the outing.

div.head: TRAVELLING _ON THE. CRAP AT RUNCORN.
div.p: TRAVELLING _ON THE. CRAP AT RUNCORN.

Before Major Hazlehurst and Mr. G. L. Wigg. at Run- corn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Andrew Ma.lcolmson, a young man, of very dilapidated appearance,was brought up on remand charged with attempting to defraud the London and North-Western Railway Company. Mr. Preston prosecuted. On the arrival at Runcorn on Thurs- day of the 12.5 train from Lime-st., to North Wales, the prisoner was found by Philip Turner, the collector, in a third class compartment, with a ticket from Lime-st. to Edge Hill. He said he had no money, but wished to get to Crewe, and if he had known they were going to examine tickets at Runcorn. he would not have come by that train.—Mr. Preston pointed out that the prisoner had been eight times convicted of similar offences, and he was sentenced to a month's hard labour, in default of paying a fine of 40s. and costs.

div.head: VIOLENT ASSAULTS ON TUE POLICE AT RUNCORN,
div.p: VIOLENT ASSAULTS ON TUE POLICE AT RUNCORN,

_ At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Major Hazlehurst and Mr. G. L. Wigg, a young man named James Fallon, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in King-st., and also 'with assaulting P.C. Edwards. He pleaded guilty. Patrick Ushin, a young man, was charged with being drunk and disorderly and also with assaulting P.C. Malkin. He also pleaded, guilty. It appeared that about seven o'clock on Satur- day night, the prisoners were fighting in King-st., and the constables went and separated them and took them into custody. Fallon lay down on the street and ki.dred Edwards very savagely, causing the limb to become quite black. Ushin was equally violent with Malkin, whom he struck with his fist and kicked, and threatened that if he could draw his knife he would stab him. He "acted like a madman." Each prisoner was fined ss. and costs for being drunk, and 10s. and costs for the assaults, or in default 21 days' hard labour.
DEATH AND FUNERAL OF CAPTAIN. G. Moss.

_ The death has occurred at Plymouth, in his 34th year, of Captain Gilbert Winter Z. Moss, of the 2nd Battalion Dorset Regiment. formerly of the Royal Fusiliers, only son of Mr. Gilbert Winter Moss, of Aigburth, Liverpool, and nephew of Sir Thomas Edwards-Moss, of Roby Hall, Lancashire. The funeral of the late Capt. Gilbert Winter Zwilchenbart Moss took place on Wedneskty, at St. Ann's, Aigburth, in the presence of a large gathering of mourning relatives and friends. The chief mourners were Mr. G. Winter Moss and Mrs. G. Winter Moss (father and mother of the deceased), Mrs. G. W. Z. Moss (widow), Miss G. W. Moss (sister), Sir John Edwards- Moss, Mr. T. Cottingham Moss, M.P., the Rev. Canon niggle, and Mrs. Diggle (sister of the deceased), Mr. Zoro Innes, and Captain Anderson. A number of the leading merchants and magistrates of the city and county were present, and beautiful wreaths of flowers covered the coffin, some of them having been sent by the deceased's fellow-officers. The funeral service was read by the Rev. Canon Livini,Aon, and the arrangements for the interment were carried out by Messrs. Woolright.and Co., of Bold-st., Liverpool.

div.head: SAD BATHING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SAD BATHING FATALITY AT RUNCORN.

Thomas Evans Reese, a boy nine years cf age, left his home in Brunswick-st., on Sunday afternoon, for the ur going to Sunday school, but instead of doing psolipeowse of to Runcorn.Cammon, with some compan- ions, Reese, J. Derbyshire, and F. Smithurn, stripped with the intention of having a bathe in the pit there ; and the former immediately jumped into the water and sank. He rose until his head was just visible, and then again disappeared and did not rise again to the surface. The boys raised an alarm, and a young man from Wid- nes came on the scene, but could not render any aid. In the course of the evening the dead body of the boy was recovered by P.C. Edwards and others. The depth of the pit is fifteen feet. On Tuesday Mr. J . E. Worsley held an inquest at the police station ; Mr. G. Ward being the foreman of the jury. Evidence bearing out the above facts was given by Emma Baguley, the mother ; Joseph Derbyshire, 49 Hope-st., and P.C. Edwards.— The Coroner said it was a very sad occurrence,and there was only one verdict to return, viz., accidentally drowned. While there was hot weather boys would bathe.—The jury returned a verdict. accordingly, and expressed their sorrow with the relatives who had lost a promising boy. SUMMER SALE now on at J. .% W. DUTTON'S Sankey-Bt., Warrington.—Advt. VIOLENT ASSAULT ON TIIE POLICE AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Police Court,on Wednesday, before Mr. A. Thomas and Dr. Steele, a flatman named Thomas Hulse, was brought up on a warrant charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Devonshire-square, on the 26th December last. He was further charged with assaulting P.C. Benfield while in the execution of his duty. P.C. Ratcliffe proved the first offence. P.C. Renfield stated that about twenty minutes past eleven on the previous night, he was on duty in front of the Police Station, when the prisoner came to him and said, "I have no- where to go ; there is a warrant out for ins, and I will give myself up, if you will wait until I go into Mersey- st." Witness walked with him to Mersey-st., when the prisoner, with an oath said, "You won't have me to, ' night," and ran away. Witness followed, and the pri- soner, placing himself close to the wall in a dark place, put out his leg, and witness fell over it. Eventually he captured the prisone:, and in the struggle the prisoner bit his arm twice, causing two ugly wounds. He also damaged his cap beyond repair. With the assistance of P.C.'s Hulse and Malkin he brought him to the Police Station. Superintendent Large said this was the sixth assault on the police within a fortnight : and the second case a biting. He must ask their Worships to deal more severely in these cases.—For being drunk and dis- orderly the prisoner was fined 10s., and costs 15 4d., or 14 days' hard labour ; and for the assault he was sen- tenced to a month's hard labour.

div.head: GOSSAGE'S TRIP TO BLACKPOOL.
div.p: GOSSAGE'S TRIP TO BLACKPOOL.

Messrs. W.-G-o-s-s-a-ge and Sons, the celebrated makers of soap at Widnes, gave their workpeople their annual trip on Saturday last. , The destination of the trip is left to the choice of the men, and by a large majority they decided upon a visit to the" Brighton of the North " Blackpool. Each workman is given two tickets, and is. 6d., and each boy is handed a ticket and is. and it may be mentioned that all who are receiving 15s. per week are included in the former list. Usually two trains have sufficed to convey the trippers on their journey, but on the present occasion three trains of 15 coaches each were chartered and just provided comfortable accommodation for the 1,400 excursionists. The first train left Widnes at a quarter to seven and thelast about half an hour later, and all had discharged their living 'freight at Blackpool by five minutes past ten. The weather was fortunately quite fine, if not so warm as could have been desired, and the Widnesians spent a pleasant day in strolling along the promenade and piers, and in viewing the numerous attractions arranged for visitors. If anything the town was too crowded for thorough enjoyment, there being no less than 28 excur- sions arrived at Talbot-road station during the day. The Gossage's excursions were despatched. in good time in the evening, and arrived at Widnes shortly after nine o'clock. The various arrangements were well conceived, and were carried out without a hitch.
