Hargreaves, J. Houghton, B. Sadler, J. Taylor, F. Liddell, J. T. Allen (clerk), I. Carr (engineer), J. Sinclair (ear- vey'or), and J. Dickson (inspector). TECHNICEI, EIYUCETION.-.-0000 OFFER.

A letter was read from Mr.. J. Morrison, hon. sec. to the Widnes Science and Art School, enclosing the follow- ing resolution unanimousfy voted by the Committee of the School That the Local Emil be respectfully requested to take into contideration, and If thought desirable, to adopt at an early date, the Techni- cal Instruction Act, 1889." He was directed to state that should the Board decide to put into operation the Act, the Committee would be prepared to, hand over to the new authority the apparatus, furnituve, and library used in the School, which has cost about £6OO. The demand for scientific and technical instruction is gradually in- creasing, and with the limited accounnodation of the school, it was impossible to teach with satisfaction seve- ral of the classes, as they are so overcrowded. All the subjects taught in the school came within the new Act, but there were other subjects, such as soap manufac- ture, mechanical engineering, gas manufacture, and Unit land steel manufacture, which ought to be placed within the reach of the industrial classes in Widnes. The Com- mittee hoped the Bcard would give the subject favour- able consideration.—The Chairman said they could riot arrive at any decision on the subject that day, and on his suggestion the letter was referred to the Generhl Purposes Committee. GAS AND WATER. _ _

The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee showed that the rainfall for the month had been 2.395 inches, and the water in stock was 5,525,109 gallons. The illu- minating power of the gas during the month had averaged 19.15scand1es.—Mr. Brown moved the adoption of the minutes, and said the increased consumption of water 'wasvery satisfaCtory, but the increased price they had to Pay for coal for the ensuing year was not very satis-- sattory. The increase was equal to a further expendi- ture of £7so.—Mr. Wright seconded the motion.—Mr. Flargreaves said there was a great deal of grumbling' anaongst small consumers of water, about the minimum'

charge of ss. per water meter. He had the names of several tradesmen who did not use more than Is. Od. worth of water per. quarter, And they considered it an injustice to have to pay ss.—Mr. Sadler said the matter was dealt with at the last meeting, and could not be re- opened without notice of motion.—Mr. Brown said ss. was the smallest minimum charge there was in the neighbourhood.—Mr. Hargreaves: It is hard to pay 55. for is. ed. worth of water.—Mr. Brown said in every other water company a higher rain was charged than at Widnes.—The Chairman said the minimum charge was fixed in order to avoid the danger of the domestic stipply of water being used for manufacturing purposes.—Mr. Hargreaves : If we consider the ratepayers dishonest in the matter it is right enough; but I think if we charge for the water used it will be quite sufficient.—The ntinutes were passed.
THRUWAY NATTERS..

The Highway Committee reported that Mr. D. Cohen' had written respecting a portable building for circus, Sic., proposed to be erected near to the Grapes Inn,in Widnes- road. Instructions were given to request that plans of the sanitary arrangeinents be submitted and that the Surveyor inspect the building. The plan of the suggested widening, &c., ot • Lugsdale-road, was submitted and approved. Mr. E. K. Muspratt agreed to give up the necessary land, about 623 squareyards, on condition the Board did the sewering and lighting. Consideration was deferred pending reply from landowners on the opposite side.—Plan of the suggested improvement of Sutton's- lane was submitted. The Leigh estate offered about 443 square yards for widening on condition that the Board bear the cost of forming about 274 square yards of the land given into a macadam road. The suggested arrange- ment and plan was approved.—The minutes were approved on the motion. of Mr. Sadler.

div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The minutes of the Health Committee contained the medical officer's report for June, which stated there were 94 births and 42 deaths, being at the respective, rates of 36.38 and 16.25 per 1,000, 22 deaths occurred amongst children under five years. Zymotic diseases caused five deaths. There had been 27 notifications of infectious disease. There were nine patients in the Fever Hospital. The Committee recommended that a laundry and drying room be provided at the Fever Hospital at an estimated cost of £250. The question of having hospital collec- tioas was deferred until more replies had been received from those communicated with in respect to the move- ment.—The minutes were approved on the motion of Mr. Carey.—Mr. Midwood remarked that the amount of money spent on the Fever Hospital was something shocking. •

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.
The Finance Committee recommended the payment ef accounts amounting to £7,983 N. 2d., and the recom- menaation was agreed to.
NEW FIRE STATION.

On the recommendation of the General Purposes Com- mittee the tender of Messrs. Sayce and Randle, on sche- dule of prices, estimated at about £2,800, for the con- struction of cottages and fire station, was accepted.

A long discussion took place as to the inclusion of ladies in the Committee, which eeveral members argued would be a source of strength. After numerous pro- positions and amendments, it was decided that the Com- mittee should be composed of ladies and gentlemen. The hon. secretary wished to fix the composition at 11 gentlemen and five ladies,but an objection being raised he withdrew his proposal, and the number of ladies to be elected was left open.—The following nominations were made t—The Vicar Dr. Gastaldi, J. Simpson, Mrs. Soulbv, J. B. Holland, E. Marshall, J. Knowles, G. Moss, Miss Isherwood. J. D. Jones, S. Pope, W. Handley, J. J. Hewitt, S. Taylor' Miss Eliza Wr,ght, Miss Andrews, 9 Miss Janet Taylor W. B. Frith, E. Imison, F. J. Norman, Miss Comerford, S. C. Beckett, A. Jordan, Rev. H. Burson, Rev. J. Holden, T. H. Annett, T. Riley, Miss Pierpoint, Rev. John Simpson, Rev. A. J. Jameson, and W. Towns. The result of the ballot was that the following were elected :—Rev. A. M. Wood, J. J. Howitt, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi. J. D. Jones, S. Taylor, Mrs. Soulby, J. B. Holland, E. Marshall, S. Pope, W. Handley, E. Imison, G. Moss, W. B. Frith, J. Knowles, and Rev. H. Burson. The Rev. J. Holden, Messrs. J. Simpson, A. Jorden, and F. J. Norman had received an equal number of votes, and a selection had to be made from these to fill up the 16th place, and the vacancy caused by the Appointment of Mr. Holland to the treasurer- ship. Eventually, Mr. Norman and Mr. Jorden were elected, on the motion of Mr. Pope, seconded by Mr. Knowles. On the proposition of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Knowles, Mr. Holland was unanimously re-appointed. treasurer. Mr. Pope proposed the re-election of Mr. Humphreys as hon. sec., and referred to his ability and Bel vices in eulogistic terms. Mr. Howitt seconded the motion,, which was supported by Mr. W. Handley, and carried by loud acclammation.—Mr. Humphreys said there had been an immense amount of work connected with the office, but it had been a labour of love, and he should have been sorry had he been unableto continue it. (Ap- plause.) He announced that Mr. Brunner had guaran- teed £l5 for the next year, in the hope that there would be two courses of lectures, and at least an equal Lumber of students. He hoped next year they would have a balance on the right side without calling upon Mr. Brunner, and to do that they must have an average of 280 persons at each lecture—last year there was 200— and he VMS sure that was not beyond the powers of an energetic committee. (Applause.)—The Chairman 'then distributed the prizes and certificates to the students, and a vote of condolence was passed to Master Harry Callister, who was unable to be present through serious illness.—The Secretary announced that the Chairman had handed him a donation of £2 2s. with which to com- mence next session.—A vote of thanks concluded the proceedings.

div.head: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES. RUNCORN CENTRE.
div.p: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES. RUNCORN CENTRE.

The annual meeting was held at the Town Hall, nn Monday evening. Mr. S. Taylor, chairman of the Board of Commissioners, presided, and there were present the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Rev. J. Holden, Rev. John Simpson, Messrs. J. Knowles, J. D. Jones, E. Marshall, J. J. Howitt, S. Pope, Tatters, J. B. Hol- land, J, H. Moulton, D. S. Garner W. Millington, W. Handley, G. Moss, T. G. Jones, W. Joynson, J. Sling- ler, W. Shaw, E. W. Humphreys (hon. sec.'„ B,;c. The Chairman expressed his pleasure at taldng the chair at a meeting called for so worthy an object, and he was glad to hear that the lectures had been so well sup- ported during the past year; and he felt confident the movement, which was not-sectarian, and intended for the general good, would have greater support in the coining year. (Applause.) The hon. sec. read a letter from Mr. F. A. Lake, apologising for non-attendance, and offering several suggestions for the consideration of the committee. He renewed his guarantee of £2 2s. (Applause.) Letters of apology had also been received from the Rev. 11. Bur- son, Mr. J. Simpson, Mr. S. C. Beckett, and Mr. F. J. Norman. The hon. sec. read the first annual report, in which he related the circumstances which led to the formation of the Runcorn Centre of the University movement. Early in last year, he said, a letter was addressed by Mr. Brun- ner, M.P., to the Free Public Library Committee, in which he drew attention to the advantages to be de- rived from the establishment ot Home Reading Circles, and further intimated his willingness to defray the fees of 30 students if that number could be got to join such a circle. The Library Committee, after fully con- sidering this generous offer, unanimously came to the conclusion that a series of University Exten- sion Lectures would prove a source of wider useful- ness, and they asked Mr, eennner if he would be willing to transfer his guaraatte* to such an object, to which he cordially ass:mated...A the same time expressing his gratification that well a course was being adopted. Subsequently a puWip rnretitil was held,under the presi- dency of the Views% the Rev. ts, M. Wood, and it was unanimously rosnived to arrange for one or more courses of University. extension Lectures to be given in the town during the water, and a Committee was appointed with Mr. J. 71, ilettand as treasurer, and 14 E. Wynne Hum- phreys as hon. secretary. The Vicar was elected chair- man. No time was lost in communicating with Mr. Sadler, the secretary of the extension movement at Oxfords with the result that they were fortunate enough to secure the services of the Rev. W. Hudson Shaw,M...A and Mr. H. J. Mac Kinder, M.A., who admittedly stood in the front rank of Extension Lecturers in their respective subjects of histoiy and science. The Committee requested Mr. Hudson Shaw to lecture upon "English Social Re- formers "and he accordingly selected the following ;-Sir Thomas Moor, John Wesley, William Wilberforce, Thos. Carlyle, Ktngsley and the Christian Socialists, and John Buskin. In addition to the sum guaranteed by Mr. Brunner other gentlemen expressed their willingness to become guarantors, and the Committee were enabled to ad- vertise courses at 2s. 6d. eack ; 6d. only being the charge for single admission, so as to bring the advantages of the movement within the reach of all. The Bethesda Lecture Hall having been secured, the first lecture was delivered on Thursday,October 3rd. In his report at the conclusion e the course, Mr. Hudson Shaw said "This first course of extension lectures held in Runcorn has been attended by very satisfactory results. The attendance was large, the organisation excellent, and the solid work accom- plished very encouraging." The examination was held on the 21st July,the examiner being Mr. A. Hassell, M.A., of Christ Church College. Oxford, and the successful can- didates were :-Passed with distinction E. J. Clayden H. Head; satisfied the examiner, E. Barlow, C. Ditchfield, M. E. Naylor, J. Stringier, A. M. Taylor. The prize was awarded to Miss E. J. Clayden. The second course commenced on January 4th, the subject being. " Physio- graphy," thetitle of the severaLlectures being The Earth's Crust, Volcanoes, Rain, Ice, The Gulf Stream, Climates, and Vegetation. Although the average attendance at this course was scarcely so large as the previous one, the interest was fully maintained whilst the number of students was largely increased. An additienal element of interest in this course was the fact that the lectures were copiously illustrated by means of the oxy-hydrogen Lime light, the slides being kindly lent by the Royal Geographical Society. The Committee were greatly in- debted to Mr. H. W. Handley fo,r his valuable services in connection with the manipulation of the lantern, and to IMr. Wm. Lea for generously supplying the oxogen free 'of charge. In his report at the conclusion of the course Mr. Mackinder said "The Runcorn centre is doing excellent work." The examination took plate on April 9th, when eleven candidates presented themselves, all of whom were successful. Mr. H. W. Bates, F.R.S., assist- ant secretary to the Royal Geographical Society, was the examiner. The following is the list of successful candi- dates :-passed with distinction H. H. Callister,Margaret C. Callister, Sarah Comerford, Wm. Epps, Darnel S. Garner, Mary E. Joynson Arthur Abram, Joseph M. Baguley, W. Leathwood, Thomas H. Parker, John Shingler. The university prize was awarded Master H. H. Callister. In connection with each course the Uni- versity Delegates sent down what is termed a "travelling library" consisting of some 50 or 60 volumes, bearing on the subjects dealt with by the lecturer, the care of which was kindly undertaken by Mr. J. D. Jones. This travelling library was much appreciated by the students, and the various books were in constant demand. In this connection the Committee felt im- pelled to express their sense of the valuable aid rendered to the movement in this centre by the action of the Free Public Library, who by procuring additional copies for their collection, of the works comprising the travelling library and of others recommended by the lecturer, assisted the students in no small degree. It was a satis- faction to the Committee to know that during the period covered by the lectures the issue of books in the history, biography, and science Section of the public library, increased more than 40 per cent, on the corres- ponding portion of the previous year. In conclusion, the report urged that the movement should be made .self- supporting, and said the Committee were strongly of opinion that the movement was a step in the right direc- tion, and that it should be carried on with redoubled energy and determination, as they were fully convinced that it was capable of great expansion, and that it could not fail to be productive of large and lasting results. The report of the Treasurer (Mr. Holland) showed that the receipts at the first course were-193 season tickets, £2425. 6d.; 11 pupil teachers, 13s. 9d.; 355 single admissions, £8 17s. 6d.; 188 syllabuses, £2 7e.; total,' £36 Os. 9d. Second course: 145 season tickets, £lB 6s. 6d.; 18 pupil teachers, £1 2s. 6d.; 358 single admis- sions, £8 18s.; 114 syllabuses, £1 85. 6d ; total £29 15s 6d. ; donations, Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., £l5 ; Mr. J. Simpson, £1 is.; sundry (per Mr. J. Knowles), 10s. ; bank interest, 9d. ; total, £l6 us. 9d.; grand total 482 as. The expenditure was as follows :-University of Oxford, let course, £2B 165.; 2nd course, £2B 75.; print- tog, advertising, £l9 Os. 10d. ; 'hire of rooms, £4 25.; miscellaneous £1 9s. 10d. ; balance in hand 12s. 4d. ; total £8283.-The reports were adopted on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. G. Moss- - Mr. E. Marshall moved that the best thanks of this meeting be given to the retiring Committee and officers for their services during the past year ;. and paid high • praise to the officials. Mr. D. S. Garner seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously-

div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

The annual meeting was held at the Cemetery, on Wednesday. Present, the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. S. Taylor, R. Morris, H. Coleburn, and W. Salkeld, secretary.—Mr. Coleburn moved, and Mr. Morris seconded, and Dr. Gastaldi supported, the appointment of Mr. Taylor to the position of chairman for the ensuing year, the speakers referring in high terms to Mr. Taylor's character and abilities. The motion was carried unanimously, and on taking the chair Mr. Taylor thanked the members for the honour con- ferred upon him During the past year the work had been conducted in a satisfact-iry manner under the pre- sideney of Mr. Morris, and he hoped the work of the coming year would be ecknally satisfactory.—On the pro- position of the Chairman, Mr. Coleburn was ifdanimously appointed vice-chairman. Mr. Coleburn, in accepting the position, said the Board had lost an excellent mem- ber in the person of Mr. James Handley.—The Secretary reported that during the three months ending June 25th, there were 100 interments, corresponding period last year 83, increase 17. The fees received during the same period amounted to 08 65.; last year, £BO Ils. ; increase, £l7 15s.—On the recommendation of the Finance Com- mittee, accounts amounting to £9 18s. 6d, were passed for payment.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Major Flazlehurst and Mr. G. L. Wigg. DRUNK.—Michael Flannery was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for being drunk. fhtootwo.—Charles Harris,a young man, was sentenced to seven days' hard labour for begging. The prisoner had stopped Inspector Bowyer in the street, and asked him to help him, as he was hard up.

Almond, Patrick Dugan, of Lugsdale-road, was fined ss. and costs in each ease.—James Ellison, of Charlotte•st., was fined ss. and costs for being drunk and refusing:to quit the Crown Inn, Birchfield-road. —John Connor, Sankey-st. ; John Sullivan, Chatham-st. ; and Michael Gmdv, Pepper-st., were each fined ss. and costs for drunkenness. . .

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

Psalms Calmar SUNDAY Scnoor„—The annual treat to elder scholars of this school was held on Wednesday. The party. numbering 130 with teachers and friends, proceeded by the 9.15 a.m. train from Frodsham to Rhyl, where they arrived safely, after a pleasant ride, at abut 1,1 o'clock. The greater part of the day was spent in visiting the many places of interest in Rhyl and the immediately vicinity. The weather turned out all that could be desired, and thus added greatly to the plea- sure of the trippers. SHOCKING Accrnmrr.—On Thursday morning, a shock- ing accident occurred to a man (whose name has not been ascertained), who was assisting a teamsman in charge of a furniture van, belonging to Messrs. Garnett and Son, of Warrington. Whilst the van was proceeding up Bridge-lane, the man who was on the off-side was knocked down, it is thought by the leading horse, and before his position was noticed, one of the fore wheels of the carriage had gone over the right leg, and a por- tion of his side. He was at once carried to Dr. Weaver's surgery, where his injuries were attended to. He was shortly afterwards removed to the Infirmary at War- rington. METHODIST FREE CHURCH.—The annual services in connection with the Sunday school were held on Sunday, when two sermons were preached by the Rev. George Thompson, of Runcorn. In the afternoon Mr. Thomp- son conducted a special service, and gave an address to parents, scholars, and friends. There was a good attend- ance at each of the services. The total collections received on behalf of the school funds realized £l5 9s. 90. The treat to the scholars took place on Wed- nesday afternoon. The children with the teachers met at the schoolroom at 1.30 p.m., whence they were con- veyed in lurries, lent by Mr. James Percival of Godscroft, who had offered them accommodation. The weather being fine, an enjoyable afternoon was spent by all. A capital tea was provided. About eight o'clock, after giving three hearty cheers for Mr. and Mrs. Percival, for their hopitality, the scholars started for home.

It is stated that the prospects of the National Rifle Association's meeting at Risley, are, from every point of view,very satisfactory. For the Queen's Prize the entries are already more than they were when the list closed at Wimbledon last year. For the St. George's they are forty less, but it is expected that post entries will bring up ' the numbers to very near if not quite the average of the last decade.
THE WARRINGTON EXTEN- SION BILL. _

Next Tuesday the Warrington Extension, Im- provement, &c., Bill will come before a special committee of the House of Commons, of which Mr. Mount is chairman, the other members being Mr. Joicey, Mr. Heath, and Mr. Maguire. The promo- ters of the Bill, the Warrington Corporation, will he represented by Mr. Pembroke Steven, Q.C., Mr. Balfour Browne, Q.C., and Mr. Fitzgerald. The gentlemen who will attend to give evidence are the Mayor (Alderman Fraucomb), Aldermen Bur- gess, _Harrison, Holmes. Sutton, and Wright; Councillors Shaw Green and Win. Pierpoint Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), T. Longdin (borough, surveyor), C. Chorley (borough treasurer), and J. L. Tunstall, and J. C. Sutton.
The parliamentary cartoon plan of the borough, which is being prepared under the supervision of the surveyor, is nearly completed. It is sixteen feet square, the scale being three feet to the mile.
orrosmoN FROM THE DARESELTRY HIGHWAY
BOARD.

At a meeting of the Daresbury Highway Board on Thursday, the Clerk (Mr. H. Linaker) said he had been requested to bring the matter of the pro- posed extension of the borough of Warrington before the Board. He had simply to report that if the proposal was carried out it would take from the Board's district a rateable value of about £3,500 and practically leave them the same length of road to main- tafn. The only road that would betaken by the borough was the length from Twentystep bridge to Wilderspool Causeway, and that, after the Ship Canal was made, would really become a main road.—The Chairman said he understood that the County Council were opposing the measure of the Warrington Corporation, and be believed the Guardians and Rural Sanitary Authority of the Runcorn Union were sending petitions against the Bill. The Bill would come forward on Tuesday, and as they were represented by Mr. Hall and Mr. Linaker, he thought they must leave it in their hands to do the best they could to protect the in- terests of the Board. He believed the Warrington Corporation was anxious to meet the various bodies who opposed them, but the time was now so short that they could not arrange terms, and the matter would have to be fought out at London between the various parties.—Mr. Hall said the extension would be a dead loss to that Board, and as there was not a pauper in the part that it was proposed to take, it would be a loss to the poor-law Union as well.—The Clerk said that with regard to the new road that would be taken by the Cor- poration at Lower Walton, the Ship Canal Company would pay a capital sum sufficient for its maintenance. —The Chairman said he supposed the whole question was one of compensation,—Mr. Hall said that when it was proposed to take Grappenhall and Thelwall from the Runcorn Union it was supposed that the objections largely arose from sentiment.—The Chairman said they had only to look after the interests of the Highway Board there, and they hex; nothing to do with sentiment.—The Assistant Clerk said the only way the Board could move was by presenting a petition.—The Chairman: You will have to petition the Lords •, it is too late for the Corn- mons.—The Clerk said the County Council promised them their assistance; unless the Board made a stand they would be ousted.—Mr. J. Darbyshire thought it was a case in which the Board should present a strong peti- tion.—lt was then agreed, on the proposal of the Chair- man, seconded by Mr. Cliffe, that the Clerk be instructed

to take the necessary proceedings for presenting a peti- tion to the House of Lords against the proposed exten- sion of Warrington —A committee, consistingof Mr. Hall, Mr. Burgess, and Mr. Cliffe, was appointed to advise the Clerk in the matter. RUNCORN UNION PETITION AGAINST THE BILL.

A special meeting of Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton Workhouse' on Thursday, for the pur- pose of considering the Warrington Extension Bill. Colonel Ashton presided, and there were present the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi J. W.Bnowles, P. Speakman, C.C., J. Weir, C. Phillips, J. Btandreth, H. Linaker (clerk), and H. G. Linaker (deputy clerk).

div.head: GROUNDS OF 013.INCTION.
div.p: THE GROUNDS OF 013.INCTION.

The Clerk said the Corporation of Warrington were applying to Parliament for power to extend the borough, and that extension would include a part of the township of Appleton, and part of the township of Walton Infe- rior, in the Runcorn Union. The rateable value of that part of Appleton proposed to be absorbed was £2,991 9s. 7d.. and of Walton £329, or a total of £3,320. This would mean a loss to the Union on the poor rate—assum- ing the poor rate to be Is. 4d. in the L—a loss of £221 Bs. Bd. per annum. There were no paupers in receipt of relief in those parts of the two townships which the Cor- poration proposed to take. The Corporation pro- posed in the Bill to take half of the Canal, and that would have taken from the Union a further rateable value ol £1,200; but they had now given that up, and instead they were going to make the boundary on the north side of the canal, leaving suffi- cient land for a towing path.—Mr. Speakman: Have they given you that in writing 7—The Clerk,. The,- given it in writing so far as a letter goes.- the proposed alteration wo-" . -.nu% were said ITnion.—The r' • Ds a serious loss to the . vierir concurred and said the expenses of rthe Union would be precisely the same.—Mr. Mclntyre : The loss to the Sanitary Authority would be larger than to the Union.—The Clerk: So far as Appleton is con- cerned the loss will be larger. The Highway Board would also be seriously affected.—Mr. Speakman suggested that a small committee be appointed to deal with the matter, because there' was very little time to lose and they ought to do all in their power to sustain the County i Council n their opposition to the Bill. He could not think for a momeat that the legislature would pass an enactment to denrive one county for the benefit of another, especially when he saw that the outskirts of LiVerpool had deteated the Liverpool extension Bill. He thought there was great wisdom in meeting that morning to protect the interests of the Union in the County of Chester.—Mr. Brandreth asked if there had not been some idea of adding Grappenhall and Latchford to the Runcorn Union.

div.head: LETTER FROM THE TOWN CLERK OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: LETTER FROM THE TOWN CLERK OF WARRINGTON.

The Clerk, in reply read the following letter he had received: "Dear Sir,—Warrington Extension Bill. As requested by you at the interview to-day I send you herewith a statement shewing the area, populace, and rateable value of the districts proposed to be added to the Borough and the area, populace, and rateable value of the parts of the parishes in ths Union of Warrington 'which, on the recommendation of the Boundary Com- missioners, are to be added to the Union of Runcorn Parishes proposed to be added to the Union of Runcorn viz. Latchford and Grappenhall ; area 3,458 populaticn 1,593, rateable value £15,407; less part of the township of Latchford proposed to be included in the borough, area 185, population 86, rateable value 21,577, leaving an area of 3,273, population 1,507, and rateable value £13,830. Part of the township of Apple- ton proposed to be included in the borough ; area, 51, population 483, rateable value £3,041. Part of the township of Lower Walton proposed to be included in the borough : area 27, population 45. rateable value £250; giving a total of area 78, population 508; rateable value £3,291. I should point out that the Cerportion propose to alter southern boundary of the borough from the centre to the north side of the canal. This will reduce the area of the parts proposed to be added to the borough. It appears to me that the question between your authority and the Corporation is one purely of account and as the Bill already provided for the adjustment of accounts by the Local Government Board your authority is in every way protected.—Yours truly, J. Lyon Whittle."— The Clerk said the Board could not act on an assumption of this sort ; they must take things as they were now The Boundary Commissioners would deal with the matter referred to in the letter.—Mr. Brandreth said in this matter they were fighting Warrington Corpora- tion; with regard to Grappenhall and Latchford they would have to fight Warrington Guardians. —Mr. Speak- man said they had not to deal with ahything prospec- tive. Mr. Linaker and himself were at Chester on Saturday and had an interview with Mr. Potts, the Clerk of the Peace, and he advised them that what the Rural Sanitary Authority had done was all in order but it was for the Union to take action. That was the reason of this special meeting being called.—The Chair- man thought the Board ought to at once

LODGE A PETITION against the Bill, and show a firm front, leaving the Corporation too offer terms.—Mr. Speakman moved, Mr. Knowles seconded, and Dr. Gastaldi supported a resolu- tion that the Union lodge a petition against the Bill in Parliament.—On the motion of Mr. Weir, seconded by Mr. Brandreth, the following were constituted a Com- mittee to deal with the subject :—Col. Ashton, Messrs. Mclntyre, Knowles, Speakman, John Whitlow and John Weir.
PENKETH. TANNING COMPANY'S TIL/P.

The employ6s of the Penketh Tanning Company, Limited; had their annual trip on Saturday, going this year to Southport. At 7.40 a.m. 160 of the tanners, their wives, and children left Sankey sta- tion, and arrived at Southport about nine o'clock. As the day was fine, they enjoyed themselves to the utmost. Various places of interest were visited, and at 9.5 p.m. the return journey was commenced Sankey being reached about 10 p.m.

The trial, in Paris, of eight Russian subjects, on the charge of possessing or manufacturing explosives, was concluded on Saturday. Most of the accused were sen- tenced to three years imprisonment. At Fermov Quarter Sessions, on Thursday,a militiaman named Riordan, convicted of groaning at the police, was sentenced to six month's imprisonment, in default of finding bail to be of good behaviour. by WEATHER IN THE STATES.—A New York telegram, of Wednesday. says the previous day was the hottest experienced in the United States for twenty years. In New York and many other places the thermometer regis- tered more than 100 degrees Fahrenheit in the shade. There has been great loss of life and destruction of pro- perty in different States owing to storms and cyclones.

div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

THE STONE-TIIROWING NUISANCE. Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, two lads named George and Wm. Dunbobbin, brothers, were summoned for throwing stones in Crossley-st., on the 4th inst., and for doing wilful damage to property belonging to William Philip Chorley. Evidence was given to the effect that the lads were seen throwing stones, and Mr. Chorley said that his property had in this manner been considerably damaged. The Bench ordered that the elder prisoner, George, shauld receive twelve strokes with the birch rod, and that his brother should have six strokes. ' A MILITIAMAN TRIES TO STAB A SENTRY. At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, a militiaman named Richard Windle was charged with having been drunk and disorderly at Orford barracks on the previous afternoon, and with having attempted to stab a private named Matthews. Prisoner was one who assembled for the annual training of the Kings (Liver- pool) Regiment, but before going to the barracks he got drunk. Arrived at the barrack gates he created a dis- turbance, and attempted to stab Matthews, who was on sentry duty, with a pocket-knife. For having been drunk prisoner was fined ss.- and costs, and for the second offence he was sent to prison for twenty-eight days.

ASSAULTS ON THE POLICE. Two charges of assault on the police were investigated by the Warrington magistrates on Tuesday, Michael Kelly, ailabourer, was charged with being drunk and disordesy in Bridge-st. on the previous night,and assault- ing P.C. Corcoran. The officer stated he was called to a public-house to eject the defendant, who became very disorderly when outside, and witness was obliged to take him into custody. He struck the officer in the mouth, and also kicked him several times. A fine of 10s. and costs was inflicted.—William Woods, a shoemaker, living in Hall-st., was charted with being drunk and disorderly in that street, on the previous night and assaulting Constable Meacock. That officer said he found the defendant in a yard near his house. He was drunk and wanted to fight his neighbours. Witness requested him to go into the house, but he refuse 3 to do so, and struck him, and also threatened to knock off his head. Defend- ant also set a dog upon him, and it attempted to bite his I the officer's leg.) Defendant was fined ss. and costs.

AN UNHAPPY MARRIAGB. On Saturday' at the Warrington Police Court, Cornelius Enoch Smith, a compositor, was charged with deserting his wife, and leaving her and her tws children chargeable on the Union. Mr. Basil Shearer, inquiry officer, stated that the wife called upon him on Wednes- day in a destitute condition, and was admitted to the Workhouse. Smith surrendered himself on Friday, and now told the magistrates he would take his children out of the workhouse, but not his wife. The magistrates said he would have to take both his wife and children out of the Rouse. The magistrates also advised thewife to try and control her tongue, and not show such temper as she exhilited in court, as such conduct could not but tantalise her husband. Ultimately Smith promised to take his family out of the Workhouse, and the case was adjourned for a month to see if he fulfilled his promise PILFERING IN THE MARKET. It the Warrington Police Court, on Monday morning, a lad of nine years of age, named John Bennett, living with his parents in Pierpoint-st., was charged with I stealing from the Market-place, on Saturday evening, a I basket containing a fowl, 13 eggs, 61bs. potatoes, and a quantity of fruit and flowers, value ss.' belonging to Sarah Jackson. Three other lads namedPatrickMoran (12), Robert Evans (10), and John Gordon McMinnies Burton (10), were also included in the charge, but the Chief Constable intimsted that so far as he was con- cerned, he only charged Bennett with the theft. The latter had implicated the others, but there was no evi- dence to show that they had had anything to do with the matter. An errand boy named Pearson was sent with the basket of produce to the market, and whilst there he asked Bennett to mind it for a minute. On his return Bennett and the basket were missing. When apprehended Bennett implicated the other boys, saying I that they ate the strawberries, sucked the eggs, and threw the potatoes away. The fowl he took home. The Bench discharged Evans, Burton, aad Moran. Bennett's father stated that his lad was unmanageable and the magistrates ordered the boy to be detained in custody until 6 p.m., and to receive six strokes with the birch rxi.

Total Total 26 WARRINGTON v. STALYBRIDGE.—The first meeting of these clubs took place on the Arpley enclosure on Satur- day afternoon, in dull weather, before a large number of spectators. A grand wicket had been prepared, and Warrington, on winning the toss, commenced batting with S. M. and J. J. Crosfield to the deliveries of Barlow and Earle. J. .1. Crosfield was responsible for four off Barlow's first over, and then got Earle away first ball for four, but with the total at 11 he had to retire. R. Smith opened his account with a four off Earle, which he again repeated next over, but at 21 that bowler got one past him, which let in C. G. Lawton. The latter had a very short stay, for after contributing a single he was "yorked." On Jolley joining Crosfield runs came faster, each batsmam playing with confidence. The score was taken to 56 before Jolley, in trying to place a ball from Barlow, put it up, and he retired. Jefferson, who made his first appearance with the first team, hit hard and clean, and put on 13 out of the 19 scored during the partnership. He was, however, easily caught and bowled in playing forward to Barlow. Clarke opened with a single, which was shortly followed by a four, after which the scoring bccame flomewhat slower. T. Lawton super- seded Earle at 81, and a few runs later Barlow was taken off and Earle put on again at the railway end, the total being 105. Only one additional run had been added when Clarke was run out—(l3 for 106). Griffin soon retired, and Podmore was content to keep his wicket up while Crosfield did the scoring. The latter had been playing a careful and patient game, but now he began to hit out, bringing Barlow on again vice Law- ton at 118. Ten runs later Podmore was caught for three. Captain Adam was at the wicket while 26 were added, of which he had contributed 8 when he also was caught. Armstrong, who came in last, played a capital game. At 183 a double change of bowling was made, Keighley going on for Barlow and Fawley relieving Earle, but at 4.45 Mr. Crosfield for the first time this year declared the innings closed. He had played a magnificent game, taking his bat out for 74, included in which were eight fours, four threes, and four twos. As a display of patient batting his innings cannot be spoken of too highly, as only one chance was given by him, and that a very difficult one after he had passed 60. He was at the wicket two hours and a quarter. At 5.5 Barlow and Clarkson faced Jolley and J. J. Crosfield, the former opening with a maiden. A Fun was hit by Barlow off Crosfield's first ball, but with the last ball Clarkson was bowled. Buckley retired five overs later, having scored 3(2 for 10). Earle now joined Barlow, and the score mounted rapidly, for after getting Joiley away for four, he followed this up an over or two after, by driving Crosfield for six, the ball hitting the flag pole, which stopped it from going clean out of the field. At 40 Lawton relieved Crosfield, Smith displacing Jolley at 45. Lawton effected the separation, S. M. Crosfield bringing off a good catch, and Earle retired for a useful 28, composed of a six, four fours, and one two, and singles. He gave a hard chance when he had made 12. Three runs later T. Lawton, who had joined Barlow, was caught by Jefferson off C. G. Lawton's bowling. Keigh- ley came in, and S. M. Crosfield relieved Smith at 70, and Lawton gave way to J. J. Crosfield at 81. This time the change worked at once, for with his third ball J. J. Crosfield clean bowled Barlow, who had been at the wicket over an hour and a half for his 3, which in- cluded 10 twos and 18 singles (5 for 81). Ten runs later Keighley was bowled by a fast one from Jolley. He had hit four 4's, and was at the wicket forty minutes for his 16. Swann was caught by Jolley the last ball of the match, which ended in a draw in Warrington's favour. It is impossible to speak too highly of the home team's fielding, and if they will only do as well a fortnight hence, when they meet Livc here, a treat is in store for the spectators. A word ot praise is also due to Arm- strong, who stood up to every ball delivered, only letting two pass him. Score WARRINGTON. A young labourer named Trickston quarrelled w ith his fattier at Crowland, Lincoln, on Thursdoy, when he knocked tha old man down and killed him. The son was afterwards arrested. The quarrel arose about a donkey which was to run in a race at Crowland. Lieutenant Trotter, Quarter-master of the Royal Fusi- liers, committed suicide on Thursday morning, in his barrack-room, by blowing out his brains with a loaded rifle which he discharged by pressing his walking stick on the trigger. No cause is assigned for the deed. The Bradford plasterers' strike, which has lasted eight weeks, came to an end, on Monday, the masters conced- ing the full demand of Bd. per hour. '

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Aldermen Burgess and Chandley, Councillor Voisey, and Mr. R. Garnett. DRUNKENNESS.—SamueI Tynan, charged with having been drunk in Dial-st., on the previous day, was lined ss.

and Mists. BROGING.—Andrew Cotter, charged with begging in Winrnarleigh-at.. on the day previous, was sent to pri- son for seven days, with hard labour. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Francomb), Alderman Harrison, and Alderman Sutton. DRUNKENNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—Samuel Porter, in Market-Place. on Saturday, fined 55., including costs ; Peter Dooley, 31ersey-st., on Saturday night, discharged; Michael Connelley, Buttermarket-st., on Saturday night, fined 10s. and costs; Margaret Sheridan, in Bank Park, on Saturday afternoon, dismissed on promising to leave the town ; Martin Callighan, in New-road, on Saturday, lined 19s. and costs ; John Mullen, in St. James's-street, on the 30th ult., fined 10s, and costs; Catherine Far- rell and Bridget McDonough, in Hill-street, on the 2nd Inst., each fined ss. and. costs; William Preston and Michael Preston, in Bank-street, on the 27th ult., each fined 10s. and costs; William Curley and Thomas-Curley, in Bridge-street, on the 27th ult., each fined 10s. and costs. FURIOUS Daiwa:a—William Burke, summoned for having furiously driven a horse and cab, in the New- road, Latchford, on the 27th ult., fined ss. and costs. TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett and Mr. E. M. DRUNKENNESS .—Patrick Casey, brought up in custody on a charge of having been drunk in Lyme-st., on the night before, was fined 55., including costs.—Ellen Raithwaite, for having been drunk and disorderly in Corporation-street, on the previous night, was cautioned and allowed to go. NEGLECT or WORK.—Mary Waterworth was summoned for neglecting her work as a servant of Andrew Johnson, fustian cutter, who claimed is. as damages. She said that. she would return to work, and the Bench adjourned the case for a week to see if the promise was kept.

WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. P. Stubs. VAGRANCY.—John Clarke (10), was charged with sleeping in an outbuilding at Croft early that morning.— P.C. McMullen stated the facts of the case, but his worship' in consideration of the prisoner's age, dis- chargeelhim on his promise to take shelter in the work- house.

MR. CAINE'S POSITION. THE GOVERNMENT A " BROKEN-POWN FAILURE." Mr. W. S. Caine, replying to a correspondent who asked if it were true that he had adopted the Home Rule platform, says :—"My position towards the Home Rule question is surely now sufficiently definite. All I can say is, that I shall in future in Irish, as well as other ques- tions, co-operate with the main body of the Liberal party, who will at the general election certainly be called by the country to take the place of the present broken-down failure. The country is weary to death of this Irish con- troversy. The Unionists have been asked by the country to settle it, and have failed. Mr. Gladstone will now have to do it, and those Unionists who are still Liberal must either help him to do it or become Tories.' • Mr. Caine, writing to a Sheffield gentleman, says, con- cerning his intentions for the future :—"I am not going to bother about a constituency just now. I have had between fifty and sixty letters, begging me to go, I should think, to every constitneney in the United King- dom which is still without a Liberal candidate; but I am going to wait a bit, and take a look round. I have had a long, five-page letter, closely-written, from Mr. Gladstone, written spontaneously on seeing my words to the reporter of the Press Association about himself. He virtually invites me back to the party on my own terms, and, of course, I am practically at one with him and with all my old friends. lam very busy, and can- not do more than give you my heartfelt thanks for the kind help and sympathy you gave me at a time whenthe value of such sympathy and help was very precious.-1 shall never forget it.—Yours very truly, W. S. CAINE."

CRICKET.

Shrewsbury is still well to the top of the season's batting record with an average of 68.68 for each'of nine- teen innings. A. J. Webbe comes next with an average of 43.66. Some other averages stand thus :—A. Hornby, 26.66 ; A. Ward. 2621; F. Ward, 25 ' • Sugg, 2394; Dr. W. G. Grace, 2388; Briggs, 21; Murdoch, 17.88. Attwell heads the bowling list with an average of one wicket for every 10.32 runs. S. M. J. Woods comes a close second with an average of 10-58. Brigg's wickets have each cost 12.71 runs; Lohmann's 1239; Barnes, 18; Ulyett's, 18.9 ; Mold's, 1836; and Watson's 1932..

It looks as though the Australian team were beginning to realise their weakness, and, as a consequence, it Is said that Messrs. Spofforth and Woods are to be asked to" assist" the team in some of the remaining matches. The team would of course be known as "Australia, Past and Present." It is to be feared the Australians will not have much reason to be pleased with the financial results of their tour.

Walter Robinson we are told, continues in gobd form, and, playing for St. Helens Recreation against Brom- borough Pool, he hit a ball to square-leg, and on measur- ing to where it dropped the distance was found to be 125 yards.

YOrkshire have given another promising batsman a chance—this being H. Tinsley, brother to A. Tinsley, who has appeared for Lancashire several times this season. He is another of the Leyland stock, and did pretty well against Warwickshire, scoring 6 and 45, and bagged four wickets. His second innings was a good one his free style taking the fancy of the Birmingham quidnuncs.

The cricket match between the Australians and Leicestershire on Wednesday resulted in a victory for the colonists by an innings and 64 runs to spare. The match at Lord's between the Gentlemen and the Players was abandoned as a draw owing to the wet weather. The two days' match at Rossall between Lancashire County and Eighteen of Rossall School was concluded on the same day, the County gaining an innings victory.

CYCLING. " I am afraid," says the writer of the Cycle Jottings in the "Athletic News," "the military cyclists will not be seen to the best advantage at Bisley. I made a deter- mined effort to reach the camp last week, and though I tried four different roads, each soon degenerated into a mere sand track. I suppose there is seme other route besides the London and South-Western Railway by which heavy vehicles can reach the camp, but I failed to find one.'

"The cycling competition at the great rifle meeting is one in which the competitors will have to ride some three-quarters of a mile and fire a stipulated number 'of rounds. The first prize is a tricycle, a " Rudge," which gives its name to the competition, while £lO goes to the second man. lam given to understand that the course will be much harder than that used at Wimbledon, and that those entering will do well to get themselves in decent condition fuz4he occasion."

An enterprising youth who has been cycle stealing from letting out depots all round London, has got to know his fate. He was tried at the Surrey QuaNer Ses- sions, at Kingston, and sentenced to twelve months, with hard labour. He will find "the wheel" rather harder work than cycle riding.

MISCELLANEOUS. A team of Salford Harriers are, it is said, about to visit the United States and compete in a series of sports against the Cream of American athletes. As yet the scheme is very much in embryo, but if it is brought to a successful issue the races should be of very great interest, and the success of the English team almost a matter of certainty. Another very interesting fixture is in course of arrangement, viz., a series of races between the Spartan Harriers and Northern athletes, to be held at the Manchester Athletic Club grounds, the programme to include events at all distances from 100 yards to two miles. Such a meeting would create a very great amount of enthusiasm, and might lead to the resuscitation of the old competitions between North and South.

The race for the half mile amateur swimming championship of Great Britain took place on Saturday afternoon in Hollingworth Lake, Rochdale. No fewer than fifteen entries were obtained, and there was not a single absentee, a fact which is quite unprecedented in the history of the race. At the word go the men dived, and all seemed to touch the water together. W. Evans, of the Manchester Swan S.C., was the first to secure an advantage, and, swimming very strongly, he rapidly drew away, his nearest opponents being Smith and Schlosel. These three led throughout, Evans never being 'headed, and winning by a dozen yards from Smith in the very good time of 14min. 38sec. Mr. R. M. White- head, of Salford, officiated as starter, and Mr. J. H. Fisher as judge.

The 'following were the contestants Brickett, Unity S.C., London; W. Chesters, Stockport S.C.; A. Dickinson, Oldham Gentleman's, Oldham ; W. Evans, Manchester Swan, Manchester (150 yards champion) ; B. A. Hart, Caustons A.C., London; E. C. N. Heaton, Sefton S.C. Liverpool ;T. Jones,Manchester Swan S.C., Manchester(22o yards champion) ; W. B. Knowles, Sefton S.C., Liverpool; A. M. Langdon, New College, Oxford (1,000 yards Ulph champion) ; T. Roberts, Holloway S.C. London; J. Manion. Huddersfield, Amateur Champion of America • F: C. Schlotol, Surbiton S.C. London; A. Smith, TyldeslyS.C.,Tyldesley, Champion Of the Mersoy; J. Waring, Everton S:C., Liverpool; J: Worthington, Y.M.C.A.S.C., Manchester.

-- Is this not rather excessive deference to royalty P The Prince of Wales should have attended a cycling meeting at Paddington bn Saturday, but it turned out wet and His Royal Highness could not put in an appearance, and so the sports had to be postponed until Wednesday. There were, it is said, several Irish and Scottish ama- teurs who had journeyed all the way from their native heaths to take part in the meeting, and one can imagine that their feelings were mixed in regard to the postpone- ment.

Another big football balance sheet. Blackburn Rovers have lately held their annual meeting, and a very satis- factory balance sheet was shown, for the treasurer's statement showed a balance in hand of £307 14s. 9d., the prat on the year's working being 82 4s. 7d. Their players have cost £1,07135. W.—not a heavy item con- sidering the quality. The club have spent £2,745 I 19s. Bd.

div.head: I CITY LICENSE EXTINGUISHED.
div.p: I CITY LICENSE EXTINGUISHED.

An appeal against the decision of the City Justices in extinguishing a public-house license was heard on Satur- day, at the City of London Quarter Sessions.—Mr. Poland, Q.C., and Mr. Humphreys appeared for the apel- lant, Mr. Nathaniel Cook ; Mr. Besley and Mr. Forrest Fultoa, M.P., were for the respondents.—Mr. Poland said the house in question the Horse and Trumpeters, Crutched-friars was left the will of a Mr. Kitching ih 1555 to the Saddlers' Company for the purposes of charity, and had been licensed ever since until March last. In 1889 the license was renewed to a Mr. Green, who held a lease from the Saddlers' Com- pany for 21 years from 1877 at a rental of £225 per annum. The house did not pay, as well as it formerly did, and so the lease was surrendered, and Mr. Cook was taken as a tenant at a reduced rental of £125 a year. The house had been closed for a little time, and in March the appellant took possession, but when he applied for the transfer at the adjourned day the justices refused his application on the ground that the neighbour- hood had changed, and there was no longer any demand for a licensed house at this spot, and, therefore, the license was refused, and the house had been closed ever since. The appellant felt certain he would have no difficulty in making the house pay at the reduced rental. If the court upheld the decision of the court below the charity would be a serious loser, as the pro- perty would not be worth more than £4O per annum. The appellant, in his evidence, said under his affree- ment with the Saddlers' Company he was ta spend £250 on doing up the house, but ha intended spending, another £4OO upon it, which he obtained from a tramway com- pany for damages for personal injuries. In cross-exam- ination, he said he did not know that the Commercial Brewery'ComPany lost £2,000 over the house, and were glad to get out of it at the price.—Mr. Beesley urged that this was an attempt to resuscitate an old and defunct license, which the justices in their discretion refused on account of the neighbourhood changing -So as to leave no demand for a public-house, and in so doing hatLexercised their strict legal rights. No one would, he subuitted, be a loser if the Court upheld the decision of the justices, as he hoped they would.—Sir It. Fowler: The appeal is dismissed, with costs.

SIR W. HARCOURT ON TRH POLITICAL SITUATION.— Sir W. Harcourt, speaking at a dinner given to him, on Wednesday night, at the National Liberal Club, by the Liberal and Radical candidates for the metropolis, said the Government were sinking fast, and the Barrow election had paralysed their whole frame. The Liberal Unionists were rejoining the Liberal party, and they would be received back with the right hand of fellowship. Mr. Caine had come back, no longer able to bear the intolerable yoke of the Liberal Unionist alliance with the Tory party.

div.head: PROGRESS OF THE SHIP
div.p: THE PROGRESS OF THE SHIP
CANAL. The "Umpire "of last Saturday gives an article —well and profusely illustrated—descriptive of the present state of things on the Ship Canal. From this article the following extracts are taken.

div.head: MANCHESTER AND SALFORD DOCKS.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER AND SALFORD DOCKS.

Salford Docks! Hew strange a sound these words have! I wonder what one of the old handloom weavers who used to throw the shuttle in a Safford cellar wsuld say if he could " revisit the pale glimpses of the moon," and see how the scene of his favourite walks is changed. He would surely imagine himself in another planet alto- gether ; for no one, however intimate his knowledge of the district to the west of Salford might have been, could now recognise his whereabouts if dropped down on the Canal side of Trafford Park. Here lie the huge docks that are to contain the argosies which we all look to to bring increased prosperity to industrial Lancashire. Where Pomona—the former scenes of great horse shows, athletic festivals, political demonstrations, and other junketings of not quite so staid a character—once stood, huge basins now lie exposed, and steam navvies, shriek- ing and puffing locomotives, and a small army of men, have been busily at work the whole livelonr, day. Almost all the work of excavatihç has been done by the steam navvies, of which altogether there are no less than 67 at various points on the works. One of these can fill 750 wagons a day, each wagon holding 5 tons, thus representing 3,750 tons for a day's:work of 12 hours; or, to put it another way, each "devil," as the steam navvy is familiarly called, can do the work of 2,000 men. It is not too much to say that without these marvellous machines the canal could never have been made, as the Engineer, Mr. Leader Williams, calculated that there were over 44,000,000 cubic yards of soil and rock to be removed in the four years allowed for the construction of the water-way. Up to this present writing upwards of 30,000,000 cubic yards have been excavated, a goodly portion of this being from the docks and locks at the two ends of the canal. The end of the principal dock is within 40 yards of the. Bridgewater Canal, and by means of steam cranes goods can be unloaded from ocean-going ships and placed on the canal barges, which will then be able to take them right up to the centre of the city, and thence, still by water, to Bolton, Bury, Rochdale, Ashton-under-Lyne,

, and other more distant:. towns. The visitor who sees the enormous dock area at this end will probably wonder how the letting of the water into the docks when completed is to be managed. The answer is to be found in the important work which has been carried on in the river close by since November last. Along the centre of the river bed two rows of piles are driven, extending nearly from Mark Addy's Bridge to Trafford-road Bridge, the space between the rows being filled in with clay, rubble, etc. There are some 5,000 or 6,000 piles in all, of 12in. by 12in. timber, the whole being tightened up by wedge-shaped pieces of wood, known as' keys." The piles are driven in in pairs, this plan being practicable owing to the immense weight of the " monkeys," or hammers, each of which weighs upwards of 1 tons. By these piles—known as " sheet piling "—the river is reduced to half its normal width, the other half being available for future opera- tions,which will consist of breaking down the river bank and excavating the bottom to the required depth. When the powers that be order the waters to be let in which it is said will be in a few months now, it is easy to see how simply and safely the task can be accomplished. The work has been going on day and night hereabouts, and steady progress has been made. By the side of Trafford- road—in fact, on the site of the ()Id roadway—the pre- parations for a large swing bridge are being pushed forward with energy. The bridge will turn on the centre of a pile and wings, in shape something like the letter E. The mpterial is to be concrete—a substance, by the way, which I found in great demand at many other portions of the Canal works. THE LOCK GATES.

- -- Arriving opposite the racecourse, I noticed that the ponderous gates for the locks are not fax from comple- tion, a big staff of men having been constantly en- gaged on the work. These gates, like others at Latch- ford, Irlatn, Barton and Eastham, are constructed throughout of a wood known as greenheart, belonging to the laurel family, which flourishes in British Guiana. This wood is of exceedingly close texture, and is about 10lb, per foot heavier than water, and is almost imper- vious to decay. It is, however, very poisonous, a I scratch caused by it producing a very ugly wound. This poisonous quality is, however, neutralised by a solution of permanganate of potash, which the work- men take care to apply in any case of injury from splinters, &c. At the three gate sheds at Sailor& Thel- wall, and Eastham, enormous quantities of this timber are cut up. The logs are in some instances 50ft. and 601 t. long, 22in. square, and weigh nearly 4 tons. TRH BARTON ACITJEDIICT.

Just before arriving at Barton there is a long stretch of Canal in a finished state, the bed being covered with ' water. At Barton, Brindley's famous aqueduct will soon be supplanted by a swing bridge. A short diversion of the Bridgewater Canal will be made at this spot, and the length of the Bridgewater over the Ship Canal will then be formed in the manner of a long moveable iron, trough, somewhat deeper in the centre than at the two ends, which will be filled with water to a depth equal to that of the Canal itself, and fitted at either end with water- tight gates. Similar gates will also be fixed at either end of the approaches from the Canal. Upon its com- pletion, the central portion of Brindley's aqueduct will be removed, the ends only being allowed to remain. The manner of working the new aqueduct will be as follows: —The operator in charge of the machinery will,on seeing an approaching steamship, cause the four water-tight gates at the ends of the trough and of the approaches to be closed, and will then, by means of hydraulic machinery, cause the trough to revolve for a quarter of a circle upon the rollers which will support it, thus leaving a perfectly clear passage for the vessel Through this passage up or down goitv, vessels will be able readily ,to steam, and when clear of aqueduet the process will be reversed-that is to say, the attendant will cause , the trough to turn back into its otiginal position, and will have the water-tight gates opened once more, when the line of the Bridgewater traffic will be clear again. after a brief interval, and without any loss of the water , in the Canal. ,

div.head: FINISHED PART.
div.p: A FINISHED PART.

Walking along by Stickin's Island, I notice the walls of the Canal are completed, and a very good idea may here be obtained of the appearance the Canal will present when finished. The locks themselves are very backvrard. At this point there is a very interesting bit" in the locks of the old Canal raised up above the bed of the Canal—a " bit" much beloved of artists who see in it a subjecb which is absolutely unique.

div.head: EXTENSIVE PUMPING OPERATIONS.
div.p: EXTENSIVE PUMPING OPERATIONS.

The walk along the Canal from here is very enjoyable, as the rails of the " overland route "—that is, the line that runs through from Manchester to the sea—are carried close along the Canal side for some miles. There is a good deal of excavating yet to be done at the junc- tion of the Barton and lrlam sections, at which point, if I may judge from the quantity of water forced up by a powerful pump, there seems to have been sonie fear of flooding. An official tells me that it is necessary to pump over a hundred million gallons of water out of the different sections of the works every day in order to keep them sufficiently dry for working in.

div.head: RAILWAY DEVIATIONS.
div.p: RAILWAY DEVIATIONS.

I don't find anything particular to note until I come to the Boat House at learn (a place to snake a note of), and on to the deviation of the Cheshire Lines Railway between Liverpool and Manchester. Near the Boat House Inn, a river diversion is being vigorously carried out. When this is finished the river will be compelled out of its course, and the Canal cut right through its bed from Calama,nca to Irlam, and from Calamanca to Hulme's Lock. , There are five railway deviations or " liftings "es route, and at each of these, embankments have to be made on both banks of the Canal, two miles each in length, and brick piers built to carry girder bridges at a height of 751 t. above the future level of the water. Near the confluence of the Mersey and Irwell—a very pretty bit of scenery—at Partington, coal tips are being built to provide accommodation for loading six steamer sim- ultaneously. Storage will also be provided here for pil sprags and other timber required for collieries. Just before reaching Cadishead I come along another section of the" big cot" nearly finished, but at the crossing of the Glazebrook and Stockport railway over the river and canal, the excavations have scarcely begun. The arches in course of, construction here look to be of unusual height, but Vflaether this is more apparent than real I cannotsay. Some of the mechanise used in the con- struction of the Forth Bridge is employed at this point. At Cadishead there are some very pretty river views, and at Cadishead also there is a hostelry that provides most excellent refreshments for the inner man—a hos- telry at which visitors to the Ship Canal should not fa" 1 , to call.

div.head: LATCHFORD LOCKS.
div.p: LATCHFORD LOCKS.

Another walk of nearly three miles lands me at the site of the Latchford Locks, where the tidal waters from the sea will end, and the canal—as a canal—will com- mence. It is impossible in the short space at my dis- posal to describe the work being carried on here. Suffice it to say that everything is being pushed on with the greatest poskible speed. THE STAPP Alen PLANT. ' , At Warrington, when resting the metaphorical sole of the foot, I met With a gentleman who gave me the fol- lowing facts :—There are on the works 170 locomotives, 245 steam cranes, 130 portable and other steam engines, over 200 steam pumps, about 6,200 wagons, 52 pile- driving engines, and an "overland route" of railway and sidings not far short ef 250 miles in length. There are about 170 horses, and nearly 15,000 men and boys on the works. Over 10,000 tons of coal, and about the same quantity of cement, are used per month. In this connection Alderman Bailey', one of the most persistent and indefatigable workers connected with the scheme, tells me that the steam employed is of about 50,000 horse-powee. To the same gentleman lam indebted for certain plans, showing the comparative size of the canal at a glance :-.-The minimum width of the canal at bottom is 120 ft., and the average width of the canai at
water level is 172 ft. the bottom width of canal between Barton and Manchester (two and a half miles) is in- creased to 170 ft., whilst the minimum depth all along is 26ft.

WARRINGTON TO RUNCORN. Starting again for awalk from Warrington to Runcorn along the course of the canal, I first notice that at Arpley the cutting for the diversion of the river is complete, and holds water, so to speak,the excavation having been flooded during a storm some months back. The devi- ation of the railway lines running into Bank Quay Station, so as to enable them to cross over the canal at a sufficiently high level, is the chief work hereabouts. The deviation of the line which runs from Warrington through Moore to Crewe is making good progress. The work begins at the arches in Slutcher's-lane—expressive name —and will be carried on high embankments at a gradient of 1 in 135 to a new bridge crossing the river at Walton Arches, and thence by means of a new viaduct over the Ship Canal, from thence the line descends to regain its old route. The Irch over the river will be 160 feet span. The old canal is at this point now filled up. At Acton Grange things are very busy. Enormous quantities of material, from huge masses of rock to tenpenny nails, are on hand. Engines are rushing hither and thither, and men and machines alike are working at high pressure. The • continuity of the embankment is interrupted here by a bridge, but as you go westward you come across the big heap again, having the cutting on your left hand. This latter is practically complete, and ready for flooding. Nature has been doing some little in that direction this last week or two,. It was doting it, in fact, when I was there, and I sineerely wished it wasn't. Another railway deviation—the Daresbnry line over the Moore line—is nearly complete, the fine bridge (the Tunnel Bridge), being quite finished. The Moore-lane Bridges, for the railway, are nearly out of hand, and the Canal Swing Bridge at Moore is in pro- gress. A little past Bob's Bridge we come across a sec- tion of the Canal pipeway—a rather important feature in connection with the Canal construction—which is to convey the waters of the Mersey and Irwell Canal to Runcorn, where they are required for the use of certain works. The walk from Warrington so far has been a hard and a wet one, and not of very great interest. Consequently the sight of the pretty village of Moore is indeed a pleasant one. Jokes on the Ship Canal are so extremely rare, that the only one I met with is worth re- cording here. On my way I met a navvy, and asked him how far I was from Moore. He told me " Mebbe a mile or so." Later on I again asked a navvy the same question. "Why," he said, "every fellow that comes along is alike. Every man Jack of em reminds me of Jem the Badger and his ale can." "How's that?" " They all ask for Moore." Not much of a joke about it, per- haps, but as a Ship Canal joke it is worth preserving. Moore is a pretty place, and the Red Lion certainly increases its attractiveness, so far, at any rate, as a thirsty and wet Special Commissioner is concerned. I don't know whether there are many inhabitants here- abouts, but I see none, and the whole place has a drowsy look about it that is inexpressively suggestive of contentment, peace, and rest. The contrast between the busy scenes I have passed through and this is very great—and pleasant Withal. From Moore to Runcorn I get a welcome lift, and consequently escape the striding from sleeper to sleeper, which, after the first mile or two, is apt to become monotonous, and a weariness to the flesh, or, at any rate, that portion of it that lies about the small of the back and the calves of the legs. I saw nothing worthy of mention en route, save a look of stagnation, and, in places, desolation. The sight of this section would just suit some of our Liverpool friends. They would attempt to find in it an augury of the future. But they would be wrong for all that, as a transformation scene is, I was told, about to be intro- duced here which will make things hum. WORE AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn, matters are at last assuming a more stir- ring appearance—they have been very quiet for some time. One of the most interesting features here is the lock at Old Quay, the construction of which may now be understood by the visitor, by means of which vessels will be able to enter the canal from the river at any state of the tide. Piling, with iron pilings and concreting of the river wall, is used here, a similar method of double walls being also adopted opposite the Bridgewater Dock to form a lock to facilitate the passing of vessels from the Bridgewater to the Ship Canal, and vice-versa. The gates for the Runcorn and Weston locks are being made at Weston Point, where the stone-work of the Weaver sluice is making great headway, and is showing itself to be a piece of very excellent work. The old Weaver jetty has been done away with, being replaced by a mit pier nearer Weston Marsh Lock.

PROGRESS AT EASTRAM. My last day's day's exploration began at the seaward end of the Canal—Eastham to wit; and as I walked along by the entrance locks, I was absolutely amazed at the progress that has been made since my last visit, some seven months ago. It is almost beyond belief that human energy could do so much in so short a time. The Canal starts from the estuary of the Mersey eight miles within the entrance, just above the old Eastham Ferry slip. A straight training bank, 900 yards in length,from the pier to the Canal gates, will have alongside it a channel 600 yards wide to admit ships into the Canal at low water of the lowest tides—a thing which the Liver- pool docks cannot do. A circumstance of some importance in regard to the size of vessels and the advantages of the Canal may be noted, as it relates to vessels like the " City of Paris." She is 580 ft. long, and some time ago she was refused entrance to the Liverpool docks because the North Docks which are the only docks there capable of accommoda- ting a steamer of her magnitude, are exposed to such strong tidal currents that the entrance is a dangerous operation. There is risk not only' of damage to the vessel, but also to the entrances of the docks, and in consequence the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board refused admission. On the Ship Canal, however, such a vessel could at least go as far as Runcorn and there dis- charge her cargo with complete immunity from the risks existing now at Liverpool. Although the Canal will accommodate vessels of this magnitude, it is well to remember that the daily average of vessels entering and leaving Liverpool is 434 tons. In the Eastern trade, the average vessel is 2,500 tons, and only almost one in fifty exceeds 3,000 tons. These the Canal can take easily. There will always be in the Canal a depth of 20ft. of water as far up as Latchford, beyond which point the tideway will hot extend. The actual length of the Canal which passes through the estuary is 13 miles 420 yards. The locks at Eastham are of three sizes, to suit the various vessels which will pass in, and so economise water. The largest of these is on the land side and is 600 ft. by 80ft. ; the middle one is 3501 t. by 50ft., and the smallest one, nearest the river, is 150 ft. by 301 1. The locks are divided by concrete piers 30f1. in width, where will be placed the arrange- , merits for opening and shutting the gates by hydraulic, ; power. In addition to the ordinary gates each lock is provided with an extra :pair of storm gates, which will be used only in rough weather, and which, by shut- ting from the outside against the lock sills,will resist the attack. of even the heaviest waves—which are here, at times, of enormous power—and prevent the tidal or ordinary gates being forced open. Each tidal gate is 46ft. in depth, whilst the largest is 401 t. wide. The largest pair are calculated to weigh 500 tons, but the storm „eates will be nearly 600 tons. I say " calculated " advisedly, as there does not seem to be a pair of scales in Eastham large enough to hold them. These gates are made in the sheds in sections, put together, then taken to pieces, well painted, and stored until they are put together again in position. Those now in their places are sources of endless wonder to visitors. The erection of the patent sluices is going on, as is that of an iron pier to divide the bywash into two equal portions. Between this Icier and the dock walls will be fixed iron gates to work up and down, by which the flow of water can be controlled with the greatest ease. As soon as this work is done, and the lock gates fixed in position, the outer hank will be removed, and Up water allowed to come right up to the lock entrances, feady for admission into the locks proper when the time comes. From Eastham to Pool Hall Bay the cutting is virtually complete, and will, according to Mr. Leader Williams, to whose skill and resistless energy the present forward state of the works may be said to be due, be filled with water in six months time. At Pool Halt a good deal of rock will require blasting and removing; but these places; which now strike the visitor as being somewhat backward, will, on the completion of other portions, have more men put on them, and soon be brought far- ward level with the rest of the work. At Ellesmer e Port the piling for the training wall is pushed on at every low tide, though it will have to be continued for a considerable length—nearly a mile, I was told, remaining to be done before the winter storms come on. Beyond Ellesmere Port the peat and sandstone are being removed as quickly as possible—work sometimes being carried on in the night.

div.head: CANAL TO BE COMPLETED IN TIME.
div.p: THE CANAL TO BE COMPLETED IN TIME.

A very general question heard on all sides is, " Will the Canal be completed in time " For those who have been over it from end to end, and noticed carefully what has been done up to now, and what there still remains to do, there can only be an answer in the affirniative. The heaviest part of the work is finished. What portion of the cutting remains to be excavated is chiefly, as a navy said, " soft " stuff that a" devil," either American or German, will make short work of. There appears to be abundance of material on every hand, and sufficient labour available. If any more is wanted it can he had without difficulty, if I may judge from the number of men I met by the Canal seeking work. By the way, I could not help noticing what a large number of the navvies I met and spoke with were from the South of England. The Irish, too, were present in goodly num- bers,but were far inferior in physique to the Southerners. I saw no Scotchmen.

CHRISTIAN KINGDOM SOCIETY. Sir,—Will you kindly allow me to bring the Christian Kingdom Society under the notice of your readers. Its aim is taemphasise the importance of individual respon- sibility and to afford opportunities to Christians of all classes and parties to take counsel together en questions affecting the public welfare. It is an outcome of the spirit of the times ; men of all denominations are longing for a bond of union based upon thus influencing for good all with whom they associate. At its conferences, i which are held monthly n different districts of London and various large towns, doctrinal matters are excluded, but all other phases of political and social life are freely discussed. The unsectanan and non-party spirit of the Society and its association with various philanthropic movements have gained for it the sympathy of men of all classes. Leaflets and further information may be had, on application by post card, to the address given here- with.—Yours truly,
ALEX. H. SMITH.
20, St. Bride-st., London, B.C.

WARRINGTON BANDS. Sir,—Would you allow me a short space in your valu- able paper to say a few words on the above. I was very much pleased to see a letter in your paper of last week pointing out what the bands of Warrington should do to get the sympathy of the people. I mustsay that I never heard the bands of Warrington play so well for the last five years as they did on last Walking Day, and it is a great pity now that Walking Day is over if the people cannot have the pleasure ot hearing some of these bands again. I must say that it was a very good suggestion that I read in your paper by one who signed himself "Musical," and I think that his suggestion ought to be taken up and worked upon. It would bring some of our bands more to the front, and not so much of their time would be spent in their practice rooms. I think that if the leaders and secretaries of the bands in Warrington were to com- bine themselves together, along with the Park Musical Committee, no doubt they would be able to frame a good brass band contest at the end of the season, say about September. The proceeds of such contest to be given to the Park Musical Committee, for I have no doubt that this hard worked and striving set of men do not get the support which they ought from the public to help them in their noble work. I have no hesitation in saving that f a brass band contest was to take place for the above named object it would be well patronised by the public, and I would further suggest that if such a contest did take place that it should not only include the bands in Warrington, but take a radius of about four or five miles around Warrington, in order that Lvmm, Widnes, Earlestown, and other places might participate in such contest.—l am, yours truly, A LOVER OF MUSIC.
