div.p: DARESBURY lIIGRWAY BOARD.

A meeting of this Board was held in the Sessions Room at Daresbury, on Thursday afternoon. Mr. J. C. Parr presided, and there were also present Messrs. J. Cliffe (vice-chairman), E. Greensll, J. Parr, T. Hall, T. S. Burgess, W. Bradford, J. Derby- shire, J. L. Jones, E. Clarke, J. Massey, J. Clarke, C. W. Phil ps, J. Lea, W. Tickle, J. S. Rigby, P. Derby- shire, P. Tickle, R. Tickle; 11. Linaker (clerk), E. G. Linaker (assistant clerk). TUE LATE CIIAIIIMAN. The Chairman said that, before they began business, he should like to express the satisfaction which, he was sure, they all felt on seeing Mr. E. Greens!! once more with them, and to express the very fervent hope that he would be entirely restored to health and strength. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: AN BNCROLCIIMENT.
div.p: AN BNCROLCIIMENT.

The County Surveyor wrote inquiring as to an inten- ded encroachment on the main road 200 or 300 yards on the Warrington side of the Sessions House at Daresbury. He (the County Surveyor) had been informed that in 1885 the Highway Board gave permission to Sir Gilbert Greenall to enclose the land in question.—The Assistant Clerk said they had replied that the Board did not give permission but that they decided not to interfere.—The Clerk: We said we never gave permission.—Mr. T. S. Burgess said that Sir Gilbert Greenall pet a drain across the road, and also provided iron places for the grids.— Mr. J. Darbvshire said he was surveyor when the subject was before the Board, and he considered that Sir Gilbert Greenllll. had made a very great improvement in the highway at the point referred to, for previous to the improvement it was a very dangerous place. It was fully consented to by the Highway Board that then existed.— The Chairman thought all the Board had to do was to leave things as they were. The County Surveyor could take his own course.—The subject then dropped.
THE SHIP CANAL COMMITTEE CHAIRMAN._
-- -- The Ship Canal Committee reported that Mr. T. S. Burgess had been elected chairman of the Committee. -

div.head: TTIE MAINTENANCE OF THE NEW ROAMS..
div.p: TTIE MAINTENANCE OF THE NEW ROAMS..

In the report of the Ship Canal. Committee it was stated that the Clerk had had an interview with Messrs. Grundy, Kershaw, and Co., solicitors to the Ship Canal Company, to discuss with them the clauses for the pro- tection of the Board in the Company's Various Powers Bill. One of the arrangements made was that as soon as the new roads to be constructed by the Company within the district of the Highway Board were completed by the Company and certified as satisfactory by the surveyor of the Board, the Company should pay to the Board such a capital sum of money as might be agreed upon, or be settled by the chairman of Quarter Sessions for the County of Chester as suffi- cient to produce when invested in government or other securities in which Highway Boards were entitled to invest money an income sufficient to provide for the increased expenses which will be incurred by the Board as compared with the expense of maintaining the present roads.

SOME SHIP CANAL ROADS NOT IN ACCORDANCE WITH PLANS. A letter was read from Mr. F. Monks calling attention to a new road made by the Ship Canal Company near Walton, and which he believed had not been made in accordance with the original plans. The deviations made the road both dangerous and undesirable for conveyances driving from Hill Cliffe to Warrington, as it would have two sharp corners to turn, which could easily be avoided. By order of the Ship Canal committee, Mr. Leader Williams had been written to in reference to this com- plaint, and he replied that the alteration to the road had been made on the suggestion of the Ship Canal Committee itself, as it would be an improve- ment.—Mr. T. S. Burgess said he well remembered Mr. James Parr making the suggestion, but it was not put upon the minutes of the Committee. The alteration was certainly an improvement for people going to Ches- ter, but it was rather bad for people coming from Hill Cliffe.—The Chairman said if the alteration had been made by the sanction of the Ship Canal Committee it would be hard for the Board to turn round now and say they did not approve of it.—Mr. James Parr agreed with this.—lt was agreed to refer tke matter to the Ship Canal Committee.—The ship Canal Committee also brought under the notice of the Board the fact that the Ship Canal Company had denarted from their deposited plans in the making of the new road at Morris Brook. In a letter on this subject, Mr. Leader Williams wrote that plans of the alteration had been submitted to the late surveyor, and that the making of the road had been carried out under his inspection. In regard to this the late surveyor (Mr: Peerman), had been written to by the Clerk, and he replied that he had never had any plan of the alteration submitted to him, or he should have called the Committee together.—The Chairman : Is this a serious matter ?—Mr. W. Bradford thought it was a serious matter, as the alterations made very awkward turns in the road.—The Chai!man asked if it was quite clear the Company had deviated from their original plans.—The Clerk said it was quite clear. They had gone round the end of a building and the plans showed that they must go through the building. was decided that the Ship Canal Company should be informed. that the Board were determined to adhere to the original plans with regard to this road.

The Coroner's inquest on the bodies of Mrs. O'Connor and her four children, who were poisoned at Seapo.int, County Dublin, was concluded on Thursday. The jury found that death had been caused by the eating of mussels taken from a pond which had been impregnated with sewage matter, and they recommended that immediate steps should be taken to have the pond filled up. They also took occasion, to express their sincere ITlnpathy with )&r. O'Connor in his addiction,.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAMRDAY, JULY 12, 1890.

THE CHESHIRE POLICE ADMINISTRATION. THE EVIDENCE AGAINST O'DONNELL. A • SCENE. His Honour Sir Horatio Lloyd presided. on Saturday, at Chester Castle, at the sixth sitting of the sub-com- mittee of inquiry into Mr. Slater Lewis's charges against the Cheshire police, the other members of the comn.ittee present being Messrs. Duncan Graham, James Tomkin- son. C. Lister, and Joseph Beckett. , Mr. Fletcher (for the police) first called Dr. McDougall, of Runcorn, who said that during a 22 ye:..rs' residence in Runcorn he had been for a considerable time in attend- ance on several members of the family of Superintendent Hollingworth, whom he knew,since he was an inspector. During that period he had had many opportunities of judging of Hollingworth's character, and certainly had no suspicion that he was a drunkard. As medical officer of health for the district, he wished to take exception to a statement by ex-Invector O'Donnell in May last that he had had great difficulty in regard to brothels; that the town was in a very immoral state ;and that the police had great difficulty in dealing with them in conseque ice. That was not a true statement, for to his knowledge there was not a single brothel in Runcorn. Since the Criminal Law Amendment Act was passed in 1887, lodging house inspectors were appointed, who brought home to the owners of the houses the fact that the penalties would be enforced, with the result that they were done away with. In this work he had had the valuable assistance and support of Superintendent Hol- lingworth. It was not due to the exertions of ex- Inspector O'Donnell that thediminution of these houses occurred. He was a mischievous and interfering person. and created a very unfavourable impression in the divi- sion, which had become still stronger in consequence of the aspersions he was endeavouring to cast upon the police.—James Collier, assistant overseer of Weston, stated that during a long acquaintance with Holling- worth he had never seen him intoxicated.—George Hayes, stationer, said he had never seen Hollingworth drunk. He had never had reason to complain of in- sufficiency of police protection in Runcorn. Be had known the superintendent for a long time, but had always considered him a sober man.—Edwin Tuckey, a barge owner, Runcorn, gave corroborative evidence, saying he had seen as much of the superintendent as any man in Runcorn, and had never seen him the worse of liquor. He had never heard any com- plaint of the Runcorn police force being drunken. W. Hankinson' mineral water manufacturer, and a member of theßuncam Board of Commissioners, also deposed to an acquaintance with Hollingworth, whom he had never seen under the influence of drink. He was a respectable officer, and discharged his duties most effi- ciently. If O'Donnell had done his work less 'officiously be would have got on better. As it was, he was so un- popular that he had to go about the town with a body• guard of two constables, whilst the present inspector did his duty quietly and incurred no opprobrium.— William Anderton, keeper of the Anchor Inn, Runcorn, wasthen called, and denied that Hollingworth had ever been drunk in his house.--Superintendent Hollingworth was next examined. He stated that he had, been 25 years in the Cheshire constabulary, and before that time had experience in police work at Manchester for four years. He denied that the charge made against him by ex-Constable Wright, of conducting himself im- properly with an immoral woman in a police cell, had the slightest foundation. With regard to the charge made against him of having been drunk on licensed pre- mises at the Anchor Inn, be said he had just called after hours to ascertain what was the cause of the noise in the yard of the house, and found that there were some cleaning operations going on, when he encountered Inspector O'Donnell on passing out. O'Donnell said, " It's all right," and turned back. Relations between himself and the inspector had been strained for some time back. Shortly afterwards, O'Donnell made a vague complaint of his conduct to witness, who told him to put any charge or complaint in writing and he would forward them to the chief con- stable. He denied in the police court that he had been drunk in Wilson's Hotel. O'Donnell got all the town ablaze three months after he came there without any cause whatever. Before he came the magistrates had such an interest in suppressing drunkenness that they never fined men less than 10s. and costs, but after O'Donnell had been there three months it was generally 2s. 6d. and costs.—By Mr. Beckett: How do you connect that with O'Donnell ? Witness : That is my opinion.—Mr. Lewis :It was a reduction for a large order. (Laughter.) —ln cross-examination by Mr. Lewis he admitted having been Zned 2s. and reprimanded for drunken- ness in Nantwich, 1889. He refused to say whether he had ever been drunk except on that occasion, but said he had never been reported for drunkenness besides that. There were exceptional circumstances in that case. His boy had just been killed on the railway, and he ad- mitted giving way to drink then.—Mr. Lewis complained that he had not been supplied with a rolice instruction book, although he had repeatedly asked for one. —Colonel Hamersley said he could not spare one.— Mr. Lewis: That is a very lame excuse.—Colonel Ham- ersley: It is true. sir.—Mr. Lewis : I don't believe it ; that 13 the plain English of it.—Colonel Hamersley: You may not believe it. After that expression from Mr. ' Lewis, I will not say any more.—The Chairman: We have conducted this inquiry so far—Mr. Lewis: I have said I do not believe that he cannot spare the book. —Colonel Hamersley (to Mr. Lewis) : Say it outside.— The Chairman said he hoped they would not exhibit any display of feeling in this way.—Colenel Hamersley : Well, when a man calls you a liar.—Mr. Lewis: I did not call you a liar ; I said I did not believe you could not spare a copy.—The Chairman said a copy I had been in the hands of the Committee all week.— , Colonel Hamersley : Yes, I can get a cepy for each member of the committee.—Mr. Lewis: Then why did you say that you could not spare one for me ?—Colonel Hamersley: 1 decline to give you a copy.—Mr. Lewis: Well, I said I did not believe you, and I don't.—Colonel Hamersley: Say it outside.—On the resumption of the sitting, after half-an-hour's adjournment, Mr. Lewis said: Just whilst the few last unfortunate words were being said, the Chief Constable said he would like me to make use of those words outside. I would like to ask him as chief-constable of the county what he meant by that? He said it as chief-constable of the county, and it is inciting to a breach of the peace. —The Chairman: When a gentleman, whether he is the chief-constable— Mr. Lewis (to Colonel Hamersley): lam not afraid of you, Colonel Hamersley, and it is a most improper thing to be said.—The Chairman : You must remember, Mr. Lewis, that you begun this by say- ing you did not believe Colonel Hamersley. It is natur- ally irritating.—Mt. Lewis : But it does not follow that Colonel Hamersley should make use of remarks like that, and threaten personal violence.—Members of the Com- mittee : I didn't hear it.—Mr. Fletcher : It is only mak- ing mischief.—Mr. Lewis: It is not. Everybody heard ' it. Ask the shorthand writer or anybody. Mr. Fletcher.—Some things are better nct heard.—Mr. Lewis: I quite agree with you. Philip Speakman, a member of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, was then called, and stated that he had been acquainted with Hollingworth for a considerable time, and had never heard the slightest hint that he was an intemperate man. He thought it only right, in the interests of Superintendent Fiollingworth, to make that statement, having been in RULICOIn all his life, and known him as inspector and superintendent.—TheChair- man asked Mr. Lewis whether he had any hope of closing the inquiry that evening.—Mr. Lewis said he did! not wish to hurry it to a close, but to sift it to the bot- tom.—The Chairman said there were other things to be considered—the time and expense. The inquiry was extending to an inordinate length, and if they could not finish that day it would be most difficult to fix another. —Mr. Lewis said it was a great sacrifice of time and money to him, which he could ill-afford, but he wished the truth to be got at and the thing thoroughly bot- toined.—Mr. bFletcher said he was afraid he must ask for another adjournment, for three of his witnesses who could not be there that afternoon.— The Chairman said they wese prepared to sit till seven if they could finish that day. It was a serious loss of time, and for the last hour Mr. Lewis had not advanced the inquiry one atom by his cross-examination of Holling- worth.—Mr. Ashton, Clerk to the Runcorn magistrates, was then called. He had never seen Hollingworth to be in the slightest under the influence of drink; he was always a very efficient officer, and compared favaurably with any other superintendent they had had at Runcorn; He had never heard of such a thing as cases being ad- journed to get a particular tribunal. He had never seen him fall asleep in Gourt.—Mr. Fletcher : Perhaps Mr. Lewis was not cross-examining.—P.C. Pickford then denied that he had ever told Inspector O'Donnell that a woman whom he took to jail had made a complaint to him of Hollingworth misconducting himself when in a cell.—P.C. Mason was next examined, and stated in the I course of his evidence that the constables habitually screened ex-P.C. Joseph Wright, the " drunkenest " man in the section, from discovery by the sergeant. He " would not take the responsibility"' of reporting him. He was not a sneak, and Wright was an old man and had a farnilv.—P.C. Wooley, of Runcorn, said that 0' Donnell used constantly to annoy the constables by whistling for them. One evening he whistled, and they all ran up, thinking murder was being committed. When he came up, O'Donnell abused him shamefully, and said to hint, Wooley, you are either a wise man or a fool." Witness said, "I may be a bit of both; but what do you mean?" He then Said, "You have seen Superintendent Hollingworth corn- ing out of the Wilson Hotel drunk?" Witness said "No, I have not." He then said, "I have reported the superintendent, and you shall never look behind you if you will back me out." Witness replied that he would not tell a lie for anybody, and told him it he said any more he should report him. Witness did report him.— Mr, Beckett: What was the whistling for P—Witness : I could never find out what it was for.—The object would be to see if the men were on the alert? I think it was I fear. I never knew him to go about the streets alone. He was hated so much that he dared not go alone.--Fhe next witness, Sergeant Gosling, stated that O'Donnell ' had tried to give the cases of one constable to another to prove. He had given evidence in one case, and made it appear as though an offence was committed in two streets when it occurred inside one house. He had also reported constables going on duty for being drunk when they were "solid and sober." His cursing and swearing at the men had caused tumoral to resign. Qn one occasion

he taxed Superintendent Hollingworth, in the presence of witness and two other men with being drunk. One said, "You are not drunk ; " another," You are certainly not drunk ; " and witness said, "If he says you are drunk he will say anything."—Other witnesses having been callei , the inquiry was adjourned for three weeks.

THE RAINFORD TRAGEDY. (Continued from page $.) STATEMENT BY THE FEMALE PRISONER. The second stage in elucidation of the Rainford tragedy was entered upon yesterday morning at the Prescot Police Station. when the prisoners, John Duckworth Pickavance, and his wife, Mary Jane Pickavance, were brought up charged with the wilful murder of Henry Granger Poster, at Rainford, on Monday. Intense inter- est still continued to be manifested in the case, and though the facts were brought out pretty fully at the inquest, it was expected that further disclosures would he made at the magisterial inquiry. Numbers of people assembled at the entrance to the court, and before the business commenced the small courtroom was filled with spectators, great anxiety being evinced to catch a glimpse of the prisoners. Mr. J. 0. Swift, solicitor, St. Helens, has been instructed to appear for the prisoners. At a I quarter-past eleven Captain Willis tcok his seat on the bench. It was not until half-past eleven o'clock that the pri- soners made their appearance in the dock. Little change was noticed in their demeanour. A constable in uniform stood between the prisoners, both of whom were very composed. The male prisoner hung down his head, arid did not even look up when Superintendent Barker orm- ally stated that the prisoners were charged ,with the wilful murder of Mr. Foster. Without further preface and before Mr. Segar, who represented the relatives of the deceased, had taken his seat, the superintendent pro- ceeded to call witnesses. The first to enter the box was Alice Leigh, house- keeper to deceased, who deposed to the visit of the pri- soners to deceased's house on the the Sunday night. The housekeeper added nothing to her statement before the coroner. While confident that Mrs. Pickavance was one of the two who asked for Air. Foster, she could not iden- tify the man. Mr. Seger having intimated that although anxious on behalf of the deceased's relatives to give every assistance, he had no right to take part in the in- quiry. Mrs. Morris, landlady of the Old Saddle beer- house, detailed how the prisons obtained admission to her house on the Sunday night. She recounted the con- versation, and the significant remark of the male pri- soner, "I don't know whether we shall be here again. We are both in the same business." Then came John Woods, who witnessed the attack on Mr. Foster, from the field close to Rainflrd Station. He heard shots fired, and seeing a man throw up his arms and fall, ran to the high- way where he found Mr. Foster lying on the road. His assailants had run away. When Mr. Foster fell a man was firing at him from a few yards' distance, aLd the woman was about ten yards further away. He could, not identify either the man or the woman. Up to this time, the only question Mr. Swift had asked was put to the witness Morris, who said she knew the female prisoner when in Mr. Foster's service, which she left about August last. Another witness of the murder. John Grace, farmer, was also too far off to be able to identify Foster's assailants. He stated that on hearing the firing of shots he saw two men on the road struggling in close quarters, Foster having his arm up to try and save himself. At this time the woman was about twenty yards from the two men, but she turned back about half-way, and subsequently both the man and the woman ran away towards Rainford Village. The next witness was Mr. Alfred Pennington, of Mun- caster-hall, who was driving in his trap to Rainford Station on Monday morning, and passed and repassed Mr. Foster within a few hundred yards of the scene of the murder. He afterwards drove the injured man home to Brook-lodge. Ellen Riding, who lives at Brook-cottage, proved find- ing two bullets on the roadway, near to pools of blood, and Edward Davies, collier, deposed to discovering two bullets and three cartridge cases, the latter having some distance apart on the road, by which the assailants had made their escape. The police next called a witness who had not been before the coroner. It turned out to be Henry Hutch- logs, a youth about 18, a brother of the female prisoner. His evidence was that he visited prisoner's house in Prescot about a fortnight ago, when the male prisoner brought down stairs two revolvers of different sizes, one of which was loaded in its five chambers. Pickavance unloaded the revolver in witness's presence, and he could say the spent cartridges produced were similar to those with which the revolver was loaded. Witness, questiontd by Mr. Swift, said the male prisoner asked him if he could get a customer for the revolver, and he promised to do what he could. Dr. Murdoch repeated the evidence as to the injuries deceased sustained, stating that the bullet which enter- ed the brain caused death. Externally deceased showed no indication of disease. While Dr. Murdoch was giving his evidence the female prisoner burst out crying and sobbed bitterly for some time. Pickavance, although dejected, paid great attention to the evidence, and had several consultations with his solicitor. The interest displayed in the proceedings became intense when Police-sergeant Smith, after recounting how he pursued and captured the prisoners at Eccleston Four- Lane Ends, went on to state the circumstances under which the female prisoner made to him the statement in which she confessed that under the threats of her hus- band she took part in the attack on Foster, and fired a shot at him. Stress was laid on the fact that prisoner volunteered the statement, and was cautioned that it might be used against her. Witness produced the state- ment which was read by the magistrates' clerk. Evi- dence of this witness concluded the case for the prosecution. The male prisoner reserved hie defence. The female prisoner said, "All I wish to say in addition to what I said to the officer, is this—Mr. Foster had seduced me and ruined me while I lived with him, and it was because my husband got to know of this that he was nearly out of his mind." The prisoners were then formally com- mitted to take their trial at the next assizes.

ARREST OF A ST. HELENS EX-TOWN COUNCILLOR. Mr. William Kirham, an ex-town councillor for St. Melens, was on Wednesday night arrested in Sunderland on a charge of leaving his family charge- able to the common funds of the Prescot Union. In 1887 Kirkham, who was an auctioneer and estate agent carrying on business in Ton- tine-st., became a representative on the Town •Council for East Sutton Ward, but soon after taking ins seat domestic differences agitated the public mind, and tradesmen were/still more affected when the rumour gained ground that he and his house- keeper had gone for a long holiday. Evidence was forthcoming that he had sailed for New York, and again later, it was rumoured that he had been seen in Liverpool. At the beginning of this week a bt. Helens man who resides in Sunderland sent word thet Kirkham, under another name, Was running an oyster shop in that town, and it was decided to send over and ascertain if the news was correct. The result was his arrest on Wednesday night. His movements since he left St. Helens have been shrouded in mystery. It appears that the Prescot Union authorities had information that Kirkham was in Sunderland four or five days since, and this was followed by-careful action. Mr. Barton, reliev- ing officer for Eccleston, in which township the Kirkhams resided, and a Prescot constable were despatched on Wednesday to, bring Kirkham to St. Helens.

THE PAROCHIAL SCHOOLS.—The results attained by the children attending these schools in their recent examina- tion by the Rev. J. Lomax and his assistants (Messrs. Parke and Webb) reflect creditably upon the headmaster and mistress and their staff of teachers. • A WOMEN'S LIBERAL ASSOCIATION FOR LTMIII.—At a meeting of the members of the Lymm Liberal Associa- tion on Monday evening at the Club-room, a committee of six members was appointed to consider the advisability of establishing a branch of the Women's Liberal Assccia- tion for Lymm and district. FOLICB COURT.—At the Police Court, On Tuesday morning, before Dr. Brabazon and Mr. T. P. Norris, John Adams (22) and William Jones (14), both of Irlam, were charged with stealing a quantity of gooseberries. value ed., from the orchard of Mr. James Warburton, at Partington, the previous day. Each of the defendants was fined 2s. ed., and costs 7s. 2d. In each instance the money was paid. Crroia TRIP.—On Monday the members of the Con- gregational Church choir, to the number of about 30, together with the Pastor (the Rev. Charles Clay), Mr. Richard Dutton (deacon), and Mr. Astley (choir master), had their annual excursion. Liverpool being the destina- tion selected. Some of the trippers went for a sail to Wales; others went across the water to New Brighton, whilst the Museum and Art Gallery were also well pat- ionized. LOYAL ORDER or ANCIENT SHEPHERDS, A..U.' WAR.. RINOTON DISTRICT.—The annual meeting of this district was held at the house of 13ro. Winstanley, Nag's Head Hotel, Lymm, on Saturday, Pro, C. S. Peter Buckley presiding, supported by D.P.C.S. Samuel Dunn, trea- surer and relieving officer, John Allen, Pro. Cor. Sec. Abel Henry Mather. There were twenty-four delegates present, representing 880 members and 44 widows. lln opening the meeting the ,Pro. C. S. congratulated the members upon the steady progress of the district, and wished every lodge a prosperous and happy year. I After the usual t business had been gone through, the following officers were elected to .serve for the following year: Pro. C.S., Sairtnel Dunn; D.P.C.S., Peter Kirk- ham ; treasurer and relieving officer, John Allen; Pro. Cor. Sec., Abel Henry Mather; trustees, James Parr, Thomas Groark, Arthur F. G. Potter; book examiners, Robert Ditchfield, and David Harris. After the new officers were installed, the best thanks of the meeting were given to Bro. Buckley, and it was further resolved that he receive the testimonial given to past officers, also to treasurer and relieving officer John Allen. The delegate to the annual meeting, P.M. G. Leigh, pre- sented his reports, showing the progress the order was making, both numerically and financially.

THE SELLING or DEBTS.—George :Newton Vernon, debt collector and agent, Warrington, sued Charles Paul, a jeweller lately carrying on business at Bewsey Cham- bers as Messrs. Armstrong and Co., for £5O damages for alleged breach of contract. Mr. Arthur Browne appeared for plaintiff and defendant made no appearance. Mr. Browne stated that on the 18th May his client saw the defendant with the object of buying some book debts from him and on the following day the defendant agreed to sell the debts, amounting to something like £250, for £ll9 10s. A deed was ordered to be drawn up and defendanbpromised to sign it. On the following Mon- day, however, he wrote stating that he had to make the , book debts over as security for cash lent. The plaintiff I then brought the present action which should have been heard on the 21st June, but four days before defendant offered to sell the debts, minus about £4O which had been paid for £95. The defendant, however, left the town, and nothing came of the matter.—Plaintiff said he expected to make £BO out of the -transaction had the book debts been assigned to him. After hearing the .evidence, his Honour gave a verdict for plaintiff for £3 13s. and costs. He held that the contract had not been entered into and he simply gave the plaintiff the costs which he had incurred through the defendant having failed to keep his promise to sign the deed of assign- ment. A CLAIM FOR FIIRNITURE.—James Brown, farmer, of Pennsylvania, America, sued Richard Milshaw, landlord of the Big Horse Shoe, Horsemarket-st., Warrington for £5O, £45 of which was for goods detained, and £5 dam- ages for detention. Mr. P. Mullholland, barrister, Liver- pool, (instructed by Messrs. P. Davies and ForshaW), represented the plaintiff, and Mr. Horridge, barrister, Liverpool, (instructed by Messrs. Ashton and Woods) appeared on behalf of the defendant. There was a counter claim of £l4l for the maintenance of plaintiff's son. James Brown, the plaintiff, said he was a farmer and carried on business in Pennsylvania, America, whither he went in 1879. His wife died a few years before and left a child, a boy. His wife had a sister named Margaret and she married a Mr. Kilshaw in 1881. The articles enumerated in the claim belonged to him. They included bcxes, drawers, stuffed birds and tamily relics. He left the articles with Miss Fairclough to take charge of, and he did not return until May of this year. She died in 1884 having meanwhile married the defen- dant. On coming to England witness called on defen- dant and pointed out the articles and said they were his and he gave a short history of each. Defendant said his wife had not told him that the things belonged to plaintiff and he would see his sister about the matter. Witness again saw him and defendant then gave him a eup, knife, some books and other articles and his wife's wedding ring. Defend- ant said as tegarded a gold watch, the witness's son had given it to „defendant's sister the day before his death, which took place last November. Defendant had since refused tolive up the other articles.—Wm. Fairclough, farmer, flurtonwood, deposed to bringing plaintiff's fur- niture to his sister's house when plaintiff went to America.—For the defence Mr. Horridge said that his client stated that he had never been in vossession of a number of the articles claimed. With respect to the other things,, they contended that there was no evidence to identify them.—His Honour, in summing up, said he considered the plaintiff had not proved his case in all particulars, but he save a verdict for plaintiff for the re- turn of the majority of tho goods. With respect to the counter claim. his Honour held that he had no jurisdic- tion. Execution was ordered to be stayed for ten days to see if the defendant commenced action in the High Court: • A BAND AS AN ADVERTISEMENT. Jacob Nagil, a German bandsman, sued "Dr. Galen," a medicine vendor, for £34 19s. 'wages owing. There was a counter claim Of £lo.—Mr. Browne represented the defendant.— Plaintiff stated that defendant was a medicine vendor, and engaged him as a Irass instrument player to play in ' the band around the town. Plaintiff and five ether players were engaged to play and were to be paid £4 10s. per week. The money now claimed was owing.—For , the defence Mr. Browne contended that plaintiff had net credited his client with all the amounts paid to him and , further that through plaintiff going away drinking the I defendant lost considerably in 'business.—Defendant stated that his name was John Bounds and he traded as Dr. Galen and travelled about with some medicine of his own known as "Mayflower." THII "DEVOURING MISCHIEF OF MILITARISM."—MV. Gladstone, acknowledging an invitation to preside at a banquet in connection with the forthcoming Interna- tional Conference on Arbitration, says it is not without regret that he foregoes an occasion of protest against the devouring mischief of militarism which is consumingthe vitals 6f Europe, and which operates even in this coun- try, although we have so many advantages for resisting it. His rule, however, is to avoid extra Parliamentary action in connection with associations out of ' doors In which, officially or otherwise, he has been called to take a prominent part.

div.p: MR. CAINE AN]) WARRINGrON.

We understand that since Mr. Caine's very definite pronouncement that nothing would please him better than to contest a constituency repre- sented by a big brewer, he has been written to by more than one elector of Warrington as to his views with regard to opposing Sir Gilbert Greenall at the next election. One of the replies received from Mr. Caine has been made 'Public, and reads as follows : " Dear Sir,-,I am much obliged to you for your kind letter, but I do not intend to take any action with regard to a constituency jus at present. I hope to spend the coming winter in India." It is needless to say that the letters which have been written to Mr. Caine from Warrington were simply the indivi- dual expressions of opinion of the writers them- selves, and were in no way authorised by the local , leaders of the Liberal party. 1

THE PHONOGRAPH AND THE WEDDING BELLS. Colonel Gouraud has presented to Mr. Stanley a phono- graph as a wedding present. There are only four phono- graphs in England. Three will be in Westminster Abbey during the wedding service. One will be placed in the tower, to record the full sound of the wedding bells. The second phonograph will be placed by the organ to note the music and the Wedding March. The third will be placed in the choir, and give the hymn as sung by the voices. These records will be presented by Colonel Gouraud to Mr. and Mrs. Stanley, so that at any time hereafter the wedding bells, the organ, and the voices will sound as on the 12th July, 1890. This is the first occasion on which the phonograph has been used to record wedding bells and the music of a marriage, service. A STEPFATHER'S PRESENT. Mr. tßobert Jones, of the Cross Foxes Inn, St. Asaoh, who married Mr. 11. M. Stanley's mother, has just sent up to Miss Tennant, Stanley's bride, a curious and yet valuable tea tray belonging to Stanley's late mother, the card of presentation being thus inscribed—'' fir oes a thangnefedd i'r ddauddyn. The favourite tea tray of Mrs. Jones, of Glascoed, St. Asaph, North Wales, mother of Henry Id. Stanley, Esq., presented to Miss Dorothy Tennant by Robert Jones, the bereaved widower, on the occasion of her marriage with his illustrious Aepson. Cross Foxes; Clascoed, July 9th, 1890." Many of the residents in the neighbourhood familiar with Stanley's boyhood take deep interest in his marriage.

div.head: OUTRAGEOUS CONDUCT IN THE PARK.
div.p: OUTRAGEOUS CONDUCT IN THE PARK.

The Warrington magistrates had before them on Mon- day a case in which a middle-aged man named Joseph Willans, an hon-planer, who lives at 18, Heaton-street, was brought up in custody on a charge of having inde- cently assaulted a girl namea Stewart, nine years of age, in Bank Park, en Saturday afternoon. He was further charged with disgraceful conduct in the presence of several children. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk) prosecuted, and Mr. Arthur Browne defended the pri- soner, who is a hunchback. From the evidence of the park keeper and other witnesses, it appeared that the prisoner was sitting with several little girls on a seat near the bandstand, where he committed the offence with which he was charged. Acting on the advice of his solicitor, the prisoner pleaded guilty to an aggravated assault, the prosecution agreeing to reduce the charge to that. Mr. Browne stated that for the last ten years the prisoner had been in the employ of the Cheshire Lines Committee, at their Battersby-lane works. He was a married man with °Re child, and had hitherto borne an , irreproachable character. . In view of the good character given the prisoner by Mr. George Walker, one of his masters, the Bench imposed a fine of £5 and costs, 31s. ed., the Mayor remarking that but for Mr. Walker's testimony the prisoner would probably have been sent to gaol for three or six months.

LATEST NEWS.
HEAVY SENTENCE FOR CRUELTY TO A CHILD.

At Sheffield Borough Sessions, on Friday morning, Thomas Lloyd and Lavinia Cousins were found guilty of neglecting and ill-treating Rose Ann M'lntyre, aged four years. Lloyd was sentenced to five years' penal servitude, and Cousins to two years' hard labour.
MID-DURHAM ELECTION: NOMINATION OF , CANDIDATES.

The nomination of candidates for Mid-Durham, to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. John Crawford, took place at Durham on Friday. Mr. John Wilson (Gladstonian Liberal) and the Hon. Vane Tempest (Con- servative) were nominated. The polling takes place next Thursday, the 17th instant. REPORTED SERIOUS ILLNESS OF MR. STANLEY. A London correspondent telegraphed last night that it was stated on good authority that Mr. Stanley was taken seriously ill of gastritis, from which he suffered when he was in Africa. ' Dr. Parke and two London doctors were attending him, and it was understood that they had grave doubts whether the explorer woald be suffi- ciently wsll to be married to-day in Westminster Abbey.

div.head: ATROCIOUS MURDER OF A MOTHER.
div.p: ATROCIOUS MURDER OF A MOTHER.

John Hart, of Ballyneale, county Kilkenny, on Thurs- day killed his mother, with whom he was living, cutting her to pieces. Some fishermen on Friday discovered the mangled woman with the son lying on her body, as they alleged, eating the flesk. When arrested he said he was sorry he did it. He was taken to New Ross and remanded on the capital charge. Some time ago he was refused admittance to a lunatic asylum. The doctors say ho is sane.

div.head: FATAL RACE FIGHTING IN GEORGIA.
div.p: FATAL RACE FIGHTING IN GEORGIA.

- NEW Yorm, FamA.v.—A serious fight has occurred at I Griffin, Georgia, between whites and negroes. Several men of each race were assembled at a drawing-off pond for the purpose of catching fish when a dispute arose as to their respective rights over certain parts of the lake. Words were soon supplemented by six shooters, and in a melee which resulted sixteen of the opponents werg killed. The incident threatens to engender a race war through- out the country. EXTRAORDINARY OUTRAGE BY AN IRISH

div.head: POLICEMAN.
div.p: POLICEMAN.

At Tipperary, Constable Palmer was charged with wrecking a number of houses at Rathnaveen. He ran amuck late at night and smashed the windows of houses with stones and threatened to kill one of the occupants. The defendant did not appear, and it was announced he had left the country. In his absence .he was sentenced to two months' imprisonment, and ordered to pay com- pensation and heavy fines. _

div.head: TFIE-LONDON POSTMEN.
div.p: TFIE-LONDON POSTMEN.

At the Gene;til—Po;t—O-tiCe the carriers and sorters I arrived in good time on Friday morning, and the work seemed to proceed smoothly. The reports from the dis- trict offices, too, were satisfactory to the authorities, who anticipated that throughout the day all the deliver- ies would be made with little or no delay. The Parcels Office at Mount Pleasant presented its normal appearance on Friday morning. All the men who were expected turned up to time, and worked without a hitch, whilst some of the discharged men begged to be reinstated.

div.head: MORE TROUBLE AT THE LONDON DOCKS.
div.p: MORE TROUBLE AT THE LONDON DOCKS.
- At the Royal Albert Docks the British India Steam- ship Company's men refuse •to discharge the Queensland liner Jumna unless the men discharged are again taken . .

on. On the arrival of this vessel on Friday the passen- gers had to carry their own baggage ashore. The Dockers' Union and Stevedore Society support the action of the men. At the Royal Victoria Docks, London, on Friday morning, the labourers employed by the Turner line, trading with New York and Boston, struck work. The British Indian Company's men still hold out, and others threaten to strike.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.—FRIDAY. AFFAIRS IN IRELAND.—Lord CAMPERDOWN drew atten- tion to the recent occurrences in the town of Tipperary and on the Ponsonby estate in the County of Cork, and attention to the action of the Land League. He said, after all attempts on the part of the Ponsonby trustees had faileil,Mr. Smith Barry earned the hatred of the National League by coming to the rescue. The existing dis- content and all which followed he laid at the door of the National League.—The MARQUIS Of LONDONDERRY attacked Earl Spencer for having thrown over the whole of his opinion in regard to Irish affairs in favour of Irish nationalists.—Earl SPENCER justified his statement that the frish were entitled to combine its legal way to get rents lowered,—Lord ASHBOURNE connected Mr. Gladstone's political necessities with the change.—Earl KIMBERLEY believed Home Rule for Ireland would before long be- come law.—Earl CADOGAN thought Earl Spencer and his friends should use their influence with the National League to stop outrage.—The subject then dropped. The House then adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS—Patna:. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. UN/TEDSTATES TARIFF.—Mr. FERGUSSON informed Mr. Howard Vineent that the Government had reason to believe the German Government did not at present con- template any action respecting the new United States TELE INLAND REVENUE OFFICERS.—Mr. GOSCHEN, reply- ing to Sir John Puleston, said he was examining the petition of the Inland Revenue officers. THE ANGILO-GERMAN AGREEMENT.—Mr. SMITH, reply- ing to Mr. Channing, said he could not say anything as to the negotiations with France respecting Zanzibar, nor could he undertake to postpone the Anglo-German Agree- ment Bill until these negotiations were concluded. THE LONDON POSTMEN.—Mr. RAIKES, replying to Mr. Conybeare, said he that day received a deputation of postmen of E. C. district and promised to consider care- fully their representations. The interview was likely to lead to very good results. (Cheers.)—Mr. SMITH, reply- ing to Mr. Buxton, said he could not relieve heads of post office of responsibility by granting a Committee. (Renewed cheers.)—Mr. CONYI3EARE gave notice to move the adjournment of the House, but Mr. Raikes having said he had promised to carefully consider the represen- tations of postmen, Mr.Conybeare withdrew the notice. THE MANAGEMENT OF VOLUNTARY SCHOOLS.—Mr. Charles Acland obtained leave to introduce a Bill to amend the law respecting the management of voluntary schools' and it was read a first time. THE GOVERNMENT AND IRELAND.—The HMSO again into Committee on the Chief Secretary's vote.—Mr. Blume continued his speech in opposition to the policy of the Government in Ireland, which he had not finished when progress was reported the previous night. He arraigned the Government for cooking statistics in order to show Ireland was disturbed or quiet as suiteff the movement. Speaking of the money vote for public works in Ireland, he said he favoured pubic works on natural and economic systems, but he warned them that such a system could only be obtained under a native Government.—Mr. Balfour denied the charge of cooking statistics as baseless and absurd. It would be obvious to all men that Government had vindicated the laws and protected the weak against the strong. They had done more than any other Govern- ment to improve the material, prosperity of the poorest people in the south and west of Ireland, and they had made larger contributions towards the settlement of the Irish Land question than had ever been attempted or even dreamed of by Irish reformers in the past.—Mr. T. P. O'CoNnon said the effect of the Irish policy of the Government had been to convert electors of Great Bri- tain to Home RUle.
I-LEFT SITTING.]

div.p: THE SHIP CANAL AND THE COAL

TRADE. The "Colliery Guardian" gives some particulars with reference to the advantages, so far as the cost of carriage and delivery of coal alongside steamer, which the canal will offer to the coal trade. South Wales coal can her' brought to Warrington, there placed upon the ship Canal, and taken alongside steamer in the Ship Canal at the same price that it is now taken alongside at Liver- pool. South Yorkshire coal, which is nearly equal for bunker purposes to South Wales steam Coal, will cost 3s. per ton less alongside steamer in the Ship Canal than South Wales coal is delivered alongside steamer at Liver- pool, and Lancashire coal could be placed alon,gside steamer in the canal at is. 4d. per ton less than it . can be delivered alongside steamer at Liverpool It may be further stated that although the canal corn; pony are giving facilities for shipping coal from a great number of the Lancashire collieries, as well as from all the South Yorkshire collieries, they have not provideei for those collieries which have access to the London and North-Western Railway Company's system. It is well known that whilst the railway companies never hsd syrre • pathy with the Ship Canal movement they were net :5e . antagonistic as to stake their own interest in opPee'nf; it. The London and North-Western Railway Company have, however, been very bitter opponents to their enter- prise all along, and as a consequence the directors of the Ship Canal Company are not sufficieatly in touch with the directors of the London and North-Western Railwl Company to enable them to provide for the exchange traffic between the two companies, and such arrang!: ments as may be made will very much depend upon tuo pressure which the colliery owners may bring to be.ars upon the railway company in securing tipping facilit to meet the requirements of their trade.

THE PLEURO- PNEUMONIA OUTBREAK. There have been no fresh outbreaks of pleuro- pneumonia during the week within the limits •of the borough, but the disease seems to be creating considerable havoc among the caul,- of farmers located in the country district roundabout. The restrictions that were at once adopted in the borouogh yet remain in force, however, and in con- sequence the half-yearly cattle fair, which in the ordinary course of things would have taken place • next Thursday, will not be held. It is confidently hoped that, so far as the borough is concerned, the decisive measures that were taken to arrest and stamp out the disease have been successful. On Saturday afternoon, by order of the county . authorities, 17 Cows and heifers belonging to Mr. William Bennett, of Bruche Hall, Padgate, were slaughtered. None of the animals were diseased, but, iris stated, they had been in contact .with others which had been previously slaughtered. Pleuro-pneumonia has also broken out on the pre- mises of Mr. George Gleave, Healey head Farm, Burtonwood. One• animal out of fourteen on the place has been slaughtered. Those remaining that have been in contact, will also be killed. • Mr. J. Cooper, of Tan House Farm, Burtonwood, upon whose premises an outbreak of pleuro-pneu- monia was discovered, has had to slaughter the whole of his stock of four cows. By order of the County Council, the whole of the cattle (53) pastured in Winwick Park, were on Wed- nesday destroyed in consequence of the recent outbreak of pleuro-pneumonia. The disease has also broken out on the farm of Mr. George Bower, of Appleton, where one animal has been slaughtered. There are 27 more on the same farm, and it is expected that they also will have to be slaughtered. The first case of pleura-pneumonia reported from the Widnes district his occurred at Birchali-rd., Appleton, Widnes. The occupier is Mr. William Hewitt, and one cow out of two on the premises has been attacked and killed.
